uni-bsc-bio-animal-physiology.title: Animal Physiology
uni-bsc-bio-animal-physiology.description: Full B.Sc. Zoology animal physiology syllabus: digestion and absorption, respiration and gas transport, blood, heart and circulation, excretion and osmoregulation, nerve and muscle physiology and endocrine control, with solved numericals, practicals and exam practice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc. (Zoology/Life Sciences) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Digestion and absorption
courses.summary: Structure of the human gut and glands, digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids, gastrointestinal hormones, absorption mechanisms and energy balance including BMR.
outcomes: Describe digestion in the mouth, stomach and small intestine
List enzymes with substrates, products and sites of action
Explain the role of gastrin, secretin, CCK and GIP
Explain absorption of monosaccharides, amino acids and fats
Calculate energy values and BMR estimates

scenes.text: Pavlov noticed his dogs salivated before food reached their mouths — the 'cephalic phase' of secretion.
His work on digestive glands earned the 1904 Nobel Prize.

steps.title: Mouth
steps.body: Three pairs of salivary glands (parotid, submandibular, sublingual) secrete about 1–1.5 L/day of saliva (pH about 6.8) containing **salivary α-amylase (ptyalin)** — starch → maltose, dextrins; optimum pH about 6.8, needs Cl⁻; **lingual lipase**; mucin; lysozyme; IgA. Mastication and bolus formation; swallowing (deglutition) has a voluntary oral phase and involuntary pharyngeal/oesophageal phases with peristalsis.

steps.title: Stomach
steps.body: Gastric glands: **chief (peptic) cells** — pepsinogen, gastric lipase; **parietal (oxyntic) cells** — HCl and **intrinsic factor** (for vitamin B₁₂ absorption); mucous neck cells — mucus and HCO₃⁻; **G cells** (antrum) — gastrin; ECL cells — histamine. HCl (pH about 1.5–2) kills microbes, denatures proteins and converts **pepsinogen → pepsin** (autocatalysis). Pepsin is an endopeptidase cutting at aromatic amino acids. **Rennin (chymosin)** in infants of ruminants (in humans minimal) curdles milk. Parietal cell H⁺ secretion uses the **H⁺/K⁺-ATPase** (target of proton-pump inhibitors); the 'alkaline tide' is the HCO₃⁻ entering blood.

steps.title: Phases of gastric secretion
steps.body:
- **Cephalic** (sight, smell, thought; vagus) — about 30% of secretion.
- **Gastric** (distension and peptides; gastrin) — about 60%.
- **Intestinal** (chyme in duodenum; mostly inhibitory via secretin, CCK, GIP, enterogastric reflex).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying HCl digests protein — it activates pepsin and denatures protein.
- Forgetting intrinsic factor (pernicious anaemia when absent).
- Calling pepsin an exopeptidase.

activity.prompt: Match the gastric cell to its secretion

quiz.q: Intrinsic factor is necessary for absorption of
quiz.why: Intrinsic factor binds B₁₂ so it can be absorbed in the terminal ileum.
Acid converts pepsinogen to pepsin, and pepsin then activates more pepsinogen.
Drugs such as omeprazole inhibit the parietal-cell H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, reducing acid.

quiz.q: The largest share of gastric secretion occurs in the
quiz.why: Distension and peptides in the stomach drive gastrin release, producing most of the secretion.

scenes.text: Acid chyme spurts into the duodenum, where bile and pancreatic juice neutralise and attack it.
A cascade starts with one brush-border enzyme activating trypsin.

steps.title: Pancreatic juice (about 1.5 L/day, pH about 8)
steps.body:
- **Trypsinogen → trypsin** by **enterokinase (enteropeptidase)** of the brush border; trypsin then activates chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase, proelastase and more trypsinogen.
- Trypsin cuts after Lys/Arg; chymotrypsin after aromatic residues; carboxypeptidase removes C-terminal amino acids.
- **Pancreatic amylase**: starch → maltose, maltotriose, α-limit dextrins.
- **Pancreatic lipase + colipase**: triglycerides → 2-monoglycerides + fatty acids.
- Nucleases; HCO₃⁻ neutralises acid.

steps.title: Bile
steps.body: Made by hepatocytes, stored and concentrated in the gall bladder; contains **bile salts** (sodium glycocholate, taurocholate), bile pigments (bilirubin), cholesterol, phospholipids. Bile salts **emulsify** fats and form **micelles**; about 95% recycled by the **enterohepatic circulation** (ileal reabsorption). Bile has no digestive enzymes.

steps.title: Brush border enzymes and GI hormones
steps.body:
Brush-border: maltase, isomaltase (α-dextrinase), sucrase, lactase, aminopeptidases, dipeptidases. Hormones:
- **Gastrin** (G cells): ↑ HCl, gastric motility.
- **Secretin** (S cells; first hormone discovered, Bayliss & Starling 1902): ↑ pancreatic HCO₃⁻, ↓ gastric secretion.
- **CCK** (I cells): ↑ pancreatic enzymes, gall-bladder contraction, satiety.
- **GIP**: ↑ insulin, ↓ gastric secretion. **Motilin**: interdigestive motility. **Ghrelin** (stomach): hunger.

steps.title: Worked example: lactose intolerance
steps.body: Low lactase activity leaves lactose undigested in the gut lumen → osmotic water retention + bacterial fermentation in the colon → gas, bloating and diarrhoea after milk. Curd is better tolerated because bacteria have already broken down part of the lactose.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying bile contains lipase.
- Saying enterokinase is a pancreatic enzyme (it is intestinal).
- Confusing secretin (bicarbonate) and CCK (enzymes).

activity.prompt: Order the steps of protein digestion
items: Carboxypeptidase and aminopeptidases release amino acids
Amino acids and di/tripeptides absorbed by enterocytes

quiz.why: This brush-border enzyme triggers the pancreatic protease cascade by activating trypsinogen.
CCK contracts the gall bladder and stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion when fat and protein enter the duodenum.

quiz.q: Bile salts help fat digestion by
quiz.why: They increase the surface area for lipase and carry products to the enterocyte surface.
Bayliss and Starling described secretin in 1902 and coined the term hormone.

story.title: A tennis court in your gut

scenes.text: Folds, villi and microvilli expand the small intestine's absorptive area enormously.
Each enterocyte uses sodium gradients to pull in sugars and amino acids.

steps.title: Surface amplification
steps.body: Plicae circulares (folds of Kerckring) ×3, villi ×10, microvilli ×20 — about a 600-fold increase over a simple tube (classic estimate). Each villus has a capillary network and a central **lacteal** (lymph).

steps.title: Carbohydrates and proteins
steps.body:
- **Glucose and galactose**: secondary active transport via **SGLT1** (2 Na⁺ : 1 glucose) at the apical membrane; exit by **GLUT2** basolaterally; Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains the gradient. Basis of **oral rehydration solution (ORS)**.
- **Fructose**: facilitated diffusion via **GLUT5**.
- **Amino acids**: several Na⁺-dependent carriers; di- and tripeptides by **PepT1** (H⁺-coupled), then hydrolysed inside the cell.

steps.title: Fats
steps.body: Micelles carry monoglycerides and fatty acids to the brush border → diffuse into the enterocyte → re-esterified to triglycerides in the smooth ER → packaged with apolipoprotein B-48, cholesterol and phospholipids into **chylomicrons** → exocytosed into **lacteals** → lymph → thoracic duct → blood. Short- and medium-chain fatty acids enter portal blood directly. Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K follow fats.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying glucose is absorbed by simple diffusion.
- Saying chylomicrons enter blood capillaries of villi directly.
- Forgetting that ORS works because Na⁺–glucose co-transport pulls water.

activity.prompt: Match the nutrient to its apical transport route

options: Na⁺–glucose co-transport draws water into the body
quiz.why: SGLT1 absorbs sodium with glucose, and water follows osmotically even during diarrhoea.
Their large size prevents entry into blood capillaries, so they enter lymphatic lacteals.

quiz.q: Glucose exits the enterocyte into blood through
quiz.why: GLUT2 on the basolateral membrane allows facilitated diffusion into the interstitial fluid.
Vitamins A, D, E and K are absorbed along with lipids in micelles.

lessons.title: Lab: Energy values, BMR and nutrition

scenes.text: Burning food in a bomb calorimeter shows how much energy it holds.
Even at rest, the body spends most of its daily energy just staying alive.

steps.title: Physiological fuel values
steps.body: Atwater factors: carbohydrate **4 kcal/g**, protein **4 kcal/g**, fat **9 kcal/g**, ethanol 7 kcal/g (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ). **Respiratory quotient (RQ) = CO₂ produced / O₂ consumed**: carbohydrate 1.0, fat about 0.7, protein about 0.8; mixed diet about 0.82.

steps.title: Solved example 1: energy of a meal
steps.body: A meal has 60 g carbohydrate, 15 g protein and 10 g fat. Energy = 60×4 + 15×4 + 10×9 = 240 + 60 + 90 = **390 kcal** = 390 × 4.184 = **1,632 kJ**.

steps.title: Solved example 2: RQ
steps.body: A subject consumes 250 mL O₂/min and produces 200 mL CO₂/min. RQ = 200/250 = **0.80**, consistent with a mixed diet.

steps.title: BMR
steps.body: **Basal metabolic rate**: energy use at physical and mental rest, 12 h after a meal, at thermoneutral temperature. Roughly 1 kcal per kg per hour for an adult (rule of thumb). Factors: body surface area, lean mass, age, sex, thyroid hormones (↑), fever (about 10–13% per °C), pregnancy. Measured by indirect calorimetry using about 4.8 kcal per litre O₂ consumed (mixed diet).

steps.title: Solved example 3: BMR from O₂ uptake
steps.body: Resting O₂ uptake = 0.25 L/min → per day = 0.25 × 1,440 = 360 L O₂. Energy = 360 × 4.8 = **1,728 kcal/day**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 9 kcal/g for protein.
- Forgetting to convert minutes to a day (× 1,440).
- Confusing BMR with total daily energy expenditure.

activity.prompt: A snack has 30 g carbohydrate, 5 g protein and 12 g fat. Energy in kcal?

quiz.why: Fats are more reduced than carbohydrates, so oxidation releases about 9 kcal per gram.

quiz.q: RQ of pure fat oxidation is about
quiz.why: Fat needs more oxygen per carbon dioxide released, giving an RQ near 0.7.
Thyroid hormones and raised body temperature both speed up cellular metabolism.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Respiration, blood and circulation
courses.summary: Lung volumes and ventilation, O₂ and CO₂ transport with the oxygen dissociation curve and Bohr effect, regulation of breathing, blood composition, haemostasis and blood groups, the cardiac cycle, ECG and cardiac output.
outcomes: Calculate lung volumes, capacities and alveolar ventilation
Explain the oxygen dissociation curve, Bohr and Haldane effects
Describe the coagulation cascade and ABO/Rh blood groups
Explain the cardiac cycle and ECG waves
Compute cardiac output and mean arterial pressure

scenes.text: A student breathes normally into a spirometer, then takes the deepest breath possible and blows it all out.
The trace shows tidal volume, reserves and vital capacity.

steps.title: Volumes and capacities (typical adult male)
steps.body:
- Tidal volume (TV) about 500 mL; inspiratory reserve (IRV) about 3,000 mL; expiratory reserve (ERV) about 1,100 mL; residual volume (RV) about 1,200 mL.
- **Vital capacity VC = TV + IRV + ERV** (about 4,600 mL).
- **Inspiratory capacity = TV + IRV**; **functional residual capacity FRC = ERV + RV**; **total lung capacity TLC = VC + RV** (about 5,800 mL).
- Anatomical dead space about 150 mL.

steps.title: Solved example: ventilation
steps.body:
TV = 500 mL, rate = 12/min, dead space = 150 mL.
Minute ventilation = 500 × 12 = **6,000 mL/min**.
Alveolar ventilation = (500 − 150) × 12 = **4,200 mL/min**. Rapid shallow breathing (TV 250, rate 24) gives the same minute ventilation but alveolar ventilation only (250 − 150) × 24 = **2,400 mL/min** — less efficient.

steps.title: Regulation of breathing
steps.body: Medullary respiratory centres (dorsal and ventral respiratory groups) and pontine centres (pneumotaxic, apneustic). **Central chemoreceptors** (medulla) respond mainly to H⁺ in CSF arising from **CO₂** — the main drive. **Peripheral chemoreceptors** (carotid and aortic bodies) respond to low PO₂ (below about 60 mmHg), high PCO₂ and H⁺. **Hering–Breuer reflex**: stretch receptors limit inspiration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including residual volume in vital capacity.
- Saying low O₂ is the main stimulus in healthy people (it is CO₂).
- Ignoring dead space when calculating alveolar ventilation.

activity.prompt: TV = 450 mL, dead space = 150 mL, breathing rate = 16/min. Alveolar ventilation in mL/min?

quiz.why: It is the maximum volume exhaled after a maximal inspiration and excludes residual volume.
Functional residual capacity is the air left after a normal expiration.

quiz.q: The main chemical drive for breathing is
quiz.why: Central chemoreceptors respond to CO₂-induced changes in CSF pH.
Stretch receptors in the lungs signal via the vagus to terminate inspiration.

scenes.text: At 3,500 m in Leh, a visitor feels breathless; arterial O₂ saturation drops.
Over weeks, the body raises red-cell numbers and 2,3-BPG to adapt.

steps.title: Oxygen transport
steps.body: About 98.5% of O₂ is carried bound to **haemoglobin** (4 haem groups, cooperative binding), 1.5% dissolved. Each gram of Hb binds about 1.34 mL O₂. The **oxygen dissociation curve** is **sigmoid**; P₅₀ about 26–27 mmHg in adult blood. **Rightward shift** (lower affinity, more unloading) by ↑ PCO₂, ↑ H⁺ (**Bohr effect**), ↑ temperature and ↑ **2,3-BPG**. Foetal Hb (HbF) binds 2,3-BPG weakly → left-shifted curve, helping O₂ transfer across the placenta. CO binds Hb about 200–250 times more strongly than O₂.

steps.title: Solved example: O₂ content
steps.body: Hb = 15 g/dL, saturation 97%: bound O₂ = 15 × 1.34 × 0.97 = **19.5 mL/dL**; dissolved = 0.003 × 100 mmHg = 0.3 mL/dL; total ≈ **19.8 mL O₂/dL**. Venous blood at 75% saturation holds 15 × 1.34 × 0.75 = 15.1 mL/dL, so tissues extract about 4.7 mL/dL at rest.

steps.title: CO₂ transport
steps.body: About 70% as **HCO₃⁻** (carbonic anhydrase in RBCs: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻; HCO₃⁻ leaves the RBC in exchange for Cl⁻ — the **chloride (Hamburger) shift**), about 20–23% as **carbaminohaemoglobin**, about 7–10% dissolved. **Haldane effect**: deoxygenated Hb carries more CO₂ and H⁺.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying a right shift means higher affinity.
- Confusing Bohr (CO₂ affects O₂) with Haldane (O₂ affects CO₂).
- Saying most CO₂ is carried bound to haem iron.

activity.prompt: Does each factor shift the O₂ dissociation curve right or left?

quiz.why: Carbonic anhydrase in red cells rapidly converts CO₂ to bicarbonate, which travels in plasma.

options: CO₂/H⁺ lowering Hb affinity for O₂
quiz.why: In active tissues raised CO₂ and acidity cause haemoglobin to release more oxygen.
Band 3 protein swaps bicarbonate out of the RBC for chloride in.

quiz.q: O₂ content with Hb 12 g/dL at 100% saturation (ignoring dissolved)
quiz.why: 12 × 1.34 = 16.08 mL of oxygen per decilitre.

scenes.text: A small cut bleeds for a minute and then stops on its own.
Behind it: vessel spasm, a platelet plug and a cascade of clotting factors.

steps.title: Composition
steps.body: Plasma about 55% (water about 90–92%, plasma proteins albumin, globulins, fibrinogen), formed elements about 45%. RBC about 4.5–5.5 million/µL (life span about 120 days), WBC about 4,000–11,000/µL (neutrophils most numerous, 40–70%), platelets about 1.5–4 lakh/µL. Normal Hb: about 13–17 g/dL men, 12–15 g/dL women.

steps.title: Haemostasis
steps.body:
1. **Vascular spasm**.
2. **Platelet plug**: adhesion to collagen via von Willebrand factor, activation, release of ADP and thromboxane A₂, aggregation.
3. **Coagulation**: intrinsic (factor XII, contact) and extrinsic (tissue factor + VII) pathways converge on **factor X → Xa**; prothrombinase (Xa + Va + Ca²⁺) converts **prothrombin → thrombin**; thrombin converts **fibrinogen → fibrin**; factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin. Ca²⁺ (factor IV) is needed at many steps; vitamin K needed to make II, VII, IX, X.
4. **Fibrinolysis**: plasmin dissolves the clot.
Anticoagulants: heparin (with antithrombin), citrate/oxalate/EDTA (chelate Ca²⁺) in lab tubes. Haemophilia A — factor VIII deficiency; B — factor IX.

steps.title: Blood groups
steps.body: **ABO** (Landsteiner, 1900): antigens on RBCs, naturally occurring antibodies in plasma. A — anti-B; B — anti-A; AB — none (universal recipient for RBCs); O — anti-A and anti-B (universal donor for RBCs). **Rh**: Rh-negative mother with Rh-positive foetus may be sensitised at first delivery; in later pregnancies anti-D IgG crosses the placenta → **erythroblastosis fetalis**; prevented by anti-D immunoglobulin given to the mother.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling AB the universal donor.
- Saying the first Rh-positive baby is usually affected.
- Forgetting vitamin K–dependent factors.

activity.prompt: Order the final common pathway of coagulation
items: Factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin into a stable clot

quiz.q: Haemophilia A is deficiency of factor
quiz.why: Classic haemophilia is X-linked deficiency of factor VIII.
Removing free Ca²⁺ stops the calcium-dependent steps of the cascade.

quiz.q: A person of group B has in plasma
quiz.why: People carry antibodies against the ABO antigen they lack, so group B has anti-A.

quiz.q: Erythroblastosis fetalis is prevented by giving
options: Anti-D to Rh-negative mother after delivery
quiz.why: Anti-D removes foetal Rh-positive cells before the mother's immune system becomes sensitised.

lessons.title: Lab: Cardiac cycle, ECG and cardiac output

scenes.text: A stethoscope picks up two sounds per beat — valves closing.
An ECG strip shows P, QRS and T waves marching across the paper at 25 mm/s.

steps.title: Conduction and cardiac cycle
steps.body: Myogenic heart: **SA node** (pacemaker, about 70–80/min) → atria → **AV node** (delay about 0.1 s) → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres. Cardiac cycle at 75 beats/min lasts **0.8 s**: atrial systole about 0.1 s, ventricular systole about 0.3 s, ventricular diastole about 0.5 s. Phases: isovolumetric contraction → ejection → isovolumetric relaxation → filling. **S1 (lub)**: AV valves close at start of systole. **S2 (dub)**: semilunar valves close at start of diastole.

steps.title: ECG
steps.body: **P** — atrial depolarisation; **PR interval** 0.12–0.20 s (AV conduction); **QRS** — ventricular depolarisation (< 0.12 s; atrial repolarisation hidden); **T** — ventricular repolarisation. Heart rate from a regular ECG at 25 mm/s = **1,500 / (R–R interval in small 1-mm squares)** or 300 / large squares.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. **Cardiac output** = HR × stroke volume = 72 × 70 mL = **5,040 mL/min ≈ 5 L/min**.
2. **Stroke volume** = EDV − ESV = 120 − 50 = **70 mL**; ejection fraction = 70/120 = **58%**.
3. **Mean arterial pressure** ≈ DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3 = 80 + (120 − 80)/3 = **93 mmHg**.
4. R–R interval = 20 small squares → HR = 1,500/20 = **75 beats/min**.

steps.title: Regulation
steps.body: Cardiac centre in the medulla; sympathetic (noradrenaline, β₁) ↑ rate and force; vagus (acetylcholine) ↓ rate. **Frank–Starling law**: greater end-diastolic stretch → stronger contraction. Baroreceptor reflex (carotid sinus, aortic arch) buffers blood pressure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assigning S1 to semilunar valves.
- Saying the T wave is atrial repolarisation.
- Forgetting to convert mL/min to L/min.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Excretion and osmoregulation
courses.summary: Nitrogenous wastes and the ornithine cycle, nephron structure, glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption and secretion, renal clearance, the countercurrent mechanism, hormonal control (ADH, RAAS, ANP) and osmoregulation in aquatic and terrestrial animals.
outcomes: Relate ammonotelism, ureotelism and uricotelism to habitat
Describe urine formation along the nephron
Calculate net filtration pressure, clearance and filtration fraction
Explain the countercurrent multiplier and urine concentration
Compare osmoregulation in freshwater and marine fishes

lessons.title: Nitrogenous wastes and the urea cycle

scenes.text: A fish simply lets ammonia diffuse out of its gills into the surrounding water.
A bird embryo inside a sealed egg cannot do that — it stores waste as insoluble uric acid.

steps.title: Types of excretion
steps.body:
- **Ammonotelic**: ammonia; very toxic, very soluble, needs much water (bony fishes, aquatic invertebrates, tadpoles).
- **Ureotelic**: urea; less toxic, soluble, made in the liver at an energy cost (mammals, adult amphibians, cartilaginous fishes, turtles partly).
- **Uricotelic**: uric acid; least toxic, nearly insoluble, excreted as a paste with little water (birds, reptiles such as lizards and snakes, insects, land snails).
Many animals switch: a tadpole is ammonotelic, the adult frog ureotelic.

steps.title: Ornithine (urea) cycle — Krebs & Henseleit, 1932
steps.body: In liver mitochondria: NH₃ + CO₂ + 2 ATP → **carbamoyl phosphate** (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I) → + ornithine → **citrulline** (ornithine transcarbamoylase). In cytosol: citrulline + aspartate + ATP → **argininosuccinate** → **arginine** + fumarate → arginase → **urea** + ornithine. Net cost: 3 ATP (4 high-energy bonds) per urea. Fumarate links to the TCA cycle.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Urea contains 2 N atoms: one from NH₃ (via carbamoyl phosphate) and one from **aspartate**. Molar mass of urea CO(NH₂)₂ = 12 + 16 + 2(14 + 2) = **60 g/mol**; so 30 g urea per day ≈ 0.5 mol, carrying 1 mol N = 14 g nitrogen.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying urea is made in the kidney (it is made in the liver).
- Calling birds ureotelic.
- Forgetting aspartate as the second nitrogen donor.

activity.prompt: Classify the animal by its main nitrogenous waste

quiz.q: The urea cycle occurs in the
quiz.why: Hepatocytes contain the full set of urea-cycle enzymes split between mitochondria and cytosol.
Arginase hydrolyses arginine into urea and ornithine, regenerating the carrier.
Insoluble uric acid can be stored or excreted with very little water.

quiz.q: The second nitrogen of urea comes from
quiz.why: Aspartate condenses with citrulline to donate its amino nitrogen.

scenes.text: Your kidneys filter about 180 L of plasma every day.
Yet you pass only about 1.5 L of urine — more than 99% is reabsorbed.

steps.title: Nephron
steps.body: About one million per kidney. **Renal corpuscle** (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule) → **proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)** → **loop of Henle** (descending thin, ascending thin and thick) → **distal convoluted tubule (DCT)** → **collecting duct**. Cortical nephrons (about 85%) have short loops; **juxtamedullary nephrons** have long loops with **vasa recta**, essential for concentration. **Juxtaglomerular apparatus**: JG cells (renin) of the afferent arteriole + macula densa of the DCT.

steps.title: Glomerular filtration
steps.body: Filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane, podocyte slit diaphragms. **Net filtration pressure** = P_GC − (P_BS + π_GC). Typical: 55 − (15 + 30) = **10 mmHg**. **GFR** about 125 mL/min (180 L/day). Autoregulation by myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback.

steps.title: Tubular processing
steps.body:
- **PCT**: reabsorbs about 65% of Na⁺ and water, ~100% glucose and amino acids (secondary active), most HCO₃⁻; secretes H⁺, organic acids/bases (e.g. penicillin, PAH). Glucose appears in urine when plasma glucose exceeds the **renal threshold** (about 180 mg/dL).
- **Descending limb**: permeable to water, not to salt.
- **Thick ascending limb**: impermeable to water; NKCC2 pumps Na⁺, K⁺, 2Cl⁻ out (target of furosemide) — 'diluting segment'.
- **DCT**: Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransport (thiazide target); Ca²⁺ reabsorption under PTH.
- **Collecting duct**: aldosterone-regulated Na⁺ reabsorption/K⁺ secretion; **ADH** inserts aquaporin-2 channels for water reabsorption.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the ascending limb is permeable to water.
- Forgetting oncotic pressure opposes filtration.
- Saying glucose is normally present in urine.

activity.prompt: Glomerular capillary pressure 60 mmHg, Bowman's space pressure 18 mmHg, plasma oncotic pressure 32 mmHg. Net filtration pressure (mmHg)?

quiz.q: Most filtered sodium is reabsorbed in the
quiz.why: About two-thirds of filtered Na⁺ and water are reclaimed in the proximal convoluted tubule.
Loop diuretics block the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter, the main salt pump of the medulla.
Modified smooth muscle JG cells of the afferent arteriole release renin.
ADH acts via V2 receptors to place aquaporin-2 water channels in collecting-duct membranes.

lessons.title: Lab: Renal clearance and the countercurrent mechanism

scenes.text: Inulin, a plant sugar, is filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted — a perfect GFR marker.
A kangaroo rat's long loops of Henle make urine several times more concentrated than ours.

steps.title: Clearance
steps.body: **Clearance C = (U × V)/P**, where U = urine concentration, V = urine flow (mL/min), P = plasma concentration. Inulin clearance = GFR. **PAH clearance** ≈ renal plasma flow (RPF, about 625 mL/min). **Filtration fraction = GFR/RPF** (about 0.2). If C_x < GFR the substance is net reabsorbed (glucose ≈ 0, urea about 50–60% of GFR); if C_x > GFR it is net secreted. Creatinine clearance is used clinically to estimate GFR.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. Inulin: U = 30 mg/mL, V = 1 mL/min, P = 0.24 mg/mL → C = 30 × 1/0.24 = **125 mL/min** (= GFR).
2. PAH: U = 12.5 mg/mL, V = 1 mL/min, P = 0.02 mg/mL → C = 12.5/0.02 = **625 mL/min** (RPF). Filtration fraction = 125/625 = **0.20**.
3. Urea: U = 6 mg/mL, V = 2 mL/min, P = 0.2 mg/mL → C = 6 × 2/0.2 = **60 mL/min**, less than GFR → urea is partly reabsorbed.

steps.title: Countercurrent multiplier
steps.body: Thick ascending limb pumps NaCl into the interstitium without water → interstitium becomes hyperosmotic; descending limb loses water to it, so fluid inside becomes concentrated; flow carries it round the hairpin, multiplying a small horizontal gradient (about 200 mOsm) into a vertical one from about 300 mOsm/kg (cortex) to about **1,200 mOsm/kg** (inner medulla) in humans. **Urea recycling** from the inner medullary collecting duct adds to the gradient. **Vasa recta** act as a countercurrent **exchanger**, preserving the gradient. With ADH, collecting-duct fluid equilibrates with the medulla → concentrated urine.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to multiply U by V.
- Calling vasa recta the multiplier.
- Saying clearance has units of mg/min (it is mL/min).

activity.prompt: Creatinine: U = 1.2 mg/mL, V = 1.5 mL/min, P = 0.015 mg/mL. Clearance in mL/min?

lessons.title: Hormonal control and osmoregulation in animals

scenes.text: A marine bony fish loses water to the sea and must drink salt water.
A freshwater fish is flooded with water and must pump salts in.

steps.title: Hormonal regulation
steps.body:
- **ADH (vasopressin)**: hypothalamus → posterior pituitary; released when plasma osmolality rises or volume falls; deficiency → **diabetes insipidus** (large volumes of dilute urine).
- **RAAS**: ↓ BP/Na⁺ → renin → angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → (ACE, mainly lungs) → **angiotensin II** (vasoconstriction, thirst, ADH) → **aldosterone** (Na⁺ retention, K⁺ secretion).
- **ANP** from atria (stretch) → natriuresis, inhibits renin and aldosterone.

steps.title: Osmoregulation
steps.body:
- **Freshwater teleost** (hyperosmotic to medium): gains water, loses salts → copious dilute urine, large glomeruli, active ion uptake by gill **chloride (ionocyte) cells**, does not drink.
- **Marine teleost** (hypo-osmotic): loses water → drinks sea water, excretes salt actively through gill chloride cells, small/aglomerular kidneys, little isosmotic urine with Mg²⁺/SO₄²⁻.
- **Marine elasmobranchs**: retain **urea and TMAO** to be slightly hyperosmotic; rectal gland secretes NaCl.
- **Salmon/eels** (euryhaline) switch strategies with cortisol and prolactin.
- Desert mammals (kangaroo rat): long loops, metabolic water, very concentrated urine. Marine birds/reptiles: **salt glands**.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: 'Fresh fish don't drink; sea fish drink and spit salt from gills.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying freshwater fish drink much water.
- Confusing diabetes insipidus (ADH) with diabetes mellitus (insulin).
- Placing ACE in the kidney only.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Nerve, muscle and endocrine physiology
courses.summary: Resting and action potentials with the Nernst equation, impulse conduction and synaptic transmission, the sliding filament mechanism of skeletal muscle contraction, and the hypothalamo–pituitary axis with major endocrine glands and hormone action.
outcomes: Calculate equilibrium potentials with the Nernst equation
Explain the ionic basis of the action potential and saltatory conduction
Describe chemical synaptic transmission at the neuromuscular junction
Explain excitation–contraction coupling and the sliding filament theory
Describe hormone classes, mechanisms and the major endocrine disorders

scenes.text: Hodgkin and Huxley pushed a wire inside a squid giant axon nearly 1 mm wide.
They recorded the rise and fall of the action potential and explained it with Na⁺ and K⁺ currents (Nobel Prize 1963).

steps.title: Resting membrane potential
steps.body:
About **−70 mV** in neurons (inside negative). Causes: (1) K⁺ concentration gradient (inside about 140 mM, outside about 5 mM) and high resting K⁺ permeability via leak channels; (2) low Na⁺ permeability; (3) **Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase** (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in — electrogenic, maintains gradients); (4) impermeant intracellular anions.
**Nernst equation** (37 °C): **E_ion = (61.5/z) log₁₀([ion]out/[ion]in)** mV.

steps.title: Solved example: Nernst
steps.body:
K⁺: E_K = 61.5 log(5/140) = 61.5 × (−1.447) = **−89 mV**.
Na⁺ (out 145, in 15 mM): E_Na = 61.5 log(145/15) = 61.5 × 0.985 = **+61 mV**.
Resting potential (−70 mV) lies close to E_K because resting K⁺ permeability is highest.

steps.title: Action potential
steps.body: Stimulus reaches **threshold** (about −55 mV) → voltage-gated **Na⁺ channels open** (positive feedback) → depolarisation overshoot to about +30 to +40 mV → Na⁺ channels **inactivate**, voltage-gated **K⁺ channels open** → repolarisation → **after-hyperpolarisation** → resting. **All-or-none**; **absolute refractory period** (Na⁺ inactivation) then relative refractory period. Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) blocks Na⁺ channels.

steps.title: Conduction
steps.body: Unmyelinated: continuous, slow (about 0.5–2 m/s). Myelinated: **saltatory** from node to node of Ranvier, fast (up to about 120 m/s). Velocity increases with diameter and myelination.

steps.title: Solved example: conduction velocity
steps.body: Stimulating a nerve at two points 10 cm apart gives latencies of 4 ms and 6 ms. Velocity = 0.10 m / 0.002 s = **50 m/s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the pump directly creates most of the resting potential (it mainly maintains gradients).
- Forgetting the sign in the Nernst ratio (out/in for cations).
- Saying a stronger stimulus gives a bigger action potential.

activity.prompt: At 37 °C, [K⁺]out = 4 mM and [K⁺]in = 160 mM. Calculate E_K in mV using E = 61.5 log(out/in).

quiz.q: The rising phase of the action potential is due to
quiz.why: Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels lets Na⁺ rush in and depolarise the membrane.
The pufferfish toxin plugs the outer pore of voltage-gated sodium channels.
Action potentials jump between nodes of Ranvier because myelin insulates internodes.

quiz.q: Two recording points 6 cm apart with latency difference 1.5 ms give velocity

lessons.title: Synaptic transmission and the neuromuscular junction

scenes.text: South American hunters tipped arrows with curare; struck animals fell limp but their hearts kept beating.
Curare blocks acetylcholine receptors on skeletal muscle.

steps.title: Chemical synapse
steps.body: Action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal → voltage-gated **Ca²⁺ channels** open → Ca²⁺ triggers fusion of vesicles (SNARE proteins) → neurotransmitter released by exocytosis → binds postsynaptic receptors → **EPSP** (e.g. glutamate, ACh at nicotinic receptors) or **IPSP** (GABA, glycine) → summation (spatial, temporal) at the axon hillock → removal by enzyme (acetylcholinesterase) or reuptake (noradrenaline, serotonin). One-way conduction and synaptic delay (about 0.5 ms).

steps.title: Neuromuscular junction
steps.body: Motor end plate: ACh binds **nicotinic receptors** (ligand-gated cation channels) → end-plate potential → muscle action potential. **AChE** hydrolyses ACh. Drugs/toxins: **curare** (blocks receptors → paralysis), **botulinum toxin** (blocks ACh release), **organophosphates** (inhibit AChE → excess ACh), **myasthenia gravis** (autoantibodies against ACh receptors; treated with AChE inhibitors such as neostigmine).

steps.title: Main neurotransmitters
steps.body: ACh, noradrenaline, dopamine, serotonin (5-HT), glutamate (main excitatory in CNS), GABA (main inhibitory in brain), glycine (inhibitory in spinal cord), neuropeptides (substance P, endorphins), nitric oxide (gaseous).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Na⁺ entry triggers vesicle release (it is Ca²⁺).
- Confusing curare (receptor block) with botulinum (release block).
- Saying synapses conduct both ways.

items: Action potential reaches the motor nerve terminal

End-plate potential triggers muscle action potential

quiz.why: Calcium entering the terminal activates the vesicle fusion machinery.

quiz.why: Inhibited acetylcholinesterase lets ACh accumulate, overstimulating muscles and glands.

quiz.why: GABA opens chloride channels and hyperpolarises neurons.

scenes.text: Hours after death, muscles stiffen.
Without ATP, myosin heads stay locked onto actin — proof that ATP is needed to release, not just to pull.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Muscle → fascicles → fibres (multinucleate) → **myofibrils** → **sarcomeres** (Z-line to Z-line, about 2–2.5 µm). **A band** (myosin thick filaments, constant length), **I band** (actin only), **H zone** (myosin only), **M line**. Thin filament: actin + **tropomyosin** + **troponin** (TnC binds Ca²⁺, TnI inhibitory, TnT binds tropomyosin). **T-tubules** and **sarcoplasmic reticulum** (terminal cisternae) form triads.

steps.title: Sliding filament theory and cross-bridge cycle
steps.body: Huxley & Niedergerke and Huxley & Hanson (1954). Muscle AP spreads into T-tubules → **DHP receptors** couple to **ryanodine receptors** → Ca²⁺ released from SR → Ca²⁺ binds **troponin C** → tropomyosin moves exposing myosin-binding sites → myosin head (with ADP + Pi) binds actin → **power stroke** (Pi then ADP released) → new **ATP binds** and detaches the head → ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the head. Relaxation: SERCA pumps Ca²⁺ back into SR. During contraction **I band and H zone shorten; A band stays constant**.

steps.title: Twitch, summation, tetanus
steps.body: Single twitch: latent period, contraction, relaxation (frog gastrocnemius about 0.1 s total). Repeated stimuli → **summation** → **tetanus** (fused). **All-or-none** applies to a single fibre; whole-muscle force graded by recruitment of motor units. Fibre types: slow oxidative (red, myoglobin-rich), fast glycolytic (white). Energy: creatine phosphate, glycolysis (lactate), oxidative phosphorylation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the A band shortens.
- Saying ATP is needed only for the power stroke (it is needed for detachment).
- Saying Ca²⁺ binds tropomyosin.

options: Lack of ATP to detach myosin
quiz.why: Without ATP, myosin heads cannot release from actin and the muscle locks rigid.

quiz.why: Ryanodine receptors on the SR release stored Ca²⁺ into the cytosol.
When stimuli arrive before relaxation, twitches summate into a sustained contraction.

scenes.text: In iodine-poor sub-Himalayan regions, swollen necks were once common.
Universal salt iodisation sharply reduced iodine-deficiency disorders.

steps.title: Hormone classes and mechanisms
steps.body:
- **Peptide/protein** (insulin, GH, ADH) and **catecholamines** (adrenaline): water-soluble, bind **cell-surface receptors** → second messengers (**cAMP** via Gs/adenylyl cyclase — Sutherland; IP₃/DAG/Ca²⁺ via Gq) or receptor tyrosine kinases (insulin).
- **Steroids** (cortisol, aldosterone, oestrogen, testosterone) and **thyroid hormones**: lipid-soluble, bind **intracellular receptors** that act as transcription factors.
Feedback: mostly **negative** (e.g. T₃/T₄ inhibit TRH and TSH); positive in the LH surge before ovulation and oxytocin in labour.

steps.title: Hypothalamus–pituitary
steps.body: Hypothalamic releasing/inhibiting hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine) reach the **anterior pituitary** via the hypophyseal portal system → TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, GH, prolactin. **Posterior pituitary** stores ADH and oxytocin made in hypothalamic neurons (supraoptic, paraventricular nuclei).

steps.title: Major glands and disorders
steps.body:
- **Thyroid** (T₃, T₄; calcitonin): hypothyroidism — cretinism (child), myxoedema (adult); goitre (iodine deficiency); hyperthyroidism — Graves' disease (exophthalmos).
- **Parathyroid** (PTH): raises blood Ca²⁺; deficiency → tetany.
- **Adrenal cortex** (glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, androgens): Addison's (deficiency), Cushing's (excess cortisol). **Medulla**: adrenaline, noradrenaline ('fight or flight').
- **Pancreatic islets**: β cells insulin (↓ glucose), α cells glucagon (↑ glucose), δ cells somatostatin. Diabetes mellitus type 1 (autoimmune β-cell loss) and type 2 (insulin resistance).
- **GH**: gigantism/acromegaly (excess), pituitary dwarfism (deficiency).
- **Pineal**: melatonin (circadian rhythm). **Gonads**: testosterone, oestrogen, progesterone.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying ADH is made in the posterior pituitary (it is stored and released there).
- Placing steroid receptors on the cell surface.
- Confusing cretinism with dwarfism due to GH.

outcomes: Recall key formulae and normal values in physiology

scenes.text: Physiology numericals repeat the same ten formulas.
Know them and their units, and most problems take two lines.

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body:
- Minute ventilation = TV × rate; alveolar ventilation = (TV − dead space) × rate.
- VC = TV + IRV + ERV; TLC = VC + RV; FRC = ERV + RV.
- O₂ content = Hb × 1.34 × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PO₂.
- Cardiac output = HR × SV; SV = EDV − ESV; EF = SV/EDV.
- MAP ≈ DBP + (SBP − DBP)/3; pulse pressure = SBP − DBP.
- Net filtration pressure = P_GC − (P_BS + π_GC).
- Clearance C = UV/P; FF = GFR/RPF.
- Nernst E = (61.5/z) log(out/in) at 37 °C.
- Conduction velocity = distance/time.
- RQ = CO₂/O₂; energy = 4/4/9 kcal per g.

steps.title: Normal values (adult, approximate)
steps.body: Hb 13–17 g/dL (M), 12–15 g/dL (F) · RBC 4.5–5.5 million/µL · WBC 4,000–11,000/µL · platelets 1.5–4 lakh/µL · BP 120/80 mmHg · HR 60–100/min · GFR 125 mL/min · urine 1–2 L/day · fasting glucose 70–100 mg/dL · blood pH 7.35–7.45 · bleeding time 2–7 min (Duke method about 1–3 min) · clotting time 4–10 min (capillary/Lee–White ranges vary by method).

steps.title: Unit discipline
steps.body: Write the formula, substitute with units, then box the answer with units — examiners award marks at each step.

lessons.title: Lab: Haemocytometer counts and haemoglobin estimation

scenes.text: The Neubauer chamber's ruled grid holds a fixed, tiny volume of diluted blood.
Count a few squares, multiply by dilution and volume factors — that's your count per µL.

steps.title: RBC count (improved Neubauer)
steps.body:
Dilute blood **1:200** with Hayem's fluid using the RBC pipette (draw to 0.5, then diluting fluid to 101). Charge the chamber; count RBCs in **5 medium squares** of the central large square = **80 smallest squares**. Each smallest square = 1/400 mm² × 0.1 mm depth = 1/4,000 mm³.
**RBC/µL = N × dilution × 4,000 / 80 = N × 200 × 50 = N × 10,000**.

steps.title: Solved example: RBC
steps.body: N = 480 cells in 80 small squares → RBC = 480 × 10,000 = **4.8 million/µL** (normal).

steps.title: WBC count
steps.body:
Dilute **1:20** with Türk's fluid (acetic acid lyses RBCs, gentian violet stains nuclei). Count in the **4 corner large squares** (each 1 mm² × 0.1 mm = 0.1 mm³; total 0.4 mm³).
**WBC/µL = N × 20 / 0.4 = N × 50**. Example: N = 150 → **7,500/µL**.

steps.title: Haemoglobin by Sahli's acid haematin method
steps.body: Add 0.1 N HCl to the graduated tube up to the 2 mark (or 10% mark), add 20 µL blood with the Hb pipette, mix and wait 10 min (Hb → brown acid haematin), dilute with distilled water drop by drop until the colour matches the standard comparator, read Hb in g/dL at the lower meniscus. Sources of error: colour matching subjectivity, fading of standards, timing; modern labs use cyanmethaemoglobin (Drabkin's) photometry.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting cells touching all four borders (count only those on two chosen borders — e.g. top and left).
- Using the WBC factor for RBCs.
- Reading Sahli's tube immediately without the 10-minute conversion time.

lessons.title: Lab: Blood group, blood pressure and salivary amylase

scenes.text: A drop of blood mixed with anti-A clumps instantly — blood group A.
Starch plus saliva stops turning iodine blue after a few minutes at 37 °C.

steps.title: Blood grouping (slide method)
steps.body: Place three drops of blood on a clean slide; add anti-A, anti-B and anti-D sera separately; mix with separate sticks; observe agglutination within 2 minutes. Agglutination with anti-A only → A; anti-B only → B; both → AB; neither → O; anti-D positive → Rh⁺.

steps.title: Blood pressure (auscultatory)
steps.body: Seated subject, cuff at heart level on upper arm; palpate radial pulse and inflate about 30 mmHg above disappearance; deflate at about 2–3 mmHg/s while listening over the brachial artery. First **Korotkoff sound** = systolic; disappearance (phase V) = diastolic. Record after exercise to show the rise in systolic pressure and pulse.

steps.title: Salivary amylase activity
steps.body: Set tubes with 1% starch + diluted saliva at different temperatures (0, 37, 70 °C) and pH (buffers 4, 6.8, 9). Every minute, remove a drop onto iodine on a spot tile; the **achromic point** is reached when no blue/black colour appears. Shortest achromic time = optimum (about 37 °C, pH about 6.8). Boiled saliva shows no activity (denatured enzyme); 0 °C slows activity reversibly.

steps.title: Worked example: BP readings
steps.body: Rest 118/78 → MAP = 78 + 40/3 = **91 mmHg**; after exercise 140/80 → pulse pressure **60 mmHg**, MAP = 80 + 60/3 = **100 mmHg**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the same stick for all antisera (cross-contamination).
- Placing the cuff below heart level (falsely high).
- Taking blue colour as 'complete digestion' — it means starch still present.

steps.title: Viva quick answers
steps.body:
- Why is O the universal donor? Its RBCs lack A and B antigens.
- Why does Hb carry O₂ cooperatively? Binding of one O₂ changes subunit conformation (T → R), raising affinity of others.
- Why are mammalian RBCs enucleate? More space for Hb, flexible biconcave shape.
- Why does urine become dilute after drinking water? ADH falls and collecting ducts become water-impermeable.
- What is a motor unit? One motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies.

scenes.text: For a few weeks every human embryo has pharyngeal pouches and a tail.
These embryonic marks are shared with a fish, a frog and a tiny sea squirt larva.

steps.title: Fundamental characters
steps.body:
At some stage of life all chordates have:
1. **Notochord** — a dorsal, flexible rod of vacuolated cells in a sheath, derived from chordamesoderm; replaced by the vertebral column in most vertebrates.
2. **Dorsal hollow (tubular) nerve cord** — formed by neurulation from ectoderm, dorsal to the notochord.
3. **Pharyngeal gill slits** (pouches/clefts).
4. **Post-anal tail**.
Also: endostyle (→ thyroid in vertebrates), ventral heart, closed circulation (in vertebrates), enterocoelous coelom, deuterostome development.

steps.title: Classification outline
steps.body:
Phylum Chordata
- **Protochordata (Acraniata)**: Subphylum **Urochordata/Tunicata** (Herdmania, Ascidia, Salpa, Doliolum, Oikopleura); Subphylum **Cephalochordata** (Branchiostoma).
- Subphylum **Vertebrata (Craniata)**: Division **Agnatha** (Class Cyclostomata: Petromyzon, Myxine) and Division **Gnathostomata** — Superclass Pisces (Chondrichthyes, Osteichthyes) and Superclass Tetrapoda (Amphibia, Reptilia, Aves, Mammalia).

steps.title: Chordates vs non-chordates
steps.body: Nerve cord dorsal, hollow and single in chordates vs ventral, solid and often double in non-chordates; heart ventral vs dorsal; notochord present vs absent; gill slits present vs absent (except hemichordates); haemoglobin in RBCs vs often dissolved in plasma or other pigments.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying adults of all chordates retain the notochord.
- Listing 'vertebral column' as a fundamental chordate character (only vertebrates).
- Placing Balanoglossus in Chordata in modern schemes.

story.title: A tadpole that becomes a sack

scenes.text: A free-swimming ascidian larva has a notochord, nerve cord and tail.
It settles head-first on a rock and loses most of them, becoming a sessile filter-feeding bag.

steps.title: Herdmania: structure
steps.body: Sessile marine ascidian (Indian coasts, e.g. Herdmania pallida); body enclosed in a **test (tunic)** containing **tunicin** (a cellulose-like polysaccharide) — hence 'tunicates'. Two openings: **branchial (oral) siphon** and **atrial siphon**. Large **pharynx** perforated by **stigmata** (gill slits) with ciliated bars; **endostyle** in the ventral groove secretes mucus; **dorsal lamina** rolls the mucus–food string to the oesophagus. Atrium surrounds the pharynx. Heart reverses beat direction periodically. Single **neural ganglion** with neural gland (proposed homologue of pituitary). Hermaphrodite.

steps.title: Retrogressive metamorphosis
steps.body: The tadpole larva (non-feeding, lives a few hours) has: notochord in the tail, dorsal hollow nerve cord, sense organs (ocellus, statocyst), and **adhesive papillae**. On settlement: attaches by papillae; tail is resorbed with notochord and most of the nerve cord; sense organs lost; nerve cord reduced to a ganglion; pharynx enlarges with more stigmata; rapid growth of the region between adhesive papillae and mouth rotates the body so siphons point upward. Called **retrogressive** because the larva is more advanced (free-living, with chordate features) than the adult.

steps.title: Significance
steps.body: Garstang's hypothesis proposed that vertebrates arose from an ascidian-like larva by **paedomorphosis** (larva becoming sexually mature without metamorphosis), as seen in Larvacea (Oikopleura).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the adult Herdmania has a notochord.
- Confusing branchial and atrial siphons: water enters through the branchial siphon.
- Calling tunicin chitin.

scenes.text: Branchiostoma, the lancelet, buries in sand with only its mouth exposed.
It shows all four chordate characters throughout life — a textbook diagram come alive.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Fish-like, laterally compressed, translucent; no paired fins, no distinct head. **Notochord** extends to the tip of the snout (beyond the nerve cord — hence 'cephalochordate'). **Myotomes** V-shaped (<-shaped), segmental. **Oral hood** with buccal cirri; **wheel organ** (ciliary tracts) and **velum** with velar tentacles; large pharynx with over 100 pairs of gill slits; **endostyle**; **atrium** opening by an **atriopore**. Notochord cells are muscular (contractile) in Branchiostoma.

steps.title: Other systems
steps.body:
- Feeding: ciliary filter feeder; **Hatschek's pit** (in the roof of the oral hood) is a proposed homologue of the adenohypophysis.
- Circulation: closed but no heart; contractile vessels; colourless blood.
- Excretion: **solenocytes** (protonephridia) in about 90 pairs of nephridia — unusual for a chordate.
- Nervous: dorsal hollow nerve cord with a slight cerebral vesicle; photoreceptor pigment spots.
- Reproduction: sexes separate, segmentally arranged gonads (about 26 pairs), external fertilisation.

steps.title: Affinities
steps.body: Chordate characters in typical form, segmented myotomes and ventral endostyle relate it to vertebrates; lack of a head, brain, paired eyes, kidneys and heart shows it is primitive. Molecular phylogenies place urochordates (not cephalochordates) as the sister group of vertebrates, though Branchiostoma still models the ancestral body plan.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:

- Forgetting that its excretory organs are protonephridia with solenocytes.
- Saying the notochord stops at the brain.

scenes.text: Zoologists once searched for chordate ancestors among annelids, arthropods and echinoderms.
The strongest clues came from larvae and, later, DNA.

steps.title: Annelid and arthropod theories
steps.body: Proposed by Dohrn/Semper (annelid) and Gaskell/Patten (arachnid). Idea: invert a segmented protostome so the ventral nerve cord becomes dorsal. **Objections**: annelid nerve cord is solid and ventral with the gut passing through the nerve ring; no notochord or gill slits; mouth would have to form anew; protostome vs deuterostome development; coelom schizocoelous not enterocoelous.

steps.title: Echinoderm (Garstang's larval) theory
steps.body: Garstang (1928) proposed that chordates arose from a **dipleurula/auricularia-like larva**: ciliated bands moved dorsally and fused to form a dorsal neural tube; adoral ciliary band became the endostyle; the larva acquired a notochord and muscular tail for swimming; paedomorphosis fixed the larval form. Support: deuterostome development, enterocoely, radial indeterminate cleavage, similar larvae (tornaria/auricularia), creatine phosphate in muscles of both echinoderms and chordates.

steps.title: Modern view
steps.body: Deuterostomia = Ambulacraria (Echinodermata + Hemichordata) + Chordata. The common deuterostome ancestor probably had pharyngeal slits (present in hemichordates and chordates, lost in living echinoderms). Within chordates, cephalochordates branch first; urochordates are closest to vertebrates. Fossil evidence: Cambrian chordate-like forms such as Pikaia (Burgess Shale) and early vertebrates such as Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia (Chengjiang).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming any one theory is proven.
- Ignoring developmental (embryological) evidence.
- Citing Pikaia as a vertebrate.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Agnatha and Fishes
courses.summary: Cyclostomes (Petromyzon and its ammocoete larva), cartilaginous and bony fishes (Scoliodon, Labeo), scales and fins, accessory respiratory organs, swim bladder and Weberian ossicles, migration and parental care in fishes.
outcomes: Distinguish Agnatha from Gnathostomata
Compare Chondrichthyes and Osteichthyes
Classify fish scales and fins
Describe accessory respiratory organs of Indian air-breathing fishes
Explain migration types and parental care in fishes

scenes.text: A lamprey clamps its round sucker on a fish and rasps through the skin with horny teeth.
Its larva, the ammocoete, was once described as a separate animal.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body: Jawless (**Agnatha**), eel-shaped, no paired fins, no scales, circular suctorial mouth with horny epidermal teeth, persistent notochord, cartilaginous skeleton, **single median nostril**, gill pouches (7 pairs in Petromyzon, 1–16 in hagfishes), two semicircular canals (lamprey) or one (hagfish). Petromyzon (lamprey) — ectoparasite, anadromous; Myxine (hagfish) — marine scavenger, produces large amounts of slime.

steps.title: Ammocoete larva
steps.body: Freshwater, burrowing filter-feeder lasting several years; has an oral hood, velum, **endostyle** (becomes thyroid at metamorphosis), protochordate-like ciliary-mucous feeding. Its resemblance to Branchiostoma is cited as evidence that vertebrates descend from a cephalochordate-like ancestor.

steps.title: Agnatha vs Gnathostomata
steps.body: Agnatha: no jaws, no paired fins, single nostril, gill pouches with endodermal gills, notochord persists. Gnathostomata: jaws from the mandibular arch, paired fins/limbs, paired nostrils, three semicircular canals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling lampreys true fishes with jaws.
- Forgetting the endostyle–thyroid transformation.
- Saying hagfish have a larval stage like ammocoete (they develop directly).

lessons.title: Chondrichthyes vs Osteichthyes; scales and fins

scenes.text: The dogfish shark Scoliodon has rough skin, a ventral mouth and five gill slits on each side.
The rohu Labeo has smooth overlapping scales and a single operculum covering its gills.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
**Chondrichthyes** (Scoliodon, Torpedo, Pristis, Trygon): cartilaginous endoskeleton, **placoid scales**, ventral mouth, 5–7 pairs of naked gill slits (no operculum), **heterocercal tail**, no swim bladder (buoyancy from oily liver), spiral valve in intestine, claspers in males, internal fertilisation, urea retention (ureosmotic) in marine forms.
**Osteichthyes** (Labeo, Catla, Anabas, Hippocampus): bony skeleton, **cycloid/ctenoid/ganoid** scales, terminal mouth, gills covered by **operculum**, usually **homocercal** tail, **swim bladder** present, mostly external fertilisation.

steps.title: Scales
steps.body:
- **Placoid**: dermal denticles of dentine + enamel-like vitrodentine with pulp cavity; homologous to teeth (sharks).
- **Cosmoid**: extinct lobe-fins; living coelacanth has modified ones.
- **Ganoid**: rhomboid with ganoine layer (Lepisosteus, Polypterus, Acipenser plates).
- **Cycloid**: thin, circular, smooth margin (Labeo, Catla).
- **Ctenoid**: comb-like posterior margin (Anabas, perches).
Age can be estimated from growth rings (**annuli**) on cycloid/ctenoid scales.

steps.title: Fins and tails
steps.body: Median fins: dorsal, anal, caudal; paired fins: pectoral and pelvic. Tail types: **protocercal** (vertebral axis straight, equal lobes — cyclostomes, larvae), **heterocercal** (axis into larger upper lobe — sharks, sturgeon), **homocercal** (externally symmetrical, axis upturned and shortened — most teleosts), **diphycercal** (secondarily symmetrical — lungfishes).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling placoid scales epidermal (they are dermal with an epidermal enamel cap).
- Saying sharks have an operculum.
- Confusing homocercal (externally symmetrical) with protocercal.

lessons.title: Accessory respiration, swim bladder and Weberian ossicles

scenes.text: In stagnant paddy fields of India, the climbing perch gulps air at the surface.
Without access to air it would drown — its gills alone are not enough in oxygen-poor water.

steps.title: Accessory respiratory organs (Indian examples)
steps.body:
- **Anabas testudineus** (climbing perch): **labyrinthine organ** in a suprabranchial chamber from the first epibranchial.
- **Clarias batrachus** (magur): **arborescent (dendritic) organs** from 2nd and 4th gill arches.
- **Heteropneustes fossilis** (singhi): long **air sacs** extending backwards into the body muscles.
- **Channa (Ophiocephalus)**: paired suprabranchial chambers.
- **Amphipnous cuchia** (cuchia eel): paired air sacs above gills.
- Lungfishes (Protopterus, Lepidosiren, Neoceratodus) use lungs (modified swim bladder).

steps.title: Swim bladder
steps.body: Gas-filled sac dorsal to the gut. **Physostomous** (open duct to gut — carps, catfish) or **physoclistous** (closed — perches; gas exchanged via **red gland/rete mirabile** and oval). Functions: hydrostatic (buoyancy), respiration (lungfishes), sound production, hearing.

steps.title: Weberian ossicles
steps.body: In Cypriniformes and Siluriformes (Ostariophysi), a chain of four small bones — **claustrum, scaphium, intercalarium, tripus** — derived from the first vertebrae connects the swim bladder to the inner ear. Swim bladder vibrations are transmitted to the perilymph, improving hearing sensitivity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the labyrinthine organ is in Clarias (it is in Anabas).
- Saying Weberian ossicles are ear bones like mammalian ossicles — they are vertebral derivatives.
- Writing that all fishes have a swim bladder.

lessons.title: Migration and parental care in fishes

scenes.text: Each monsoon, hilsa shoals swim up the Hooghly and Padma from the Bay of Bengal to spawn.
Far away, European eels cross the Atlantic to breed in the Sargasso Sea.

steps.title: Types of migration
steps.body:
- **Anadromous**: sea → freshwater to breed (salmon, Hilsa ilisha, lamprey).
- **Catadromous**: freshwater → sea to breed (Anguilla eels → Sargasso Sea).
- **Potamodromous**: within freshwater.
- **Oceanodromous**: within the sea (tuna, herring).
- **Amphidromous**: between fresh and salt water, not for breeding.
Causes: breeding, feeding, climatic/seasonal change. Navigation cues: olfaction (salmon home to natal stream by smell), sun, geomagnetism, currents. Hormonal changes (thyroid, gonadotropins, cortisol) prepare osmoregulation.

steps.title: Parental care
steps.body:
- **Nest building**: stickleback (male builds nest and guards eggs), Channa.
- **Mouth brooding**: Tilapia (Oreochromis) females, Arius males.
- **Brood pouch**: male **Hippocampus** (seahorse) and pipefish carry eggs.
- **Egg attachment to body**: Kurtus (male carries eggs on a forehead hook).
- **Viviparity**: Scoliodon (placenta-like yolk sac), Gambusia, guppy.

steps.title: Conservation
steps.body: Dams like Farakka block migratory routes of Hilsa; fish passes/ladders and seasonal fishing bans aim to protect breeding stock.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping anadromous and catadromous.
- Saying the female seahorse carries the brood.
- Calling Gambusia oviparous (it bears live young).

courses.title: Unit 3 · Amphibia and Reptilia
courses.summary: Origin of tetrapods, amphibian orders and parental care, neoteny in Ambystoma, reptile characters and skull types (temporal fossae), poisonous and non-poisonous snakes of India and the biting mechanism.
outcomes: Explain the origin of tetrapods from lobe-finned fishes
Classify amphibians and describe parental care and neoteny
Classify reptiles by temporal fossae
Distinguish poisonous from non-poisonous snakes and describe snake venom types
Describe the biting apparatus of a viper

scenes.text: About 375 million years ago, Tiktaalik propped itself up in shallow water on sturdy fins with wrist-like bones.
Its descendants gave rise to frogs, salamanders and caecilians — and eventually to us.

steps.title: Origin of tetrapods
steps.body: Tetrapods evolved in the Late Devonian from **sarcopterygian (lobe-finned) fishes** related to Osteolepiformes (Eusthenopteron). Transitional fossils: **Tiktaalik** (fish–tetrapod intermediate with neck and robust fins), **Acanthostega** and **Ichthyostega** (limbs with 8 and 7 digits respectively, still largely aquatic). Pre-adaptations: lungs, internal nostrils (choanae), bony lobed fins with humerus–radius–ulna pattern, labyrinthodont teeth.

steps.title: Living amphibian orders
steps.body:
- **Anura/Salientia**: frogs and toads, tailless adults, long hind legs (Rana / Hoplobatrachus tigerinus, Bufo/Duttaphrynus, Hyla, Rhacophorus).
- **Urodela/Caudata**: salamanders and newts, tailed (Ambystoma, Salamandra, Triturus; India: Tylototriton in the north-east).
- **Apoda/Gymnophiona**: limbless caecilians (Ichthyophis, Uraeotyphlus — Western Ghats, North-east).
General characters: moist glandular skin without scales (except some caecilians), cutaneous + pulmonary respiration, three-chambered heart, 10 pairs of cranial nerves, two occipital condyles, ammonotelic larvae/ureotelic adults, mostly external fertilisation and aquatic larvae.

steps.title: Neoteny
steps.body: Retention of larval characters in a sexually mature animal. **Axolotl** (Ambystoma mexicanum) remains aquatic with external gills and breeds; metamorphosis can be induced by **thyroxine** (or iodine), showing that low thyroid activity in its cold, iodine-poor environment causes neoteny. Permanent neoteny (cannot metamorphose): Necturus, Proteus.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying amphibians evolved from ray-finned fishes.
- Confusing neoteny (larva breeds) with paedogenesis in insects.
- Calling caecilians snakes or worms.

scenes.text: The male midwife toad wraps strings of eggs around his hind legs until they hatch.
In Darwin's frog, the male carries tadpoles in his vocal sac.

steps.title: Why parental care?
steps.body: Aquatic eggs and larvae face predators, desiccation and competition. Species laying fewer eggs often invest more in each, raising survival.

steps.title: Examples
steps.body:
- **Foam nests**: Rhacophorus (Indian tree frogs) and Polypedates whip mucus into foam on leaves above water.
- **Nest building / mud nests**: Hyla faber (blacksmith frog).
- **Carrying eggs on legs**: Alytes (midwife toad, male).
- **Dorsal pouch**: Gastrotheca (marsupial frog, female).
- **Skin cells on back**: Pipa (Surinam toad, female; eggs sink into dorsal skin).
- **Vocal sac brooding**: Rhinoderma darwinii (male).
- **Stomach brooding**: Rheobatrachus (gastric-brooding frog, now extinct).
- **Egg guarding/coiling**: Ichthyophis female coils around eggs.
- **Viviparity**: Salamandra atra, Nectophrynoides.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Organise answers by type (nests → carriage externally → in body cavities → viviparity) and give one Indian example (Rhacophorus, Ichthyophis).

steps.title: Common mistakes

scenes.text: A shelled amniotic egg let early reptiles breed far from water.
Openings behind the eye in their skulls tell us which lineage each belongs to.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body: Dry skin with epidermal **horny scales/scutes**, **amniotic egg** (amnion, chorion, allantois, yolk sac) with shell, internal fertilisation, lungs only, heart incompletely four-chambered (ventricle partly divided; fully in crocodiles), **one occipital condyle (monocondylic)**, 12 pairs of cranial nerves, uricotelic, ectothermic. Living orders: **Chelonia/Testudines** (turtles, tortoises), **Rhynchocephalia** (Sphenodon — tuatara of New Zealand), **Squamata** (lizards and snakes), **Crocodilia** (Crocodylus, Gavialis).

steps.title: Temporal fossae classification
steps.body:
- **Anapsida**: no temporal opening (cotylosaurs; turtles traditionally placed here).
- **Synapsida**: one lower opening bounded above by postorbital and squamosal (mammal-like reptiles → mammals).
- **Parapsida/Euryapsida**: one upper opening (ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs).
- **Diapsida**: two openings (Sphenodon, lizards, snakes with modification, crocodiles, dinosaurs, birds).
Modern molecular data place turtles within Diapsida with secondary loss of openings.

steps.title: Mesozoic reptiles
steps.body: The Mesozoic (about 252–66 million years ago) is called the 'Age of Reptiles': dinosaurs (Saurischia and Ornithischia), pterosaurs, ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs. Mass extinction at the end of the Cretaceous (66 Ma), linked with the Chicxulub impact and Deccan volcanism, eliminated non-avian dinosaurs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling mammals descendants of diapsids — they arose from synapsids.
- Saying all reptiles have a three-chambered heart (crocodiles have four).
- Listing Sphenodon as a lizard.

lessons.title: Lab: Poisonous snakes of India and the biting mechanism

scenes.text: Most snakebite deaths in India are caused by four species: cobra, common krait, Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper.
Polyvalent antivenom made in India targets exactly these four.

steps.title: Identification key (field guide level)
steps.body:
- Ventral scales broad, covering the belly width: suspect venomous colubroid features; narrow ventrals → many non-venomous (e.g. blind snakes, pythons have small ventrals).
- **Cobra (Naja naja)**: hood with spectacle mark; third supralabial touches eye and nasal.
- **Common krait (Bungarus caeruleus)**: glossy blue-black with paired white bands; **enlarged hexagonal vertebral scales** along the back; subcaudals single.
- **Russell's viper (Daboia russelii)**: three rows of dark chain-like spots; triangular head with small scales; loud hiss.
- **Saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus)**: small, serrated keeled scales producing a rasping sound; arrow/trident mark on head.
Always treat any bite as potentially venomous; identification is for study, not handling.

steps.title: Fangs and biting mechanism
steps.body:
- **Proteroglyphous**: fixed front grooved fangs (cobra, krait, sea snakes — Elapidae).
- **Solenoglyphous**: long hollow hinged front fangs on a short rotatable maxilla (vipers).
- **Opisthoglyphous**: grooved rear fangs (cat snake Boiga).
- **Aglyphous**: no fangs (rat snake Ptyas, python).
Viper strike: mouth opens wide (about 180°); muscles push the pterygoid and ectopterygoid forward, which rotate the maxilla so fangs swing erect; on biting, compressor glandulae muscle squeezes the venom gland, pushing venom down the duct and through the hollow fang.

steps.title: Venom and first aid
steps.body: Elapid venom is mainly **neurotoxic** (ptosis, paralysis, respiratory failure); viperid venom is mainly **haemotoxic/cytotoxic** (bleeding, swelling, kidney injury). First aid: reassure, immobilise the limb, remove tight items, transport quickly to a hospital for antivenom; avoid cutting, sucking, tight tourniquets or traditional remedies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the python venomous.
- Recommending incision and suction.
- Mixing proteroglyphous (fixed front) and solenoglyphous (hinged) fangs.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Aves and Mammalia
courses.summary: Archaeopteryx and bird origins, flight adaptations, feathers, bird migration, mammalian characters and subclasses (Prototheria, Metatheria, Eutheria), dentition and dental formulae, and adaptive radiation of mammals.
outcomes: Evaluate Archaeopteryx as a connecting link
List flight adaptations of birds
Explain causes and navigation of bird migration
Distinguish monotremes, marsupials and placentals
Write and interpret dental formulae

scenes.text: In 1861 a quarry worker in Solnhofen, Germany, split a slab of limestone and found a skeleton with feathers.
It had teeth, claws on its wings and a long bony tail — half reptile, half bird.

steps.title: Archaeopteryx (Late Jurassic, about 150 Ma)
steps.body:
**Reptilian characters**: teeth in jaws, long bony tail of about 20 free vertebrae, three clawed fingers, free metacarpals, simple ribs without uncinate processes, weak sternum without keel, abdominal ribs (gastralia), non-pneumatic bones (mostly).
**Avian characters**: feathers (asymmetric flight feathers), wings, furcula (wishbone), opposable hallux, beak-like jaws, fused clavicles.
Modern view: a feathered theropod dinosaur close to the origin of birds; birds are living dinosaurs (many feathered non-avian theropods found in China).

steps.title: Flight adaptations
steps.body:
- Spindle-shaped streamlined body, feathers, forelimbs as wings.
- **Pneumatic bones**; fusion of bones — synsacrum, pygostyle, carpometacarpus, tibiotarsus, tarsometatarsus.
- **Keeled sternum** for large pectoralis major (downstroke) and supracoracoideus (upstroke via a tendon pulley through the triosseal canal).
- Lungs with **air sacs** giving unidirectional airflow through parabronchi; double respiration.
- Four-chambered heart, high metabolic rate, endothermy; right aortic arch only.
- Loss of teeth, urinary bladder (most), one ovary (left) in females — weight reduction.
- Uricotelic excretion, large eyes, well-developed cerebellum.

steps.title: Feather types
steps.body: **Contour feathers** (quill/calamus, rachis, vanes of barbs with interlocking barbules and hooklets), remiges (flight feathers of wing) and rectrices (tail); **down feathers** (insulation); **filoplumes** (sensory); bristles. Moulting replaces worn feathers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Archaeopteryx had a keeled sternum.
- Calling bird bones solid — many are hollow with struts.
- Writing that birds have the left aortic arch (mammals do).

activity.prompt: Is this feature of Archaeopteryx reptilian or avian?

quiz.q: The upstroke of the bird wing is powered by the
quiz.why: Its tendon passes over the shoulder through the triosseal canal and lifts the wing.

quiz.q: The pygostyle is formed by fusion of
quiz.why: Fused terminal tail vertebrae support the tail feathers.
The systemic arch of birds curves to the right, unlike mammals.
The Solnhofen limestone dates to about 150 million years ago.

scenes.text: Every winter, bar-headed geese fly over the Himalaya to Indian wetlands.
How do they know when to leave, and which way to go?

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Latitudinal**: north–south (Siberian cranes historically to Bharatpur; Amur falcons via Nagaland to Africa).
- **Longitudinal**: east–west.
- **Altitudinal**: up and down mountains seasonally (Himalayan monal, many Himalayan birds).
- **Partial**: only part of a population migrates.
- **Irregular/irruptive** and **vagrant**.

steps.title: Causes and physiology
steps.body: Ultimate causes: seasonal food availability, breeding opportunities, avoiding harsh winters. Proximate cue: **photoperiod** changes acting via the hypothalamus–pituitary–gonad axis and pineal melatonin; pre-migratory **hyperphagia** and fat deposition; **Zugunruhe** (migratory restlessness) in caged birds.

steps.title: Navigation
steps.body: Sun compass with time compensation (Kramer's starling experiments), star compass (Emlen's indigo buntings rotate to the night-sky pattern), geomagnetic sense, landmarks, olfaction, infrasound. Study methods: ringing/banding, satellite telemetry, radar.

steps.title: India
steps.body: India lies on the **Central Asian Flyway**; important sites include Keoladeo (Bharatpur), Chilika Lake, Point Calimere and the Rann of Kutch.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying birds migrate only because of cold.
- Ignoring the role of photoperiod.
- Confusing altitudinal with latitudinal migration.

activity.prompt: Match the scientist/concept to the navigation cue

quiz.why: Changing day length triggers hormonal changes that prepare birds to migrate.

Many Himalayan birds move to lower elevations in winter and back in summer.

scenes.text: When the platypus reached Europe, naturalists thought it was a hoax — a duck's bill sewn onto a mole.
Kangaroos give birth to a bean-sized young that crawls into a pouch.

steps.title: Mammalian characters
steps.body: Hair, mammary glands, sweat and sebaceous glands, **diaphragm**, **heterodont, thecodont, diphyodont** teeth, single dentary bone in each lower jaw articulating with the squamosal, three middle-ear ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes), external pinna, seven cervical vertebrae (with few exceptions — sloths, manatees), four-chambered heart with **left aortic arch**, enucleate biconcave RBCs, dicondylic skull, 12 pairs of cranial nerves, endothermy, mostly viviparous.

steps.title: Subclasses
steps.body:
- **Prototheria (Monotremata)**: egg-laying, cloaca, no teats (milk from patches), no pinna, reptile-like pectoral girdle with interclavicle and coracoids; Ornithorhynchus (platypus), Tachyglossus (echidna) — Australia/New Guinea.
- **Metatheria (Marsupialia)**: short gestation, young completes development in a **marsupium**; mostly choriovitelline (yolk-sac) placenta; epipubic bones; Macropus (kangaroo), Didelphis (opossum), koala.
- **Eutheria (Placentalia)**: chorioallantoic placenta, long gestation; orders such as Primates, Rodentia, Chiroptera, Carnivora, Cetacea, Proboscidea, Artiodactyla, Perissodactyla, Insectivora/Eulipotyphla, Lagomorpha.

steps.title: Monotremes as a connecting link
steps.body: They link reptiles and mammals: reptilian (eggs, cloaca, interclavicle, imperfect thermoregulation) and mammalian (hair, milk, diaphragm, single dentary, three ossicles).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying marsupials have no placenta (most have a yolk-sac placenta).
- Saying all mammals have seven cervical vertebrae without exception.
- Saying monotremes have teats.

lessons.title: Lab: Dentition and adaptive radiation of mammals

scenes.text: A skull on the lab bench has no incisors in the upper jaw and broad grinding molars.
Without seeing the animal, you can say: a ruminant herbivore.

steps.title: Dental formula
steps.body:
Written for one half of upper / lower jaw as I C P M. Total teeth = 2 × (upper sum + lower sum).
- **Human (adult)**: 2 1 2 3 / 2 1 2 3 → 2 × (8 + 8) = **32**.
- **Human milk teeth**: 2 1 0 2 / 2 1 0 2 → **20**.
- **Dog**: 3 1 4 2 / 3 1 4 3 → 2 × (10 + 11) = **42**.
- **Cow/sheep**: 0 0 3 3 / 3 1 3 3 → 2 × (6 + 10) = **32** (lower canines incisiform; upper incisors replaced by a dental pad).
- **Rabbit**: 2 0 3 3 / 1 0 2 3 → 2 × (8 + 6) = **28**.
- **Rat**: 1 0 0 3 / 1 0 0 3 → **16**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: A skull has upper 3 1 4 1 and lower 3 1 3 1 (cat). Upper half = 3+1+4+1 = 9; lower half = 3+1+3+1 = 8; total = 2 × (9 + 8) = **30**. Large canines and carnassials (upper P4 + lower M1 in Carnivora) indicate a carnivore.

steps.title: Adaptive radiation
steps.body: From small, insectivorous, terrestrial ancestors, eutherians radiated in the Cenozoic after the end-Cretaceous extinction into: **cursorial** (horse, deer — digitigrade/unguligrade, reduced digits), **fossorial** (mole — spade-like forelimbs), **arboreal** (primates, squirrels — grasping hands), **volant** (bats — patagium on elongated fingers), **aquatic** (whales, dolphins — flippers, blubber, loss of hind limbs), **scansorial**. Limb modifications are a classic example of adaptive radiation and homology.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to multiply by 2 for both sides.
- Giving cows upper incisors.
- Writing the formula for both jaws together instead of upper over lower.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Comparative anatomy, practicals & exam
courses.summary: Comparative anatomy of the vertebrate heart, aortic arches and kidneys, a key-point revision sheet, practicals on specimen and bone identification, and previous-year-style questions with a final exam.
outcomes: Trace the evolution of the vertebrate heart from fishes to mammals

lessons.title: Evolution of the heart and aortic arches

scenes.text: A fish heart pumps only deoxygenated blood to the gills — a single circulation.
A mammal's heart keeps two circuits fully apart, at different pressures.

steps.title: Heart
steps.body:
- **Fishes**: two-chambered (atrium + ventricle) plus sinus venosus and conus/bulbus arteriosus; **venous heart**, single circulation.
- **Lungfishes/Amphibians**: atrium divided into two (right receives body blood, left receives pulmonary blood), single ventricle; spiral valve in conus helps separate streams — incomplete double circulation.
- **Reptiles**: two atria, ventricle partly divided by an incomplete septum (complete in crocodiles, where the foramen of Panizza connects the two systemic arches).
- **Birds and mammals**: four chambers, complete double circulation; sinus venosus incorporated into the right atrium as the **SA node**.

steps.title: Aortic arches
steps.body:
Embryos have **six pairs** of aortic arches. In tetrapods arches 1, 2 and 5 largely disappear (5 persists in urodeles).
- **Arch III → carotid arch** (internal carotids).
- **Arch IV → systemic arch**: both in amphibians and reptiles; **right** only in birds; **left** only in mammals.
- **Arch VI → pulmonary arch** (with ductus arteriosus in embryos linking it to the systemic arch; closes after birth to form the ligamentum arteriosum).

steps.title: Worked example: tracing a red blood cell (mammal)
steps.body: Vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary arch (VI) → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid (mitral) valve → left ventricle → left systemic arch (IV) → body.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the frog heart has two ventricles.
- Giving birds the left systemic arch.
- Forgetting the ductus arteriosus in fetal circulation.

quiz.why: It receives venous blood from the body and pumps it to the gills.

scenes.text: A human embryo forms three kidneys in sequence; only the last one stays.
Fish keep the second one as adults.

steps.title: Kidney types
steps.body:
Kidneys arise from intermediate mesoderm (nephrotome) in a head-to-tail sequence:
- **Pronephros**: anterior, few segmental tubules with nephrostomes opening into the coelom; functional in larvae of cyclostomes, fishes and amphibians; adult in hagfish (along with mesonephros).
- **Mesonephros**: middle region; duct = **Wolffian (mesonephric) duct**; adult kidney of fishes and amphibians (**opisthonephros**); embryonic in amniotes.
- **Metanephros**: posterior; arises from the **ureteric bud** (out-growth of the Wolffian duct) and metanephric mesenchyme; adult kidney of reptiles, birds and mammals; drained by a ureter.

steps.title: Fate of ducts
steps.body: In male amniotes the Wolffian duct becomes the **vas deferens/epididymis**; in females it degenerates. The **Müllerian duct** forms oviducts, uterus and upper vagina in females and degenerates in males (under anti-Müllerian hormone).

steps.title: Memory aid
steps.body: 'Pro–Meso–Meta = Larva–Fish/Frog–Amniote' and 'Wolffian → male duct; Müllerian → female duct'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the metanephros arises from the Müllerian duct.
- Calling the mesonephros the adult kidney of mammals.
- Forgetting that the ureter is a new duct of the metanephros.

quiz.why: Reciprocal induction between the bud and posterior intermediate mesoderm forms nephrons and collecting ducts.

steps.title: Vertebra types by centrum
steps.body:
- **Amphicoelous** (both faces concave): fishes.
- **Procoelous** (anterior concave): most frog vertebrae, lizards, snakes.
- **Opisthocoelous** (posterior concave): some urodeles, some birds.
- **Heterocoelous** (saddle-shaped): bird cervical vertebrae — allow neck flexibility.
- **Acoelous/amphiplatyan** (flat): mammals.
Frog: 9 vertebrae + urostyle; atlas without transverse processes; 9th (sacral) has a double condyle behind.

uni-bsc-bio-developmental-biology.title: Developmental Biology
uni-bsc-bio-developmental-biology.description: Full B.Sc. Zoology developmental biology syllabus: gametogenesis, fertilisation, cleavage and egg types, gastrulation in frog and chick, neurulation and germ-layer fates, extra-embryonic membranes and placenta, embryonic induction, pattern formation, metamorphosis, regeneration, ageing and teratogenesis, with practicals and exam practice. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc. (Zoology/Life Sciences) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Gametogenesis and fertilisation
courses.summary: Historical theories (preformation, epigenesis), spermatogenesis and oogenesis, sperm and egg structure, egg classification by yolk, vitellogenesis, and fertilisation: acrosome reaction, blocks to polyspermy, egg activation and amphimixis.
outcomes: Contrast preformation and epigenesis

Describe the acrosome reaction and sperm–egg fusion
