lessons.title: Concepts and history of developmental biology

story.title: A tiny man in the sperm?

scenes.text: In 1694 Hartsoeker drew a tiny curled-up human — a 'homunculus' — inside a sperm head.
Wolff, watching chick embryos, saw organs form gradually from unformed tissue — epigenesis.

steps.title: Preformation vs epigenesis
steps.body:
- **Preformation**: the organism is fully formed in miniature in the egg (**ovists**, e.g. Swammerdam, Bonnet) or sperm (**spermists/animalculists**, Hartsoeker) and simply grows.
- **Epigenesis** (Aristotle; revived by **C. F. Wolff**, 1759): structures arise progressively from undifferentiated material.
Modern synthesis: development is epigenetic but directed by inherited genetic information plus cytoplasmic determinants — 'neo-preformation' of information, not of form.

steps.title: Key concepts
steps.body:
- **Determination**: commitment of a cell to a fate (often before visible change).
- **Differentiation**: acquisition of specialised structure/function through differential gene expression.
- **Potency**: totipotent (zygote) → pluripotent (inner cell mass) → multipotent → unipotent.
- **Mosaic (determinate)** vs **regulative (indeterminate)** development: Roux's experiment (killing one frog blastomere → half-embryo) vs Driesch's (separated sea-urchin blastomeres → complete small larvae).
- **Germ plasm theory** (Weismann): germ line separate from soma.

steps.title: Model organisms
steps.body: Sea urchin, Xenopus, chick, mouse, zebrafish, Drosophila, Caenorhabditis elegans (fixed cell lineage, 959 somatic cells in the adult hermaphrodite), Arabidopsis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating Roux's result as proof of mosaic development in frogs: later work (keeping the dead cell attached vs removing it) showed regulation is possible.
- Mixing up determination and differentiation.
- Calling the inner cell mass totipotent.

activity.prompt: Match the scientist to the idea or experiment
pairs: Complete larvae from isolated sea-urchin blastomeres

quiz.why: Isolated early blastomeres could still form whole larvae, showing their fate was not fixed.
Differentiation is the visible expression of a specialised phenotype through selective gene expression.
The zygote can give rise to every cell of the embryo and the extra-embryonic tissues.

quiz.q: Ovists believed the preformed organism was in the
quiz.why: Ovists held that the miniature individual was already inside the egg.

scenes.text: A human testis makes millions of sperm every day.
An ovary releases usually one egg a month, packed with resources for the embryo.

steps.title: Spermatogenesis
steps.body: In seminiferous tubules: **spermatogonia** (2n, mitosis) → **primary spermatocyte** (2n) → meiosis I → 2 **secondary spermatocytes** (n) → meiosis II → 4 **spermatids** (n) → **spermiogenesis** (no division): Golgi → acrosome, nucleus condenses (protamines), centriole → axoneme, mitochondria → middle-piece sheath, excess cytoplasm shed as residual bodies. Supporting **Sertoli cells** (blood–testis barrier, ABP, inhibin); **Leydig cells** make testosterone (LH). FSH acts on Sertoli cells. Human cycle about 64–74 days.

steps.title: Oogenesis
steps.body: **Oogonia** multiply only before birth (in humans) → **primary oocytes** arrested in **prophase I (diplotene/dictyate)** inside primordial follicles → at puberty, each cycle one completes meiosis I just before ovulation → **secondary oocyte** + **first polar body** → arrested at **metaphase II** → meiosis II completes only after **fertilisation** → ovum + **second polar body**. One primary oocyte → **1 ovum + 2–3 polar bodies**. Follicle stages: primordial → primary → secondary → tertiary/Graafian (antrum, cumulus oophorus, corona radiata, zona pellucida).

steps.title: Worked example: counting
steps.body:
(a) 100 primary spermatocytes → 100 × 4 = **400 sperm**.
(b) 100 primary oocytes → **100 ova** (+ up to 300 polar bodies).
(c) 100 secondary spermatocytes → 100 × 2 = **200 sperm**.
(d) 100 spermatids → **100 sperm** (spermiogenesis has no division).

steps.title: Vitellogenesis
steps.body: In many vertebrates (fish, amphibians, birds), the liver synthesises **vitellogenin** under oestrogen; it travels in blood and is taken up by oocytes by receptor-mediated endocytosis and cleaved into lipovitellin and phosvitin (yolk platelets).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying spermiogenesis involves meiosis.
- Saying human eggs complete meiosis before ovulation.
- Saying Leydig cells respond to FSH (they respond to LH).

activity.prompt: How many functional ova and how many sperm together can be produced from 25 primary oocytes and 25 primary spermatocytes? (Enter total gametes.)

story.title: From a sea urchin to an ostrich

scenes.text: A sea-urchin egg is barely visible and has very little yolk.
The 'yolk' of a hen's egg is a single giant cell packed with food reserve.

steps.title: By amount of yolk
steps.body:
- **Alecithal**: almost no yolk (eutherian mammals — often called microlecithal/alecithal).
- **Microlecithal/oligolecithal**: little yolk (sea urchin, Amphioxus).
- **Mesolecithal**: moderate yolk (frog, lungfish).
- **Macrolecithal/polylecithal**: much yolk (reptiles, birds, monotremes, many fishes, insects).

steps.title: By distribution of yolk
steps.body:
- **Isolecithal/homolecithal**: evenly spread (sea urchin, mammals).
- **Telolecithal**: concentrated at the **vegetal pole**; cytoplasm and nucleus near the **animal pole** — moderately (frog) or extremely (bird, where cytoplasm forms a **germinal disc/blastodisc**).
- **Centrolecithal**: yolk central, cytoplasm peripheral (insects).
Egg membranes: primary (vitelline membrane, zona pellucida), secondary (chorion of insects, jelly coat of frog — from follicle cells or oviduct depending on definition) and tertiary (albumen, shell membranes and shell of bird from the oviduct).

steps.title: Link to cleavage
steps.body: Yolk impedes cleavage furrows (Balfour's law: cleavage rate is inversely proportional to yolk density). So isolecithal → holoblastic equal; moderately telolecithal → holoblastic unequal; highly telolecithal → meroblastic discoidal; centrolecithal → meroblastic superficial.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the frog egg macrolecithal.
- Placing the bird nucleus in the yolk centre.
- Treating the albumen as part of the egg cell.

scenes.text: Thousands of sea-urchin sperm reach an egg; one fuses first.
Within seconds the egg's membrane voltage flips, and within a minute a fertilisation envelope lifts off — no more entries.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. **Chemotaxis** (sperm-attracting peptides such as resact/speract in sea urchins; progesterone and other cues in mammals).
2. **Capacitation** (mammals): in the female tract, removal of cholesterol and glycoproteins from the sperm membrane; hyperactivated motility.
3. **Acrosome reaction**: triggered by egg jelly (sea urchin) or zona protein **ZP3** (mouse); Ca²⁺ influx → acrosomal exocytosis releases enzymes (e.g. acrosin, hyaluronidase); in sea urchins an **acrosomal process** forms by actin polymerisation carrying **bindin**, which binds species-specific egg receptors.
4. **Penetration and fusion**: sperm crosses the zona pellucida/vitelline envelope; plasma membranes fuse (mouse: sperm IZUMO1 with egg JUNO).

steps.title: Blocks to polyspermy
steps.body:
- **Fast block** (sea urchin, frog): Na⁺ influx depolarises the egg membrane from about −70 mV to about +20 mV within seconds; lasts about a minute.
- **Slow block** (**cortical reaction**): sperm-induced **IP₃** releases Ca²⁺ from ER as a **calcium wave** → **cortical granules** exocytose → enzymes and mucopolysaccharides raise the vitelline envelope into a hard **fertilisation envelope** (sea urchin) or modify ZP2/ZP3 (**zona reaction**, mammals). Mammals rely mainly on the slow block.

steps.title: Egg activation and amphimixis
steps.body: Ca²⁺ wave activates metabolism: NAD⁺ kinase, raised pH (Na⁺/H⁺ exchange), protein and DNA synthesis, completion of meiosis (in vertebrates). Male and female **pronuclei** migrate (sperm aster), meet and either fuse (sea urchin) or their chromosomes join on the first mitotic spindle (mammals) — **amphimixis**, restoring diploidy. In frogs the sperm entry point determines the dorsal side via **cortical rotation** forming the grey crescent.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the fast block is due to the fertilisation envelope.
- Saying capacitation happens in the testis.
- Forgetting the Ca²⁺ wave as the universal activator.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Cleavage, blastulation and gastrulation
courses.summary: Planes and patterns of cleavage, blastula types, fate maps, morphogenetic movements, gastrulation in frog and chick (primitive streak, Hensen's node), and early mammalian development to implantation.
outcomes: Classify cleavage by plane and pattern
Describe the frog blastula and gastrula
Name morphogenetic movements and their examples
Describe primitive streak formation in the chick
Outline mammalian cleavage, compaction and blastocyst formation

scenes.text: A frog zygote divides into 2, 4, 8 … thousands of cells in about a day, yet the embryo is no larger than the egg.
The cells get smaller each time — a morula, then a hollow blastula.

steps.title: Features of cleavage
steps.body: Rapid mitotic divisions without growth (cell cycle mostly S and M phases), increase in nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio, no change in total volume; ends at the **mid-blastula transition** (in Xenopus after about 12 divisions) when zygotic transcription begins, cell cycles lengthen and cells become motile.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
- **Planes**: meridional (through animal–vegetal axis), vertical, equatorial, latitudinal.
- **Holoblastic** (complete): **equal** (sea urchin, Amphioxus), **unequal** (frog — micromeres at animal pole, macromeres at vegetal pole); **radial** (echinoderms, amphibians), **spiral** (molluscs, annelids — oblique spindles, determinate), **bilateral** (tunicates), **rotational** (mammals).
- **Meroblastic** (incomplete): **discoidal** (birds, reptiles, fishes — only blastodisc divides), **superficial** (insects — nuclei divide without cytokinesis forming a syncytial blastoderm).

steps.title: Blastula types
steps.body:
- **Coeloblastula**: hollow sphere with a blastocoel (sea urchin, Amphioxus; frog's is multilayered with the blastocoel displaced to the animal half).
- **Discoblastula**: blastoderm over yolk with a subgerminal cavity (bird — area pellucida and area opaca).
- **Periblastula**: cellular layer around central yolk (insects).
- **Stereoblastula**: solid, no cavity (some cnidarians).
- **Blastocyst**: trophoblast + inner cell mass + blastocoel (mammals).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the embryo grows during cleavage.
- Calling frog cleavage meroblastic.
- Confusing spiral cleavage (protostomes) with radial cleavage (deuterostomes).

activity.prompt: Match the animal to its cleavage pattern

quiz.why: Cleavage partitions the egg cytoplasm into smaller cells without overall growth.
Oblique spindles in spiralian protostomes produce tiers of cells set at angles.

scenes.text: Vogt (1929) stained patches of a newt blastula with vital dyes.
Following the coloured cells, he drew a map of what each region would become.

steps.title: Fate map of the amphibian blastula
steps.body: Prepared by **vital staining** (Nile blue sulphate, neutral red — Vogt) and today by fluorescent dyes or lineage tracers. From animal to vegetal: **epidermis** (animal pole), **neural plate** (dorsal), **notochord** (dorsal marginal zone above the grey crescent), **mesoderm** (somites, lateral plate — marginal zone), **endoderm** (vegetal). A fate map shows normal fate, not commitment (potency may be broader).

steps.title: Morphogenetic movements
steps.body:
- **Epiboly**: spreading of a sheet over the embryo (animal cap ectoderm; fish blastoderm over yolk).
- **Emboly** (inward movements):
  - **Invagination**: inward folding of a sheet (sea-urchin vegetal plate).
  - **Involution**: inward rolling over a lip (amphibian mesoderm over the dorsal lip).
  - **Ingression**: individual cells migrate inside (sea-urchin primary mesenchyme; chick primitive streak).
  - **Delamination**: splitting of one sheet into two (chick hypoblast).
- **Convergent extension**: cells intercalate, narrowing and lengthening the tissue (notochord, neural plate).

steps.title: Memory aid
steps.body: 'Epi-boly spreads over, In-vagination folds in, In-volution rolls in, In-gression crawls in, De-lamination splits.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying fate maps show determined fates.
- Confusing invagination with involution.
- Forgetting convergent extension.

story.title: The most important time in your life

scenes.text: Lewis Wolpert said: 'It is not birth, marriage, or death, but gastrulation which is truly the most important time in your life.'
In a few hours three germ layers move into their final positions.

steps.title: Frog gastrulation
steps.body: Begins at the **dorsal lip of the blastopore**, formed where **bottle cells** in the grey-crescent region constrict apically and invaginate. Marginal-zone cells **involute** over the dorsal lip (future notochord and mesoderm migrate along the blastocoel roof on fibronectin); the lip extends laterally and ventrally to form a ring; animal cap ectoderm spreads by **epiboly**; vegetal yolk cells are enclosed and remain visible as the **yolk plug**. The **archenteron** (primitive gut) expands and the blastocoel is obliterated. End result: ectoderm outside, mesoderm in the middle, endoderm lining the archenteron; blastopore becomes the anus (deuterostome).

steps.title: Chick gastrulation
steps.body: Blastoderm: central **area pellucida** and peripheral **area opaca**; **epiblast** (upper) and **hypoblast** (lower, by delamination and polyingression). Cells of the posterior epiblast converge to form the **primitive streak** (with a primitive groove, ridges and anterior **Hensen's node** — equivalent of the amphibian dorsal lip/organizer). Epiblast cells **ingress** through the streak: the first displace the hypoblast to form **definitive endoderm**, the next form **mesoderm** spreading laterally; cells through Hensen's node form the head process (notochord) and prechordal plate. Epiblast left on the surface becomes **ectoderm**. The streak then regresses posteriorly as the notochord is laid down.

steps.title: Molecular note
steps.body: In Xenopus, β-catenin stabilised on the dorsal side by cortical rotation, plus vegetal VegT and Nodal-related signals, induce the dorsal mesoderm organizer (Nieuwkoop centre → Spemann organizer).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the hypoblast forms the definitive endoderm of the chick (it is extra-embryonic; definitive endoderm comes from ingressing epiblast).
- Saying the frog blastopore becomes the mouth.
- Forgetting the yolk plug.

scenes.text: An embryologist watches a human embryo in culture: 2 cells on day 2, a compact morula on day 4, a blastocyst on day 5.
Only the blastocyst is ready to implant in the uterus.

steps.title: Cleavage and compaction
steps.body: Slow (about 12–24 h per division), **rotational** and **asynchronous**; zygotic genome activated early (2-cell stage in mouse, 4–8-cell in human). At the 8-cell stage **compaction** occurs: cells flatten and maximise contact using **E-cadherin**, forming tight junctions on the outer cells. Inner cells → **inner cell mass (ICM)**; outer cells → **trophoblast/trophectoderm**.

steps.title: Blastocyst and implantation
steps.body: Trophoblast pumps Na⁺ inward, water follows → **blastocoel**. ICM later splits into **epiblast** (embryo proper — source of embryonic stem cells) and **hypoblast/primitive endoderm**. Blastocyst **hatches** from the zona pellucida and implants (human: about day 6–7) in the endometrium; trophoblast forms **cytotrophoblast** and invasive **syncytiotrophoblast**, which secretes **hCG** (basis of pregnancy tests) maintaining the corpus luteum.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: IVF and embryo transfer (first IVF baby Louise Brown, 1978; India's first, 'Durga', 1978 by Subhas Mukhopadhyay — and the first officially documented Indian IVF birth 1986), preimplantation genetic testing using trophectoderm biopsy, and identical twins from splitting of the ICM.

- Calling mammalian cleavage fast and synchronous.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Neurulation, organogenesis, extra-embryonic membranes and placenta
courses.summary: Neurulation and neural crest, germ-layer derivatives, mesoderm subdivision and somites, development of the eye as a model of induction, extra-embryonic membranes of the chick and the classification and functions of the mammalian placenta.
outcomes: Describe neurulation and neural tube defects
List derivatives of ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm and neural crest
Explain somite formation and mesoderm subdivisions
Describe extra-embryonic membranes of the chick

scenes.text: Doctors advise women planning pregnancy to take folic acid.
It lowers the risk that the neural tube fails to close in the first month.

steps.title: Primary neurulation
steps.body: The notochord (chordamesoderm) induces overlying ectoderm to thicken into the **neural plate** → edges rise as **neural folds** with a central **neural groove** (hinge points: median and dorsolateral) → folds meet and fuse dorsally forming the **neural tube**, which separates from the surface ectoderm (epidermis). The anterior tube forms brain vesicles (prosencephalon, mesencephalon, rhombencephalon), the posterior forms the spinal cord. In amniotes the tube closes first in the middle and 'zips' toward the ends (neuropores). **Secondary neurulation** (hollowing of a solid cord) forms the tail/sacral region.

steps.title: Neural crest — 'fourth germ layer'
steps.body: Cells at the fold crests undergo epithelial–mesenchymal transition and migrate widely to form: sensory (dorsal root) and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, **adrenal medulla**, **melanocytes**, craniofacial cartilage and bone, odontoblasts (tooth dentine), parts of the heart outflow septum, and thyroid C cells.

steps.title: Neural tube defects
steps.body: Failure of anterior closure → **anencephaly** (lethal); posterior → **spina bifida** (range from occulta to myelomeningocele). Periconceptional folic acid supplementation reduces NTD risk substantially (randomised trial evidence, MRC 1991).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the neural tube forms from mesoderm.
- Listing the adrenal cortex (mesoderm) as a neural crest derivative.
- Forgetting the notochord's inductive role.

lessons.title: Germ-layer derivatives, somites and eye development

scenes.text: Your skin, gut lining and muscles all trace back to three sheets of cells in a 3-week embryo.
The eye shows how they talk: brain tissue tells skin to make a lens.

steps.title: Derivatives
steps.body:
- **Ectoderm**: epidermis, hair, nails, skin glands, lens, cornea epithelium, inner ear (otic placode), enamel, anterior pituitary (Rathke's pouch), nervous system and retina (neural ectoderm).
- **Mesoderm**: notochord; **paraxial** (somites → sclerotome: vertebrae and ribs; myotome: skeletal muscle; dermatome: dermis); **intermediate** (kidneys, gonads, ducts); **lateral plate** (somatic → body wall, limb skeleton; splanchnic → heart, blood vessels, blood, gut smooth muscle); adrenal cortex, coelomic linings.
- **Endoderm**: epithelium of gut, liver, pancreas, lungs, thyroid, parathyroid, thymus, urinary bladder, urethra lining.

steps.title: Somitogenesis
steps.body: Paraxial mesoderm segments into paired blocks (**somites**) from anterior to posterior at regular intervals governed by a **segmentation clock** (oscillating Notch/Hes genes) and a wavefront of FGF/Wnt — the clock-and-wavefront model. Chick: one pair about every 90 minutes; human about 42–44 pairs form.

steps.title: Eye development
steps.body: Diencephalon outgrowth → **optic vesicle** → contacts head ectoderm → induces **lens placode** → lens vesicle; optic vesicle invaginates into a double-walled **optic cup** (inner layer → neural retina; outer → pigmented retina); lens in turn induces overlying ectoderm to form the **cornea**. A classic chain of **reciprocal/sequential induction** (Spemann's lens experiments).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the retina in surface ectoderm (it is neural ectoderm).
- Calling the heart an endodermal organ.
- Assigning vertebrae to the dermatome.

scenes.text: A chick develops in a sealed shell with no way to drink, eat or excrete outside.

steps.title: The four membranes
steps.body:
- **Yolk sac** (splanchnopleure: endoderm + splanchnic mesoderm): grows over the yolk; blood islands form first blood cells and vessels; nutrition.
- **Amnion** (somatopleure: ectoderm + somatic mesoderm, inner limb of amniotic folds): encloses embryo in **amniotic fluid** — protection from shock and desiccation, freedom of movement.
- **Chorion/serosa** (somatopleure, outer limb of folds): lies under the shell membrane; gas exchange when fused with the allantois.
- **Allantois** (splanchnopleure, outgrowth of hindgut): stores **uric acid**; fuses with chorion as the **chorio-allantoic membrane** (CAM) for respiration and calcium uptake from the shell.
Albumen is taken up via the albumen sac. Amniotes = reptiles, birds, mammals.

steps.title: CAM assay
steps.body: The vascular chorio-allantoic membrane is used in research to test angiogenesis and tumour growth, and historically to grow viruses for vaccines.

steps.title: By shape (villi distribution)
steps.body:

- **Cotyledonary**: villi in patches (cow, sheep, goat).

steps.title: By tissue layers (Grosser's classification)
steps.body:
Number of maternal layers between foetal chorion and maternal blood:
- **Epitheliochorial**: all maternal layers intact (pig, horse).
- **Syndesmochorial**: maternal epithelium eroded (cow, sheep — often reclassified as synepitheliochorial).
- **Endotheliochorial**: chorion against maternal endothelium (dog, cat).
- **Haemochorial**: chorion bathed in maternal blood (human, rodents).
- **Haemoendothelial**: only foetal endothelium remains (rabbit, rat at late stages).
Also **deciduate** (maternal tissue shed at birth — human) vs **non-deciduate** (pig).

steps.title: Functions
steps.body: Exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes; barrier (partial — alcohol, many drugs, rubella virus cross); transfer of **IgG** antibodies; endocrine: hCG, human placental lactogen, progesterone and oestrogens (after the first trimester the placenta takes over progesterone production from the corpus luteum), relaxin.

scenes.text: In 1924 Hilde Mangold grafted a dorsal blastopore lip from a pale newt into the belly side of a dark one.
A second body axis formed — mostly from host cells. The graft had organised them.

steps.title: Spemann–Mangold experiment
steps.body: Donor: dorsal lip of Triturus cristatus (unpigmented); host: T. taeniatus (pigmented) early gastrula, ventral side. Result: secondary embryo with neural tube, notochord and somites; the notochord came mainly from graft cells, while neural tube and most somites came from **host** tissue. Conclusion: the dorsal lip is the **primary organizer** that **induces** host cells and organises an axis. Spemann received the Nobel Prize in 1935.

steps.title: Molecular basis
steps.body: The organizer secretes **BMP antagonists** — **noggin, chordin, follistatin** — which block BMP-4 signalling in the ectoderm; ectoderm without BMP becomes **neural** (default model of neural induction); with BMP it becomes epidermis. Wnt antagonists (Dickkopf, Cerberus) promote head formation. Earlier, the **Nieuwkoop centre** (dorsal vegetal cells with β-catenin) induces the organizer.

steps.title: Types of induction
steps.body:
- **Instructive** vs **permissive** induction.
- **Competence**: the ability of the responding tissue to react (time-limited).
- **Sequential/reciprocal induction**: eye (optic vesicle → lens → cornea), kidney (ureteric bud ↔ metanephric mesenchyme).
- **Homeogenetic induction**: induced tissue induces the same tissue in neighbours.
- Mechanisms: paracrine factors (FGF, Hedgehog, Wnt, TGF-β/BMP families), juxtacrine (Notch–Delta), extracellular matrix.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the secondary embryo is made entirely of graft cells.
- Saying the organizer secretes BMP (it secretes BMP antagonists).
- Ignoring competence of the responding tissue.

options: Ability to respond to an inducer

lessons.title: Pattern formation: Drosophila genes, Hox and the limb

scenes.text: Ed Lewis bred Drosophila with mutations that turned halteres into a second pair of wings.
The genes responsible — Hox genes — are found in almost all animals, including us.

steps.title: Drosophila anterior–posterior hierarchy
steps.body:
1. **Maternal effect genes**: **bicoid** mRNA anchored anteriorly → Bicoid protein gradient (anterior morphogen); **nanos** posteriorly; hunchback, caudal translation controlled.
2. **Gap genes** (hunchback, Krüppel, knirps, giant): broad domains; mutants lack contiguous segments.
3. **Pair-rule genes** (even-skipped, fushi tarazu, hairy): 7 stripes; mutants lack alternate segments.
4. **Segment polarity genes** (engrailed, wingless, hedgehog): 14 stripes; define anterior/posterior halves of each parasegment.
5. **Homeotic selector (Hox) genes**: **Antennapedia complex** (lab, pb, Dfd, Scr, Antp) and **Bithorax complex** (Ubx, abd-A, Abd-B) give segment identity. Nobel Prize 1995: Lewis, Nüsslein-Volhard, Wieschaus.

steps.title: Hox genes
steps.body: Contain a 180-bp **homeobox** encoding a 60-amino-acid homeodomain (DNA binding). Show **colinearity**: order on the chromosome matches order of expression along the body axis. Mammals have 4 clusters (HoxA–D, 39 genes). Mutations cause **homeotic transformations** (e.g. Antennapedia: legs instead of antennae).

steps.title: Vertebrate limb
steps.body:
- **Apical ectodermal ridge (AER)**: FGFs, proximal–distal outgrowth (removal truncates limb).
- **Zone of polarising activity (ZPA)**: posterior mesenchyme secreting **Sonic hedgehog** — anterior–posterior (digit identity); an anterior ZPA graft produces mirror-image digit duplication.
- **Dorsal ectoderm Wnt7a**: dorsal–ventral.
- **Interdigital apoptosis** (BMPs) separates digits; reduced in ducks → webbed feet.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling bicoid a zygotic gene.
- Confusing pair-rule (7 stripes) with segment polarity (14 stripes).
- Saying AER controls digit identity (that is ZPA/Shh).

scenes.text: In 1912 Gudernatsch fed tadpoles horse thyroid tissue.
They metamorphosed early into tiny froglets.

steps.title: Changes
steps.body:
- **Regressive**: tail and gills resorbed (apoptosis, lysosomal enzymes), larval teeth and lateral line lost.
- **Constructive**: limb development, lungs, middle ear, eyelids, tongue.
- **Remodelling**: gut shortens (herbivore → carnivore), skin thickens, retina pigment switches from porphyropsin to rhodopsin, haemoglobin switches to adult type with lower O₂ affinity.
- **Biochemical**: ammonotelic → ureotelic (urea-cycle enzymes induced in the liver).

steps.title: Hormonal control
steps.body: Hypothalamus (CRH acts as the main TSH releaser in amphibians) → pituitary **TSH** → thyroid **T₄** → converted in target tissues to **T₃** (by deiodinase) → binds nuclear **thyroid hormone receptors** → gene expression. **Prolactin** acts as a juvenile (anti-metamorphic) hormone; corticosteroids enhance T₃ action. Thyroidectomy or hypophysectomy prevents metamorphosis (giant tadpoles); iodine/T₄ hastens it. Response is tissue-specific — the same hormone makes limbs grow and tails die.

steps.title: Link
steps.body: Neoteny in the axolotl (Unit on Chordates) is a failure of this axis — metamorphosis can be induced with thyroxine.

lessons.title: Regeneration, stem cells, ageing and teratogenesis

scenes.text: Cut off a salamander's leg and within weeks a new, perfect one grows from a blastema.
A thalidomide tragedy in the 1960s showed how drugs can derail limb development.

steps.title: Types of regeneration (Morgan)
steps.body:
- **Epimorphosis**: dedifferentiation of adult cells into an undifferentiated **blastema** that proliferates and re-differentiates (salamander limb, lizard tail).
- **Morphallaxis**: re-patterning of existing tissue with little new growth (Hydra).
- **Compensatory regeneration**: cells divide but keep their function (mammalian liver).
Salamander limb: wound epidermis → **apical ectodermal cap** → blastema (needs nerve supply — denervated limbs fail) → redifferentiation following positional information (**rule of distal transformation**: only structures distal to the cut regenerate). Retinoic acid can proximalise the blastema. Planaria regenerate from **neoblasts** (pluripotent stem cells).

steps.title: Stem cells
steps.body: Embryonic stem cells (ICM, pluripotent); adult stem cells (haematopoietic, intestinal crypt, skin, mesenchymal — multipotent); **induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs)** from fibroblasts using Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc (Yamanaka, 2006; Nobel 2012).

steps.title: Ageing and teratogenesis
steps.body:
Ageing theories: free-radical/oxidative damage, telomere shortening (Hayflick limit about 40–60 divisions for human fibroblasts in culture), DNA damage accumulation, insulin/IGF signalling (C. elegans daf-2 mutants live longer).
**Teratogens**: thalidomide (phocomelia — limb defects), alcohol (foetal alcohol syndrome), retinoic acid/isotretinoin, rubella virus, Zika virus (microcephaly), X-rays, mercury (Minamata). Most sensitive period: **organogenesis (about weeks 3–8 in humans)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling Hydra regeneration epimorphic.
- Saying liver regeneration forms a blastema.
- Saying teratogens are most harmful in the first 2 weeks (that period tends to be all-or-none).

scenes.text: Developmental biology is a story in order: gametes → fertilisation → cleavage → gastrulation → neurulation → organs.
Remember the order and the key experiment at each step.

steps.title: Sequence with key experiments
steps.body:
- **Gametes**: spermatogenesis (4 sperm per primary spermatocyte), oogenesis (1 ovum + polar bodies); egg types by yolk.
- **Fertilisation**: acrosome reaction, fast (electrical) and slow (cortical) blocks; Ca²⁺ wave.
- **Cleavage**: holoblastic/meroblastic; Balfour's law; MBT.
- **Blastula**: coeloblastula, discoblastula, blastocyst.
- **Gastrulation**: frog dorsal lip, chick primitive streak and Hensen's node; Vogt's fate map.
- **Neurulation**: neural plate → tube; neural crest; NTDs and folate.
- **Organogenesis**: germ-layer derivatives, somites, eye induction.
- **Membranes and placenta**: amnion, chorion, yolk sac, allantois; placenta by shape and by Grosser.
- **Mechanisms**: Spemann–Mangold; BMP antagonists; Drosophila gene hierarchy; Hox; AER/ZPA.
- **Post-embryonic**: metamorphosis (T₃), regeneration (blastema), stem cells, ageing, teratogens.

steps.title: Numbers worth remembering
steps.body: Synchronous cleavage gives 2ⁿ cells after n divisions · Xenopus MBT about the 12th division (4,096 cells) · human implantation about day 6–7 · organogenesis weeks 3–8 · about 42–44 somite pairs in humans · Hox clusters: 1 in Drosophila (split into ANT-C and BX-C), 4 in mammals.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: How many cells after 6 synchronous cleavages? 2⁶ = **64**. After 10? 2¹⁰ = **1,024**.

scenes.text: Six slides: a 2-cell, 8-cell, blastula, gastrula with yolk plug, neurula and tailbud embryo.
Identify each with two reasons.

steps.title: Identification points
steps.body:
- **2-cell / 4-cell**: meridional furrows; pigmented animal half.
- **8-cell**: first equatorial (latitudinal) furrow displaced toward the animal pole → 4 micromeres over 4 macromeres.
- **Morula / blastula (section)**: multilayered roof, blastocoel in the animal half, large yolky vegetal cells.
- **Gastrula**: crescent-shaped dorsal lip → circular blastopore with **yolk plug**; sections show archenteron and shrinking blastocoel.
- **Neurula**: neural plate and folds on the dorsal surface; sections show notochord, mesoderm and archenteron.
- **Tailbud**: elongated, tail bud, gill plates, sucker, optic bulges.
- **Tadpole**: external gills (later operculum covers them), coiled gut.

steps.title: Practical tip
steps.body: In sections, decide orientation first: dark pigment marks the animal side; the dorsal lip marks the dorsal side; then name the cavities (blastocoel vs archenteron).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Naming the archenteron as blastocoel in late gastrula sections.
- Mistaking the yolk plug for the mouth.
- Forgetting that the 8-cell stage is unequal.

lessons.title: Lab: Chick embryo whole mounts and egg windowing

story.title: A beating heart at two days

scenes.text: Cut a small window in a 48-hour incubated egg and the embryo lies on the yolk.
Under a lens, a tiny S-shaped heart is already beating.

steps.title: Whole mounts (approximate incubation ages)
steps.body:
- **18 h**: primitive streak with Hensen's node and primitive groove; area pellucida and area opaca.
- **24 h**: head fold, neural folds, notochord (head process), about 4 pairs of somites; streak regressing.
- **33 h**: brain vesicles (pros-, mes-, rhombencephalon), optic vesicles, about 12 somite pairs, heart tubes fusing, vitelline veins.
- **48 h**: cranial and cervical flexure, torsion begins (embryo turns on its left side), S-shaped beating heart, optic cups with lens placode, otic vesicles, about 24 somite pairs, amnion covering the head.
- **72 h**: C-shaped, limb buds, pharyngeal arches/clefts, eyes with lens, extensive vitelline circulation, allantois appears.
Counts vary with incubation conditions — stage embryos by morphology (Hamburger–Hamilton stages), not by hours alone.

steps.title: Windowing procedure
steps.body: Incubate fertile eggs at about 37.5 °C with humidity, turning regularly. Swab with 70% alcohol; remove 2–3 mL albumen with a syringe from the blunt end side so the embryo drops; cut a small window in the shell with fine scissors; observe the embryo; seal with tape to continue incubation, or lift the embryo on a filter-paper ring into warm saline, fix, stain (borax carmine) and mount.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ageing embryos only by hours.
- Rupturing the yolk by cutting too deep.
- Leaving out the saline step — the embryo dries and folds.

steps.title: Viva quick answers

- Function of amniotic fluid? Prevents desiccation and adhesion, cushions shocks.
- What is competence? Ability of tissue to respond to an inducer.

courses.summary: Chemical origin of life (Oparin–Haldane, Miller–Urey, RNA world), the geological time scale and fossil dating, evidence of evolution, Lamarckism, Darwinism, mutation theory and the Modern Synthesis, and an outline of human evolution.
outcomes: Explain the Oparin–Haldane hypothesis and the Miller–Urey experiment

scenes.text: In 1953 Stanley Miller sparked electricity through methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour for a week.
The water turned brown and contained amino acids — building blocks of life made without life.

steps.title: Oparin–Haldane hypothesis (1920s)
steps.body: Early Earth had a **reducing atmosphere** (CH₄, NH₃, H₂, H₂O; little free O₂). Energy from UV light, lightning and volcanic heat drove formation of simple organic molecules, which accumulated in the oceans as a **'hot dilute soup'** (Haldane's phrase). Polymers formed and aggregated into **coacervates** (Oparin) or **microspheres** (Fox, from proteinoids), precursors of cells.

steps.title: Miller–Urey experiment
steps.body: Closed glass apparatus: boiling water flask → gases (CH₄, NH₃, H₂) → spark chamber (electrodes, about 60,000 V) → condenser → trap. After about a week: amino acids (glycine, alanine, aspartic acid), and other organics. Later reanalyses of stored samples found over 20 amino acids. Criticism: early atmosphere may have been less reducing (CO₂, N₂), though volcanic and hydrothermal environments could supply reducing conditions.

steps.title: RNA world and first cells
steps.body: **Ribozymes** (Cech, Altman — Nobel 1989) show RNA can both store information and catalyse reactions, suggesting early life used RNA before DNA and proteins. Proposed sites: shallow pools with wet–dry cycles, deep-sea hydrothermal vents. Earliest evidence of life: stromatolites and microfossils about 3.5 billion years old (some claims older). Oxygenic photosynthesis by cyanobacteria led to the **Great Oxidation Event** about 2.4 billion years ago.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Miller made living cells.
- Saying the early atmosphere was rich in O₂.
- Confusing coacervates (Oparin) with microspheres (Fox).

lessons.title: Lab: Fossils, dating and evidence of evolution

scenes.text: The Siwalik hills of north India hold fossils of ancient apes, elephants and giraffes.
Radioactive clocks in rocks and bones tell us how old they are.

steps.title: Geological time scale (outline)
steps.body: **Precambrian** (to 541 Ma). **Palaeozoic** (541–252 Ma): Cambrian explosion, first fishes, land plants, amphibians (Devonian), reptiles (Carboniferous); ends in the Permian extinction. **Mesozoic** (252–66 Ma): Triassic, Jurassic, Cretaceous — age of reptiles; first mammals and birds. **Cenozoic** (66 Ma–present): age of mammals; Quaternary includes humans.

steps.title: Radiometric dating
steps.body: **N = N₀ (½)^(t/T½)**, so **t = T½ × log₂(N₀/N)**. Radiocarbon (¹⁴C, T½ ≈ 5,730 years) dates organic remains up to about 50,000 years; potassium–argon (⁴⁰K, T½ ≈ 1.25 billion years) and uranium–lead date volcanic rocks.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. A bone has 25% of the original ¹⁴C. 25% = (½)² → 2 half-lives → age = 2 × 5,730 = **11,460 years**.
2. A sample retains 12.5% → 3 half-lives → **17,190 years**.
3. Remaining fraction after 4 half-lives = (½)⁴ = **6.25%**.

steps.title: Evidence of evolution
steps.body:
- **Morphological**: homologous organs (forelimbs of whale, bat, human — divergent evolution), analogous organs (wings of insect and bird — convergent evolution), vestigial organs (human appendix, coccyx, nictitating membrane remnant, wisdom teeth).
- **Embryological**: pharyngeal pouches and tails in all vertebrate embryos (von Baer's laws; Haeckel's biogenetic law is now considered oversimplified).
- **Palaeontological**: transitional fossils (Tiktaalik, Archaeopteryx), horse evolution (Eohippus → Equus: size increase, reduction of digits, high-crowned teeth).
- **Biogeographical**: Darwin's finches, marsupials of Australia.
- **Molecular**: universal genetic code, cytochrome c and haemoglobin sequence similarity; molecular clocks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ¹⁴C to date dinosaurs.
- Confusing homologous with analogous.
- Quoting 'ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny' as literally true.

lessons.title: Theories: Lamarck, Darwin, de Vries and the Modern Synthesis

scenes.text: Lamarck: giraffes stretched their necks and passed on longer necks.
Darwin: giraffes with longer necks survived droughts better and left more young.

steps.title: Lamarckism (Philosophie Zoologique, 1809)
steps.body: Inner urge for perfection; environment creates needs; **use and disuse** of organs; **inheritance of acquired characters**. Criticism: **Weismann** cut tails of mice for about 20 generations — no tailless offspring; germ plasm is separate from soma. Neo-Lamarckism and modern epigenetic inheritance show limited, usually unstable, transmission of some acquired states, but not adaptive inheritance of use and disuse.

steps.title: Darwinism (On the Origin of Species, 1859)
steps.body: Influences: Lyell (uniformitarianism), Malthus (population growth). Points: **overproduction** (prodigality), limited resources → **struggle for existence** (intraspecific, interspecific, environmental), **variation** (heritable), **survival of the fittest** (Spencer's phrase) — **natural selection**, gradual accumulation → **origin of species**. Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea independently (joint presentation, 1858). Weakness: no mechanism of inheritance; could not explain origin of variations or vestigial organs well.

steps.title: Mutation theory and Modern Synthesis
steps.body: **Hugo de Vries** (Oenothera lamarckiana): new species arise suddenly by large mutations (saltation) — many of his 'mutants' were chromosomal variants. **Modern Synthetic Theory** (Fisher, Haldane, Wright, Dobzhansky, Mayr, Simpson, Huxley; 1930s–40s): evolution = change in **allele frequencies** caused by mutation, recombination, gene flow, genetic drift and natural selection, with **reproductive isolation** leading to speciation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Darwin knew about genes.
- Calling 'survival of the fittest' Darwin's coinage.
- Saying Weismann's experiment proved Darwin right on all points.

scenes.text: In 1974, in Ethiopia, fossil hunters found a 3.2-million-year-old skeleton they named Lucy.
Her pelvis and knee show she walked upright, though her brain was ape-sized.

steps.title: Sequence (simplified)
steps.body:
- **Sahelanthropus, Ardipithecus** (about 7–4.4 Ma): early possible hominins.
- **Australopithecus afarensis** (Lucy, about 3.9–2.9 Ma): bipedal, brain about 400–500 cc.
- **Homo habilis** (about 2.4–1.4 Ma): 'handy man', Oldowan stone tools, about 600–700 cc.
- **Homo erectus** (about 1.9 Ma–110 ka): left Africa, Acheulean hand axes, fire; Java and Peking man; about 900–1,100 cc. India: Narmada fossil at Hathnora is often attributed to archaic Homo.
- **Homo neanderthalensis** (about 400–40 ka): Europe/West Asia, about 1,500 cc, buried dead; interbred with H. sapiens.
- **Homo sapiens** (from about 300 ka; Jebel Irhoud, Morocco): about 1,350 cc average, language, art (Bhimbetka rock shelters in India have ancient paintings).

steps.title: Trends
steps.body: Bipedalism (S-shaped spine, bowl-shaped pelvis, arched foot, foramen magnum shifted forward), increase in brain size, reduction of jaw and teeth, flattening of face, chin, opposable thumb with precision grip, culture and tools. **Out of Africa** model supported by mitochondrial DNA and fossils, with some archaic admixture (Neanderthal, Denisovan DNA in modern humans).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying humans evolved from chimpanzees (we share a common ancestor about 6–7 Ma).
- Drawing a single straight-line 'march of progress'.
- Saying Neanderthals had smaller brains than us.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Population genetics, natural selection and speciation
courses.summary: Gene pool and Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium with solved numericals, forces changing allele frequencies (mutation, gene flow, genetic drift, selection), types of natural selection with industrial melanism and sickle-cell examples, species concepts, isolating mechanisms and modes of speciation.
outcomes: Calculate allele and genotype frequencies with Hardy–Weinberg
Explain mutation, gene flow, genetic drift (founder and bottleneck effects) and selection
Distinguish stabilising, directional and disruptive selection with examples
Classify pre- and post-zygotic isolating mechanisms
Compare allopatric, sympatric and parapatric speciation

scenes.text: In 1908 a mathematician (Hardy) and a physician (Weinberg) independently showed that allele frequencies stay constant unless something changes them.
This 'null model' lets us detect evolution happening.

steps.title: The principle
steps.body: For one gene with two alleles A (frequency p) and a (frequency q), **p + q = 1** and, after one generation of random mating, genotype frequencies are **p² (AA) + 2pq (Aa) + q² (aa) = 1**, staying constant thereafter if: large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration (gene flow), no selection. Deviation indicates evolution or non-random mating.

steps.title: Solved example 1: recessive trait
steps.body: 16% of a population shows a recessive trait (aa). q² = 0.16 → **q = 0.4**, **p = 0.6**. AA = p² = **0.36**, Aa = 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = **0.48**. So 48% are carriers.

steps.title: Solved example 2: rare disease
steps.body: Albinism frequency 1 in 10,000 → q² = 0.0001 → q = 0.01, p = 0.99. Carriers 2pq = 2 × 0.99 × 0.01 = **0.0198** ≈ **2%** (about 1 in 50) — far more carriers than affected individuals.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking q directly as the frequency of affected individuals (it is q²).
- Forgetting that heterozygotes carry one of each allele when counting.
- Assuming equilibrium means dominant alleles become common.

activity.prompt: A recessive disorder affects 1 in 2,500 people. What percentage of the population are heterozygous carriers? (Use 2pq, answer to 2 decimals.)

Which condition is NOT required for Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium?
quiz.why: Selection changes allele frequencies, so equilibrium requires its absence.

lessons.title: Forces of evolution: mutation, gene flow, drift

scenes.text: A small group of settlers founds an isolated community; by chance one carries a rare allele.

steps.title: Mutation and gene flow
steps.body:
- **Mutation**: ultimate source of new alleles; rates are low (often about 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁶ per gene per generation), so mutation alone changes frequencies slowly.
- **Gene flow (migration)**: movement of alleles between populations; makes populations more similar and can introduce new alleles.

steps.title: Genetic drift
steps.body:
Random change in allele frequency due to sampling in small populations (Sewall Wright). Can cause **fixation** or **loss** of alleles regardless of fitness.
- **Founder effect**: new population started by a few individuals (e.g. high frequency of Ellis–van Creveld syndrome among the Amish of Pennsylvania).
- **Bottleneck effect**: drastic reduction in population size (northern elephant seals hunted to about 20–100 individuals in the 1890s; cheetahs with very low genetic diversity). Reduced variation limits future adaptation.

steps.title: Non-random mating
steps.body: Inbreeding increases homozygosity (without changing allele frequencies itself) and exposes recessive disorders; assortative mating also alters genotype frequencies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying drift is adaptive.
- Saying gene flow increases differences between populations.
- Confusing founder effect with bottleneck.

steps.title: Types of selection
steps.body:
- **Stabilising**: favours intermediates, reduces variance (human birth weight — highest survival near average).
- **Directional**: shifts the mean (industrial melanism in Biston betularia; antibiotic and insecticide resistance; longer giraffe necks).
- **Disruptive (diversifying)**: favours both extremes (African seedcracker finch beak sizes) — can lead to polymorphism or speciation.
- **Sexual selection**: mate choice (peacock tail) and competition.
- **Balancing selection**: heterozygote advantage maintains alleles.

steps.title: Sickle-cell and malaria
steps.body: HbS homozygotes have sickle-cell disease; heterozygotes (HbA/HbS) have greater resistance to severe falciparum malaria → **heterozygote advantage** keeps HbS frequent in malarial regions of Africa and parts of India (e.g. tribal populations of central India).

steps.title: Industrial melanism
steps.body: Kettlewell's mark–release–recapture experiments (1950s) found higher recapture of camouflaged morphs: dark (carbonaria) in polluted Birmingham, light (typica) in unpolluted Dorset — consistent with bird predation. Later studies (Majerus) confirmed the selection pattern. Classic directional selection, reversed after pollution declined.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying moths changed colour by choice.
- Saying selection creates variation (it acts on existing variation).
- Calling resistance in bacteria 'Lamarckian'.

lessons.title: Species concepts, isolating mechanisms and speciation

scenes.text: African Lake Victoria once held hundreds of cichlid species that evolved within roughly the last 15,000 years.
How can one ancestor split into so many?

steps.title: Species concepts
steps.body:
- **Biological species concept** (Mayr): groups of actually or potentially interbreeding natural populations reproductively isolated from others. Limits: asexual organisms, fossils.
- **Morphological**, **phylogenetic** and **ecological** species concepts complement it.

steps.title: Isolating mechanisms (Dobzhansky)
steps.body:
**Pre-zygotic**: habitat (ecological), temporal (breeding seasons differ), behavioural/ethological (courtship songs, displays), mechanical (incompatible genitalia or flowers), gametic (sperm–egg incompatibility, e.g. bindin in sea urchins).
**Post-zygotic**: hybrid inviability, **hybrid sterility** (mule = horse × donkey, 63 chromosomes), hybrid breakdown (F₂ weak or sterile).

steps.title: Modes of speciation
steps.body:
- **Allopatric**: geographic barrier splits a population (Darwin's finches across islands; Abert's and Kaibab squirrels on either side of the Grand Canyon).
- **Peripatric**: small peripheral founder population.
- **Parapatric**: adjacent populations with a cline and limited gene flow.
- **Sympatric**: without geographic separation — **polyploidy** in plants (e.g. bread wheat hexaploid, Primula kewensis), host shifts (apple maggot fly Rhagoletis), disruptive selection in cichlids.
**Adaptive radiation**: rapid diversification into many niches (Darwin's finches, Australian marsupials, Hawaiian honeycreepers).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling hybrid sterility pre-zygotic.
- Saying sympatric speciation is impossible.
- Saying the mule is a species.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Ecosystem ecology: energy flow and biogeochemical cycles
courses.summary: Ecosystem structure, limiting factors and laws of tolerance, productivity (GPP, NPP), food chains and webs, energy flow and Lindeman's ten per cent law, ecological pyramids, and the carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles.
outcomes: Explain Liebig's and Shelford's laws
Calculate NPP and energy transfer along food chains
Distinguish grazing and detritus food chains and draw food webs
Interpret pyramids of number, biomass and energy
Describe the carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles

scenes.text: A pond near a village has algae, water plants, zooplankton, fish, frogs and herons.
Sunlight, temperature, oxygen and nutrients decide how much life it can hold.

steps.title: Components
steps.body: **Abiotic**: inorganic substances (C, N, P, water), organic compounds (humus, proteins), climatic factors (light, temperature, rainfall). **Biotic**: producers (autotrophs — phytoplankton, plants), consumers (primary — herbivores; secondary and tertiary — carnivores), decomposers (bacteria, fungi) and detritivores (earthworms). Term 'ecosystem' coined by **A. G. Tansley (1935)**.

steps.title: Laws of limiting factors
steps.body:
- **Liebig's law of the minimum (1840)**: growth is limited by the essential nutrient present in the smallest quantity relative to need.
- **Shelford's law of tolerance (1913)**: organisms have a minimum and maximum for each factor, with an optimum range between; **steno-** (narrow) vs **eury-** (wide) tolerance — e.g. stenothermal corals, eurythermal humans; euryhaline salmon, stenohaline goldfish.
- **Blackman's law** of limiting factors applies to rate processes such as photosynthesis.

steps.title: Indian example
steps.body: In many Indian freshwater lakes phosphorus (and sometimes nitrogen) limits algal growth; runoff of fertilisers and sewage removes the limitation, causing algal blooms and eutrophication (e.g. Dal Lake, Hussain Sagar).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling decomposers consumers of living tissue.
- Swapping Liebig (minimum) and Shelford (tolerance).
- Treating stenothermal as 'tolerates heat'.

scenes.text: In 1942 Raymond Lindeman measured energy at each feeding level in Cedar Bog Lake, Minnesota.
Only a small fraction passed from one level to the next.

steps.title: Productivity
steps.body:
- **Gross primary productivity (GPP)**: total rate of photosynthesis.
- **Net primary productivity (NPP) = GPP − R** (respiration of producers) — energy available to consumers.
- **Secondary productivity**: rate of new biomass formation by consumers.
Units: g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. Highly productive: tropical rain forests, estuaries, coral reefs, swamps; low: deserts, open ocean (per unit area). Plants capture only about 1–2% of incident sunlight (often quoted as about 1% of solar radiation reaching vegetation).

steps.title: Energy flow
steps.body: Energy flow is **unidirectional** (sun → producers → consumers → heat), obeying the laws of thermodynamics. **Lindeman's ten per cent law**: on average about 10% of energy at one trophic level is incorporated at the next (actual values vary roughly 5–20%). Hence food chains are short (usually 4–5 links).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. GPP = 2,500 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹, producer respiration 1,000 → NPP = **1,500 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹**.
2. Producers fix 20,000 J; with 10% transfer: primary consumers 2,000 J, secondary 200 J, tertiary **20 J**.
3. Ecological (trophic) efficiency = energy at level n+1 / energy at level n × 100: 150/1,500 × 100 = **10%**.

steps.title: Food chains and webs
steps.body: **Grazing food chain**: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk. **Detritus food chain**: dead leaves → earthworms/detritivores → birds; in many forests most energy flows through detritus chains. **Food webs** interlink chains and increase stability.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying energy is recycled like nutrients.
- Using GPP instead of NPP for energy available to herbivores.
- Applying exactly 10% as a physical law.

steps.title: Types (Charles Elton, 1927)
steps.body:
- **Pyramid of numbers**: upright in grassland; **inverted** in a tree ecosystem (one tree → many insects) or parasitic chain.
- **Pyramid of biomass**: upright on land; **inverted** in many aquatic systems (small standing crop of fast-turnover phytoplankton supports larger zooplankton/fish biomass).
- **Pyramid of energy**: **always upright**, because energy decreases at each level (second law of thermodynamics).

scenes.text: A carbon atom in your breath may have been in a dinosaur, a tree and an ocean shell.
Nitrogen from the air enters life mainly through bacteria in root nodules.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: **Gaseous cycles** (reservoir in atmosphere/ocean): carbon, nitrogen, oxygen. **Sedimentary cycles** (reservoir in rocks): phosphorus, sulphur (partly gaseous), calcium.

steps.title: Carbon cycle
steps.body: CO₂ fixed by photosynthesis (land plants, phytoplankton) → food chains → released by respiration, decomposition, combustion of fossil fuels and forest fires, volcanic activity; large ocean reservoir as dissolved CO₂/bicarbonate; long-term storage in carbonate rocks and fossil fuels. Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 ppm (pre-industrial) to over 420 ppm in recent years, driving global warming.

steps.title: Nitrogen cycle
steps.body:
1. **Nitrogen fixation**: N₂ → NH₃ by **nitrogenase** — symbiotic **Rhizobium** (legume root nodules, leghaemoglobin protects nitrogenase from O₂), free-living Azotobacter, Clostridium, cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc; Azolla–Anabaena in rice fields); also lightning and industrial Haber–Bosch process.
2. **Ammonification**: decomposers convert organic N to NH₄⁺.
3. **Nitrification**: NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ (**Nitrosomonas**) → NO₃⁻ (**Nitrobacter**).
4. **Assimilation**: plants absorb NO₃⁻/NH₄⁺.
5. **Denitrification**: NO₃⁻ → N₂ (**Pseudomonas**, Thiobacillus denitrificans) in waterlogged, anaerobic soils.

steps.title: Phosphorus cycle
steps.body: Weathering of phosphate rocks → soil phosphate → plants → animals → decomposition returns phosphate; runoff to oceans → sediments (lost from the short-term cycle) → geological uplift over long times; seabird guano returns some to land. No significant gaseous phase.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping Nitrosomonas (to nitrite) and Nitrobacter (to nitrate).
- Saying phosphorus has an atmospheric reservoir.
- Saying plants fix N₂ themselves.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Population and community ecology, biodiversity and conservation
courses.summary: Population attributes, exponential and logistic growth with solved numericals, r- and K-selection, survivorship curves, species interactions, ecological niche and Gause's principle, ecological succession, biodiversity hotspots of India and in-situ/ex-situ conservation.
outcomes: Calculate population growth with exponential and logistic models
Interpret survivorship curves and r/K strategies
Classify species interactions and explain competitive exclusion
Describe primary and secondary succession
Describe India's biodiversity, threats and conservation measures

scenes.text: Yeast cells in fresh sugar solution double rapidly at first.
Then growth slows and levels off — the curve becomes an S.

steps.title: Population attributes
steps.body: Density, natality (birth rate), mortality, age structure (pyramids: expanding, stable, declining), sex ratio, dispersal (immigration, emigration). Change: **ΔN = (B + I) − (D + E)**.

steps.title: Exponential (J-shaped) growth
steps.body: Unlimited resources: **dN/dt = rN**, where r = intrinsic rate of natural increase (b − d). Integrated: **N_t = N₀ e^(rt)**. **Doubling time t_d = ln 2 / r ≈ 0.693 / r**.

steps.title: Logistic (S-shaped) growth
steps.body: Limited resources (Verhulst–Pearl): **dN/dt = rN (1 − N/K)**, where **K** = carrying capacity. Growth is fastest at **N = K/2** (maximum sustainable yield concept in fisheries).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
1. Exponential: N₀ = 100, r = 0.1 per day, t = 10 days → N = 100 × e^1 = 100 × 2.718 = **272**.
2. Doubling time with r = 0.035 per year: 0.693/0.035 = **19.8 years**.
3. Logistic: r = 0.5, N = 200, K = 1,000 → dN/dt = 0.5 × 200 × (1 − 0.2) = **80 individuals per unit time**.
4. Maximum logistic growth rate occurs at N = K/2 = 500: dN/dt = 0.5 × 500 × 0.5 = **125**.

steps.title: r- and K-selection; survivorship
steps.body: **r-strategists**: small, many offspring, little care, early maturity, unstable habitats (insects, weeds). **K-strategists**: large, few offspring, much care, stable habitats (elephants, humans). **Survivorship curves**: Type I (high survival until old age — humans, large mammals), Type II (constant mortality — many birds, Hydra), Type III (high early mortality — oysters, fishes, many plants).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the (1 − N/K) factor in logistic growth.
- Using log₁₀ instead of ln for doubling time.
- Confusing Type I and Type III curves.

scenes.text: Gause grew Paramecium aurelia and P. caudatum together in one tube.
P. aurelia always won; P. caudatum died out — two species could not share one niche.

steps.title: Interactions (effect on species 1 / species 2)
steps.body:
- **Mutualism (+/+)**: lichens, mycorrhiza, Rhizobium–legume, pollination (fig and fig wasp).
- **Commensalism (+/0)**: barnacles on whales, cattle egret with cattle, epiphytic orchids.
- **Competition (−/−)**: intra- and interspecific.
- **Predation (+/−)**: tiger–deer; also herbivory.
- **Parasitism (+/−)**: Plasmodium, Cuscuta (plant parasite), ticks.
- **Amensalism (−/0)**: Penicillium inhibiting bacteria.
- **Neutralism (0/0)**.

steps.title: Niche and competitive exclusion
steps.body: **Habitat** = address; **niche** = profession (Elton) / n-dimensional hypervolume (Hutchinson): fundamental vs realised niche. **Gause's competitive exclusion principle**: two species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely. **Resource partitioning** allows coexistence (MacArthur's warblers feeding in different parts of spruce trees). **Connell's barnacles** (Chthamalus and Balanus) showed realised niche narrower than fundamental niche due to competition. **Keystone species** (Paine's Pisaster starfish) maintain community diversity.

steps.title: Predator–prey cycles
steps.body: Lotka–Volterra equations predict oscillations; the snowshoe hare–lynx fur-trade records (Hudson's Bay Company) show roughly 10-year cycles, though food supply also drives hare cycles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the cattle egret relationship mutualism (it is commonly treated as commensalism).
- Confusing habitat with niche.
- Saying competitive exclusion means competitors can never coexist (partitioning allows it).

scenes.text: After a landslide, bare rock is first colonised by crustose lichens.
Over centuries, mosses, grasses, shrubs and finally a forest take over.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
**Succession**: orderly, directional change in community composition over time ending (classically) in a **climax community** in balance with climate (Clements' monoclimax; Tansley's polyclimax). Stages = **seres** (seral stages); first colonisers = **pioneers**.
- **Primary**: on a bare area never colonised (rock, lava, sand dune) — slow.
- **Secondary**: after disturbance where soil remains (abandoned farmland, after fire) — faster.

steps.title: Hydrosere and xerosere
steps.body:
- **Hydrosere** (pond): phytoplankton → submerged plants (Hydrilla, Vallisneria) → floating plants (Nymphaea, Trapa) → reed swamp (Typha, Phragmites) → sedge meadow → woodland → forest climax.
- **Xerosere** (lithosere on rock): crustose lichens → foliose lichens → mosses → herbs → shrubs → forest.
Trends: increasing biomass, species diversity, soil depth and organic matter, more complex food webs, nutrient cycling becomes tighter.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Write sere stages as a flow diagram with an example plant at each stage and note the change in water level or soil at each step.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling succession on abandoned farmland primary.
- Starting a hydrosere with trees.
- Saying climax communities never change.

scenes.text: In 1973, with tigers in steep decline, India launched Project Tiger with nine reserves.
National estimates in recent surveys show tiger numbers rising again.

steps.title: Levels and values
steps.body: **Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity** (term popularised by E. O. Wilson). Diversity indices: alpha (within community), beta (between communities), gamma (regional). **Shannon index H' = −Σ pᵢ ln pᵢ**. Values: food, medicine, ecosystem services (pollination, water purification), cultural and ethical value.

steps.title: Solved example: Shannon index
steps.body: Community of 2 species with equal abundance (p = 0.5 each): H' = −[0.5 ln 0.5 + 0.5 ln 0.5] = −ln 0.5 = **0.693**. If proportions are 0.9 and 0.1: H' = −[0.9 ln 0.9 + 0.1 ln 0.1] = −[0.9(−0.1054) + 0.1(−2.3026)] = 0.0948 + 0.2303 = **0.325** — lower evenness, lower diversity.

steps.title: India's biodiversity
steps.body: One of the **17 megadiverse** countries; about 2.4% of the world's land area with roughly 7–8% of recorded species. Four of the world's **36 biodiversity hotspots** lie wholly or partly in India: **Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats & Sri Lanka, Sundaland** (Nicobar Islands). Endemics: lion-tailed macaque, Nilgiri tahr, purple frog, Malabar civet.

steps.title: Threats and conservation
steps.body: Threats (HIPPO): **H**abitat loss, **I**nvasive species (Lantana, Parthenium, African catfish), **P**ollution, human **P**opulation, **O**verexploitation; plus climate change. **In-situ**: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves (core, buffer, transition zones; e.g. Nilgiri — India's first, 1986), sacred groves, Project Tiger (1973), Project Elephant (1992), community reserves. **Ex-situ**: zoos, botanical gardens, seed and gene banks (NBPGR), cryopreservation, captive breeding (e.g. vultures, Great Indian Bustard). Laws and bodies: **Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972**, **Biological Diversity Act 2002** (National Biodiversity Authority), IUCN Red List categories (CR, EN, VU …), CITES, Convention on Biological Diversity (1992).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling zoos in-situ conservation.
- Listing Eastern Ghats as a global hotspot.
- Mixing up Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 and Biological Diversity Act 2002.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Revision, field practicals & exam
courses.summary: Key-point and formula sheet, field and laboratory practicals — quadrat sampling (density, frequency, abundance), mark–recapture (Lincoln index), dissolved oxygen by Winkler's method and Hardy–Weinberg simulation with beads — plus viva and previous-year-style questions.
outcomes: Recall key formulae in evolution and ecology
Compute density, frequency and abundance from quadrat data

scenes.text: Evolution has theories and examples; ecology has formulas and cycles.
Keep both on one page.

steps.title: Formulae
steps.body:
- Hardy–Weinberg: p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
- Radiometric age: t = T½ × log₂(N₀/N); ¹⁴C T½ ≈ 5,730 y.
- NPP = GPP − R; trophic efficiency = Eₙ₊₁/Eₙ × 100; ≈10% rule.
- dN/dt = rN; N_t = N₀e^(rt); t_d = 0.693/r; dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K); max at K/2.
- Shannon H' = −Σ pᵢ ln pᵢ.
- Lincoln index N = (M × C)/R.
- Quadrat: density = individuals/total quadrats; frequency % = quadrats with species/total × 100; abundance = individuals/quadrats where present.

steps.title: Key names
steps.body: Oparin, Haldane, Miller–Urey · Lamarck, Darwin, Wallace, de Vries, Weismann · Hardy, Weinberg, Fisher, Wright, Dobzhansky, Mayr · Kettlewell (moths) · Tansley (ecosystem), Lindeman (10%), Elton (pyramids, niche), Gause (exclusion), Hutchinson (niche), Clements (succession), Liebig, Shelford.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: For numericals: formula → substitution with units → answer boxed with units; for theory: definition → diagram → points with examples → conclusion.

activity.prompt: Match the scientist to the concept

quiz.why: Frequency reflects how widely a species is distributed across sampled quadrats.

options: Ecological pyramids and the niche concept
quiz.why: Elton described pyramids of numbers and defined the niche as an organism's role.
For exponential growth, ln 2 divided by r is the time for a population to double.

scenes.text: Students throw ten 1 m × 1 m quadrats across the college lawn and count every plant species.
In the garden, they mark snails with nail paint and come back the next day.

steps.title: Quadrat method
steps.body:
Lay quadrats randomly (random numbers for coordinates); record individuals of each species per quadrat. Compute:
- **Density** = total individuals / total quadrats studied.
- **Frequency (%)** = quadrats in which species occurs / total quadrats × 100.
- **Abundance** = total individuals / number of quadrats in which it occurs.
Raunkiaer's frequency classes A–E (0–20, 21–40 … 81–100%).

steps.title: Solved example: quadrats
steps.body:
10 quadrats; species X counts: 4, 0, 3, 5, 0, 2, 6, 0, 4, 6 (total 30; present in 7 quadrats).
Density = 30/10 = **3.0 per m²**; frequency = 7/10 × 100 = **70%**; abundance = 30/7 = **4.29**.

steps.title: Lincoln–Petersen index
steps.body: Capture M animals, mark harmlessly, release; after mixing, capture C animals, of which R are marked. **N = (M × C)/R**. Assumptions: closed population, marks not lost, marking does not affect survival or catchability, random mixing.

steps.title: Solved example: snails
steps.body: M = 50 marked; second sample C = 60, of which R = 15 marked. N = 50 × 60/15 = **200 snails**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dividing by total quadrats when computing abundance.
- Placing quadrats only where plants look interesting (biased).
- Using a toxic or conspicuous mark that changes predation.

activity.prompt: Mark–recapture: 40 fish marked and released; later 75 caught, 12 of them marked. Estimate the population size.

quiz.q: Species present in 4 of 20 quadrats has frequency
quiz.why: 4 ÷ 20 × 100 = 20 per cent of quadrats.

quiz.q: Abundance is total individuals divided by
quiz.why: Abundance describes how many individuals occur where the species is present.

options: A closed population with random mixing
quiz.why: Without closure and mixing, the marked proportion would not represent the whole population.

lessons.title: Lab: Dissolved oxygen and Hardy–Weinberg simulation

scenes.text: A water sample turns brown with Winkler's reagents and is titrated to a colourless end point.
Back in class, a bag of red and white beads becomes a population of alleles.

steps.title: Winkler's method (DO)
steps.body:
Fill a BOD bottle without air bubbles; add **MnSO₄** and **alkaline KI–azide**; Mn(OH)₂ is oxidised by dissolved O₂ to a brown precipitate; add **conc. H₂SO₄** to dissolve it, liberating I₂ equivalent to O₂; titrate a measured volume against **sodium thiosulphate** using **starch** indicator (blue → colourless).
For 0.025 N thiosulphate and 200 mL sample: **DO (mg/L) = mL of titrant used** (since 0.025 × 8 × 1,000/200 = 1).

steps.title: Solved example: DO
steps.body: General formula: DO (mg/L) = (V_titrant × N × 8 × 1,000)/V_sample. With V = 6.2 mL, N = 0.025, sample 200 mL: 6.2 × 0.025 × 8,000/200 = **6.2 mg/L** (healthy for most fish; below about 4 mg/L indicates stress). **BOD** = DO initial − DO after 5 days at 20 °C.

steps.title: Hardy–Weinberg bead simulation
steps.body: Put 60 red (A) and 40 white (a) beads in a bag (p = 0.6, q = 0.4). Draw two beads at random (with replacement) to form a genotype; record 100 'offspring'. Expected: AA 36, Aa 48, aa 16. Repeat with a small sample (e.g. 10 offspring) to show **genetic drift**; remove white beads to simulate **selection**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trapping air bubbles in the BOD bottle (raises DO).
- Adding starch too early (should be near the pale-yellow end point).
- Drawing beads without replacement in a small bag.

steps.title: Viva quick answers
steps.body:
- Why is the energy pyramid always upright? Energy is lost as heat at each transfer.
- Why do carriers of recessive alleles outnumber affected individuals? 2pq ≫ q² when q is small.
- Why are islands good for studying speciation? Isolation reduces gene flow.
- What is a keystone species? One whose impact on the community is disproportionate to its abundance.
- Why does eutrophication kill fish? Algal decay by bacteria depletes oxygen.

Zoology non-chordates syllabus: protists, sponges, cnidarians, ctenophores, flatworms, roundworms, annelids, arthropods, molluscs, echinoderms and hemichordates — organisation, type studies, life cycles, parasitology and evolutionary trends, with practicals and exam practice. courses.title: Unit 1 · Protista, Porifera, Cnidaria and Ctenophora
courses.summary: Basis of animal classification, protist locomotion, nutrition and reproduction with Paramecium and Plasmodium, the sponge body plan and canal systems, cnidarian polymorphism and metagenesis (Obelia), coral reefs and the comb jellies.
outcomes: Use symmetry, germ layers, coelom and segmentation to classify animals
Describe locomotion, nutrition and conjugation in Paramecium
Explain the life cycle of Plasmodium vivax and its link to malaria control
Compare ascon, sycon and leucon canal systems
Explain polymorphism and metagenesis in Obelia and the formation of coral reefs

scenes.text: In a drop of pond water a slipper-shaped Paramecium swims, eats, excretes and even exchanges genes — all inside one cell.
To place it and every other animal, zoologists ask a fixed set of questions about body plan.

steps.title: Criteria of classification
steps.body:
- **Level of organisation**: protoplasmic (protists), cellular (sponges), tissue (cnidarians), organ-system (flatworms onward).
- **Symmetry**: asymmetry (most sponges), radial (cnidarians), biradial (ctenophores), bilateral (Platyhelminthes onward; adult echinoderms secondarily pentaradial).
- **Germ layers**: diploblastic (ectoderm + endoderm, mesoglea between: Cnidaria, Ctenophora) vs triploblastic.
- **Body cavity**: acoelomate (flatworms), pseudocoelomate (nematodes — cavity from blastocoel, not lined by mesoderm on both sides), coelomate (annelids onward).
- **Coelom origin**: schizocoelous (split in mesoderm: annelids, arthropods, molluscs) vs enterocoelous (from gut pouches: echinoderms, hemichordates, chordates).
- **Blastopore fate**: protostomes (mouth) vs deuterostomes (anus).
- **Segmentation (metamerism)**: annelids, arthropods.

steps.title: Protista: locomotion and nutrition
steps.body: Locomotory organelles: **pseudopodia** (Amoeba — lobopodia; sol–gel conversion of cytoplasm), **flagella** (Euglena, Trypanosoma; 9+2 axoneme), **cilia** (Paramecium; same 9+2 structure, shorter and numerous, beating in metachronal rhythm). Nutrition: holozoic (Amoeba, Paramecium — food vacuoles), holophytic (Euglena in light), saprozoic, and parasitic (Plasmodium, Entamoeba, Trypanosoma, Leishmania).

steps.title: Type study: Paramecium caudatum
steps.body: Pellicle with cilia; **oral groove → cytostome → cytopharynx**; food vacuoles circulate (cyclosis) and digest food; undigested matter leaves at the **cytopyge**. Two **contractile vacuoles** with radiating canals expel excess water (osmoregulation in fresh water). **Trichocysts** for defence. Nuclear dimorphism: a **macronucleus** (vegetative functions) and a **micronucleus** (genetic). Asexual: transverse binary fission. Sexual: **conjugation** — two cells pair at oral surfaces, macronuclei degenerate, each micronucleus divides meiotically to four, three degenerate, the survivor divides into a stationary and a migratory pronucleus, migratory pronuclei are exchanged and fuse to form a synkaryon; after separation, divisions restore the nuclear apparatus, each exconjugant giving four daughter cells.

steps.title: Worked example: counting conjugation products
steps.body: Question: from one conjugating pair, how many daughter Paramecia result? Each exconjugant's synkaryon divides three times (8 nuclei: 4 become macronuclei, 3 micronuclei degenerate, 1 remains), then two cell divisions distribute them, giving 4 cells per exconjugant. Answer: **2 × 4 = 8 daughter cells**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling conjugation reproduction in the sense of increasing number at the moment of pairing — it is genetic recombination; the number rises only in the later fissions.
- Saying the macronucleus is exchanged: only migratory micronuclear pronuclei move.
- Confusing pseudocoelom (blastocoel remnant) with a true coelom.

activity.prompt: Match the protist to its locomotory organelle

quiz.why: In nematodes the body cavity is a persistent blastocoel not fully lined by mesoderm, so it is a pseudocoel.
Deuterostomes such as echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates form the coelom from outpocketings of the archenteron.

quiz.q: During conjugation in Paramecium the macronucleus
quiz.why: The old macronucleus breaks down and a new one is formed later from products of the synkaryon.

quiz.q: Contractile vacuoles in Paramecium mainly function in
quiz.why: They pump out the excess water that enters the hypertonic cell from fresh water.

lessons.title: Lab: Life cycle of Plasmodium vivax

scenes.text: A female Anopheles mosquito bites at dusk and injects thousands of sporozoites.
Some days later the patient has chills and fever every 48 hours — the rhythm of the parasite's blood cycle.

steps.title: Hosts
steps.body: **Definitive host**: female Anopheles mosquito (sexual phase, sporogony). **Intermediate host**: human (asexual phase, schizogony). Ross (1897) demonstrated the mosquito stage of malaria parasites.

steps.title: Phase in humans
steps.body:
1. **Sporozoites** injected with saliva reach the liver within about an hour.
2. **Pre-erythrocytic schizogony** in hepatocytes → thousands of **merozoites** (cryptozoites).
3. In P. vivax some sporozoites stay dormant as **hypnozoites**, causing relapses months later.
4. **Erythrocytic schizogony**: merozoite enters RBC → ring stage (trophozoite) → amoeboid trophozoite → schizont → RBC bursts releasing merozoites and **haemozoin** (malaria pigment) and toxins; synchronous bursting every **48 h** causes tertian fever. Schüffner's dots appear in infected RBCs.
5. Some merozoites become **gametocytes** (micro- and macrogametocytes), which do not develop further in humans.

steps.title: Phase in the mosquito
steps.body: Gametocytes taken up in a blood meal → in the midgut, **exflagellation** of the microgametocyte forms microgametes → fertilisation → **zygote → ookinete** (motile) → penetrates gut wall → **oocyst** on the outer gut wall → **sporogony** forms thousands of sporozoites → oocyst bursts, sporozoites migrate to the **salivary glands**. The mosquito cycle takes roughly 10–20 days depending on temperature.

steps.title: Control
steps.body: Breaking the cycle: long-lasting insecticidal nets and indoor residual spraying (vector), removing breeding water and larvivorous fish such as Gambusia (larvae), prompt diagnosis by blood smear or rapid test and treatment (blood stages), and primaquine-class drugs against hypnozoites in P. vivax.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling humans the definitive host: sexual fusion occurs in the mosquito.
- Saying male mosquitoes transmit malaria — only females take blood meals.
- Forgetting hypnozoites when explaining relapse in vivax malaria.

quiz.why: Sexual reproduction (gamete fusion) of Plasmodium takes place in the female Anopheles, which makes it the definitive host.

quiz.why: Dormant hypnozoites in the liver can reactivate weeks or months later and restart the blood cycle.

story.title: An animal that is a water pump

scenes.text: A sponge pumps a volume of water equal to its own body many times an hour through tiny pores.
Its body plan is built around that current: in through ostia, out through the osculum.

steps.title: General features
steps.body: Cellular grade, mostly asymmetrical, sessile, mostly marine. Body wall: outer **pinacoderm** (pinacocytes, with porocytes forming ostia), inner **choanoderm** of flagellated collar cells (**choanocytes**) that drive water and trap food, and between them a gelatinous **mesohyl** with amoebocytes, archaeocytes (totipotent) and scleroblasts. Digestion is intracellular. Skeleton: calcareous spicules (Calcarea), siliceous spicules (Hexactinellida, e.g. Euplectella), siliceous spicules and/or spongin fibres (Demospongiae, e.g. Spongilla, bath sponge Spongia).

steps.title: Canal systems
steps.body:
- **Ascon** (Leucosolenia): ostia → spongocoel lined by choanocytes → osculum. Simplest; limits size.
- **Sycon** (Scypha/Sycon): ostia → incurrent canals → prosopyles → radial canals (choanocytes) → apopyles → spongocoel → osculum.
- **Leucon** (Spongilla): ostia → incurrent canals → prosopyles → small flagellated chambers → apopyles → excurrent canals → osculum; spongocoel reduced. Most efficient, allows large size; most sponges are leuconoid.

steps.title: Reproduction
steps.body: Asexual: budding, fragmentation and **gemmules** (in freshwater Spongilla: archaeocytes in a resistant spicule-reinforced coat that survives drought and winter). Sexual: mostly hermaphrodite; sperm carried in water currents; larvae are **amphiblastula** (Sycon) or **parenchymula** (many demosponges). Sycon amphiblastula shows **inversion** of flagellated cells during development.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: Draw the three canal systems side by side with arrows for water flow and shade the choanocyte-lined part; the shift of choanocytes from the spongocoel (ascon) to radial canals (sycon) to chambers (leucon) is the key point.

quiz.q: The most efficient canal system is
quiz.why: Many small flagellated chambers give leucon sponges the greatest choanocyte surface and pumping capacity.
