quiz.why: The osculum is the large exhalant opening at the top through which the current exits.

lessons.title: Cnidaria and Ctenophora: polymorphism, metagenesis, corals

scenes.text: A branching Obelia colony on seaweed looks like a tiny plant, but it is a colony of animals with different jobs.
Small medusae bud off and swim away to reproduce sexually — two body forms, one life cycle.

steps.title: Characters of Cnidaria
steps.body: Tissue grade, diploblastic, radial symmetry, gastrovascular cavity with a single opening (mouth), **cnidocytes** containing **nematocysts** for prey capture and defence, nerve net, two body forms — sessile **polyp** and free-swimming **medusa**. Classes: **Hydrozoa** (Hydra, Obelia, Physalia), **Scyphozoa** (Aurelia — medusa dominant), **Anthozoa** (sea anemone Metridium, corals — polyp only).

steps.title: Obelia: polymorphism and metagenesis
steps.body: The colony has **gastrozooids** (feeding polyps with hypostome and tentacles) and **gonozooids/blastostyles** inside a gonotheca that bud off **medusae**. The perisarc (chitinous) and coenosarc connect zooids. Medusae are gonochoric and produce gametes; the zygote forms a ciliated **planula larva** that settles and grows into a new polyp colony. This alternation of an asexual polyp generation with a sexual medusa generation, both diploid, is **metagenesis** (not true alternation of haploid and diploid generations as in plants).

steps.title: Corals and coral reefs
steps.body: Reef-building corals are anthozoan polyps that secrete a CaCO₃ exoskeleton and host symbiotic **zooxanthellae** (dinoflagellates) supplying photosynthate. Reefs form in warm (about 20–28 °C), clear, shallow, sunlit tropical seas. Types (Darwin's classification): **fringing**, **barrier** and **atolls**; Darwin's subsidence theory explains the sequence fringing → barrier → atoll around a sinking volcanic island. Indian reefs: Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kachchh, Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep (atolls). Bleaching = loss of zooxanthellae under heat stress.

steps.title: Ctenophora
steps.body: Comb jellies (Pleurobrachia): biradial symmetry, eight rows of **comb plates** of fused cilia for locomotion, **colloblasts** (adhesive cells) instead of nematocysts, aboral statocyst. Lack polymorphism and are mostly bioluminescent.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing that Hydra shows metagenesis — it has no medusa stage.
- Calling colloblasts stinging cells.
- Treating zooxanthellae as parasites; the relationship is mutualistic.

lessons.title: Lab: Life cycle of Fasciola hepatica

story.title: A fluke in the sheep's liver

scenes.text: Sheep grazing on wet pasture fall ill with 'liver rot'; their bile ducts hold leaf-shaped flukes.
The missing link is a small pond snail that releases tailed larvae onto the grass.

steps.title: Platyhelminthes: key characters
steps.body: Triploblastic, acoelomate (spaces filled with **parenchyma**), bilateral, dorsoventrally flattened, incomplete gut or none, excretion by **flame cells (protonephridia)**, mostly hermaphrodite. Classes: Turbellaria (free-living Dugesia/planaria), Trematoda (flukes: Fasciola, Schistosoma), Cestoda (tapeworms: Taenia, Echinococcus).

steps.title: Fasciola life cycle
steps.body: Adult in bile ducts of sheep/cattle (definitive host) → eggs pass out with faeces → in water an egg hatches a ciliated **miracidium** → penetrates the snail **Lymnaea** (intermediate host) → **sporocyst** → **rediae** (often two generations) → **cercariae** (tailed) leave the snail → encyst on vegetation as **metacercariae** (infective stage) → swallowed by sheep → excyst in the duodenum → cross the gut wall, migrate through the liver to the bile ducts. Larval multiplication in the snail (**polyembryony**) greatly amplifies numbers.

steps.title: Worked example: amplification
steps.body: If one miracidium yields 1 sporocyst producing 8 rediae, each redia producing 20 daughter rediae and each daughter redia 15 cercariae: cercariae = 1 × 8 × 20 × 15 = **2,400** from one egg. (Illustrative numbers.) This explains why a few eggs can contaminate a whole pasture.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Naming the cercaria as the infective stage for sheep — it is the encysted metacercaria.
- Forgetting that Lymnaea is the only intermediate host in Fasciola (Taenia needs no snail).
- Writing 'coelom' for the parenchyma-filled space of flatworms.

activity.prompt: Order the larval stages of Fasciola hepatica

quiz.q: The intermediate host of Fasciola hepatica is
quiz.why: Larval multiplication of the liver fluke takes place inside the freshwater snail Lymnaea.

quiz.why: Sheep are infected by swallowing metacercariae encysted on grass.
Flame cells are protonephridial cells whose beating cilia drive fluid into excretory canals.

scenes.text: A man eats undercooked 'measly' pork and months later passes tapeworm segments.
In the same village, children playing in soil swallow roundworm eggs.

steps.title: Taenia solium (pork tapeworm)
steps.body: Body: **scolex** with four suckers and a rostellum with two rows of hooks, a neck (zone of proliferation), and **strobila** of proglottids (immature, mature with both sexes, gravid with branched uterus full of eggs). No gut — absorbs food through the tegument. Life cycle: gravid proglottids pass in human faeces → pig eats eggs (**onchosphere/hexacanth embryo** with six hooks) → embryo reaches muscles → **cysticercus** (bladder worm) → human eats raw/undercooked pork → scolex evaginates and attaches in the intestine. Humans swallowing eggs directly can develop **cysticercosis**, including neurocysticercosis (a common cause of acquired epilepsy in endemic areas).

steps.title: Ascaris lumbricoides
steps.body: Nematoda: pseudocoelomate, unsegmented, complete gut, sexes separate (male smaller with curved tail and two penial spicules), body covered by a tough **cuticle**. Single host (monogenetic). Eggs passed in faeces need about 2–3 weeks in soil to embryonate; the egg containing the **second-stage (rhabditiform) larva** is infective. Swallowed eggs hatch in the intestine → larvae penetrate the gut → liver → heart → lungs (moult; may cause Loeffler's pneumonitis) → up the trachea and swallowed → mature in the small intestine.

steps.title: Parasitic adaptations
steps.body:
- Attachment organs: suckers, hooks (Taenia), oral suckers (Fasciola).
- Thick cuticle/tegument resisting host enzymes; anti-enzymes.
- Reduced or absent gut and sense organs; absorption through body surface.
- Anaerobic respiration (glycolysis) in the low-oxygen gut.
- Enormous fecundity (a female Ascaris lays on the order of 200,000 eggs per day) and larval multiplication.
- Hermaphroditism and self-fertilisation (tapeworms); resistant egg shells; intermediate hosts for dispersal.

steps.title: Worked example: egg output
steps.body: A female Ascaris laying 200,000 eggs/day over a 12-month life produces about 200,000 × 365 = **7.3 × 10⁷ eggs**. This is why sanitation (not just treatment) is the main control measure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying pork causes cysticercosis in humans — pork causes intestinal taeniasis; eggs (faecal–oral) cause cysticercosis.
- Calling Ascaris digenetic: it has only one host.
- Forgetting the lung migration of Ascaris larvae.

scenes.text: Cut an earthworm crosswise anywhere in the middle and the slices look alike: septa, nephridia, nerve ganglia, blood vessels.
Each segment's fluid-filled coelom acts as its own hydrostatic skeleton.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body: Triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical, **schizocoelous coelomates**, **metamerically segmented** (internal septa match external annuli), closed circulatory system, excretion by **nephridia**, ventral double nerve cord with segmental ganglia, setae (chaetae) of chitin for locomotion. Development: protostome with spiral cleavage; marine forms have a **trochophore** larva.

steps.title: Classes
steps.body:
- **Polychaeta**: marine, parapodia with many setae, distinct head with tentacles, sexes separate, trochophore larva (Nereis, Aphrodite, Chaetopterus).
- **Oligochaeta**: few setae, no parapodia, hermaphrodite, clitellum and cocoon, direct development (Pheretima, Lumbricus, Tubifex).
- **Hirudinea**: leeches, fixed number of segments (33–34 in typical accounts), anterior and posterior suckers, no setae (most), coelom reduced by botryoidal tissue, hermaphrodite (Hirudinaria, Hirudo).

steps.title: Significance of metamerism and coelom
steps.body: Segmented coelom compartments allow localised changes in shape: contraction of circular muscle lengthens a segment, longitudinal muscle shortens and widens it, producing **peristaltic burrowing**. A coelom separates gut from body wall so each can move independently, provides space for organs and a fluid for transport. Metamerism also gives redundancy — damage is localised.

steps.title: Exam tip
steps.body: When asked 'metamerism in annelids', mention: true (homonomous) metamerism, origin via teloblastic growth from a posterior growth zone, segmental organs (nephridia, ganglia, setae), and locomotory advantage.

steps.title: Pheretima: external features
steps.body: About 100–120 segments; prostomium overhangs the mouth; **clitellum** in segments 14–16; one female genital pore mid-ventral on segment 14; a pair of male genital pores on segment 18; four pairs of spermathecal pores between segments 5/6 to 8/9; S-shaped setae in a ring in each segment except the first, last and clitellum.

steps.title: Internal organisation
steps.body:
- **Digestive**: mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → muscular **gizzard** (segment 8–9) grinds soil → stomach → intestine with **typhlosole** (from segment 26, increases absorptive area) and a pair of intestinal caeca on segment 26.
- **Circulation**: closed; dorsal vessel (blood forward), ventral vessel (backward), lateral hearts in segments 7 and 9 and lateral oesophageal hearts in 12–13; haemoglobin dissolved in plasma.
- **Excretion**: three kinds of **nephridia** — septal (enteronephric, open into intestine), integumentary (exonephric, open on skin), pharyngeal tufts (open into gut); excreting ammonia and urea; enteronephric habit conserves water.
- **Reproduction**: hermaphrodite but **protandrous** with cross-fertilisation; testes in segments 10–11; ovaries in segment 13; sperm exchanged during copulation and stored in spermathecae; cocoon formed by the clitellum; direct development.

steps.title: Hirudinaria: feeding adaptations
steps.body: Tri-radiate jaws make a Y-shaped incision; salivary **hirudin** (anticoagulant) keeps blood fluid; the crop with lateral caeca stores a large meal for months; anterior sucker for feeding, posterior for attachment. The coelom is reduced to canals by **botryoidal tissue**; nephridia number 17 pairs in Hirudinaria.

steps.title: Economic importance
steps.body: Earthworms aerate soil, improve drainage, mix organic matter and cast nutrient-rich soil; **vermicomposting** (often with Eisenia fetida or Perionyx excavatus) converts organic waste into compost. Medicinal leeches are still used in reconstructive surgery to relieve venous congestion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the female pore on segment 18: male pores are on 18, female on 14.
- Saying earthworms have lungs or gills — exchange is cutaneous through moist skin.
- Forgetting that earthworms are hermaphrodite yet cross-fertilise.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Arthropoda
courses.summary: Arthropod characters and classification, the cockroach (Periplaneta) as type study, insect mouthparts, respiration by tracheae, gills and book lungs, metamorphosis and its hormonal control, social insects and the prawn.
outcomes: Classify arthropods into major classes with examples
Describe the anatomy of Periplaneta americana
Compare insect mouthparts in relation to feeding
Explain tracheal, gill and book-lung respiration
Explain metamorphosis and its control by ecdysone and juvenile hormone

scenes.text: More than three-quarters of all described animal species are arthropods, most of them insects.
Their secret: a jointed, chitinous exoskeleton that can be specialised for almost any job.

steps.title: General characters
steps.body: Triploblastic, bilateral, metamerically segmented with **tagmatisation** (segments grouped into head, thorax, abdomen or cephalothorax), **jointed appendages**, chitinous **exoskeleton** shed by **moulting (ecdysis)**, coelom reduced and body cavity a blood-filled **haemocoel** with an **open circulatory system** and dorsal tubular heart, striated muscles in bundles, compound eyes in many.

steps.title: Classes (traditional scheme)
steps.body:
- **Crustacea**: two pairs of antennae, gills, mostly aquatic (Palaemon prawn, crab, Daphnia, barnacles).
- **Insecta (Hexapoda)**: head–thorax–abdomen, one pair of antennae, three pairs of legs, usually two pairs of wings, tracheae (cockroach, honeybee, mosquito).
- **Arachnida**: cephalothorax + abdomen, no antennae, four pairs of legs, chelicerae, book lungs or tracheae (scorpion, spider, ticks, mites).
- **Chilopoda**: centipedes, one pair of legs per segment, poison claws.
- **Diplopoda**: millipedes, two pairs of legs per apparent segment (diplosegments).
- **Merostomata**: Limulus (horseshoe crab), book gills — a 'living fossil'.
- Peripatus (Onychophora), often studied alongside, shows annelid + arthropod characters.

steps.title: Why moult?
steps.body: The cuticle cannot grow once hardened (sclerotised), so growth happens in steps: the old cuticle is loosened (apolysis), a new soft cuticle forms beneath, the old one splits and is shed, and the animal expands before the new cuticle hardens.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting spiders as insects (four pairs of legs, no antennae).
- Saying arthropods have a closed circulation.
- Writing that the haemocoel is a true coelom.

quiz.why: Blood fills a cavity called the haemocoel as part of the open circulatory system.

scenes.text: Survivor of 300 million years of insect history, the cockroach is the standard dissection for insect anatomy.
Pinned in a wax tray under water, its organs come into view one system at a time.

steps.title: External features
steps.body: Body: head (hypognathous, with compound eyes, filiform antennae, mandibulate mouthparts), thorax (prothorax with pronotum, meso- and metathorax each with a pair of legs and wings: leathery forewings = **tegmina**, membranous hindwings), abdomen of 10 segments with **anal cerci** in both sexes and **anal styles** only in males. Legs: coxa, trochanter, femur, tibia, tarsus (5 segments) with claws and arolium.

steps.title: Internal systems
steps.body:
- **Digestive**: mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → **crop** (storage) → **gizzard/proventriculus** with six chitinous teeth → midgut with 6–8 **hepatic caeca** → hindgut (ileum, colon, rectum). Malpighian tubules open at the midgut–hindgut junction.
- **Excretion**: **Malpighian tubules** (uric acid — uricotelic), also fat body, nephrocytes and urate cells.
- **Circulation**: open; 13-chambered dorsal heart with ostia; colourless haemolymph.
- **Respiration**: tracheae opening by **10 pairs of spiracles** (2 thoracic, 8 abdominal).
- **Nervous**: supra-oesophageal ganglion (brain), sub-oesophageal ganglion, ventral double nerve cord with 3 thoracic and 6 abdominal ganglia.
- **Reproduction**: male — testes in abdominal segments 4–6, mushroom gland, phallomeres; female — ovaries with 8 ovarioles each, spermathecae, colleterial glands forming the **ootheca** (about 16 eggs in typical accounts). Development **paurometabolous** via nymphs.

steps.title: Practical: temporary mount of mouthparts
steps.body: Remove the head, boil briefly in 10% KOH to soften, then separate labrum, mandibles, maxillae, labium and hypopharynx with needles; mount in glycerine under a coverslip and label each part.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing anal styles in females — they occur only in males.
- Saying Malpighian tubules open into the rectum.
- Calling cockroach blood red — it lacks haemoglobin.

quiz.why: There are two thoracic and eight abdominal pairs, ten pairs in total.
Anal styles are a male character, while anal cerci occur in both sexes.
Its dorsal tubular heart is divided into 13 segmental chambers with ostia.
Nymphs resemble adults and gain wings gradually through moults, which is incomplete metamorphosis.

scenes.text: A mosquito pierces skin with needle-like stylets; a housefly mops up liquid with a sponge; a butterfly uncoils a proboscis.
Each also breathes through tubes, gills or lungs that suit its habitat.

steps.title: Types of insect mouthparts
steps.body:
- **Biting and chewing** (cockroach, grasshopper): labrum, paired mandibles, paired maxillae, labium, hypopharynx — the basic type.
- **Piercing and sucking** (female Anopheles/Culex): labrum-epipharynx, two mandibles, two maxillae and hypopharynx form six stylets in a sheath made by the labium (labella at tip).
- **Sponging** (housefly): labium forms a proboscis ending in **labella** with pseudotracheae; mandibles absent.
- **Siphoning** (butterfly): galeae of maxillae form a coiled **proboscis**.
- **Chewing and lapping** (honeybee): mandibles for wax work + glossa (tongue) for nectar.

steps.title: Respiration
steps.body:
- **Tracheal system** (insects, many arachnids): spiracles → tracheae (with spiral taenidia preventing collapse) → fine **tracheoles** ending in tissues; oxygen diffuses directly to cells, so blood plays little role in O₂ transport. Ventilation by abdominal pumping.
- **Gills** (crustaceans): in prawn, phyllobranchiate gills in a branchial chamber under the carapace; water current driven by the **scaphognathite** (baler) of the second maxilla.
- **Book lungs** (scorpion, spiders): stacked lamellae like pages; scorpion has four pairs.
- **Book gills** (Limulus).

steps.title: Why insects are small
steps.body: Diffusion through tracheoles is effective only over short distances; this is one constraint on maximum insect size. Higher atmospheric O₂ in the Carboniferous coincides with giant dragonfly-like insects (wingspans around 70 cm).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the housefly bites: its mouthparts are sponging.
- Calling taenidia muscles; they are cuticular spiral thickenings.
- Saying insect blood transports most oxygen.

lessons.title: Metamorphosis, social insects and economic importance

scenes.text: A silkworm larva eats mulberry leaves for weeks, then spins a cocoon.
Inside, its body is rebuilt into a moth — controlled by two hormones in a delicate balance.

steps.title: Types of development
steps.body:
- **Ametabolous**: no metamorphosis, young like adult (silverfish Lepisma).
- **Hemimetabolous / paurometabolous** (incomplete): egg → **nymph** → adult (cockroach, grasshopper, bugs); aquatic nymphs called **naiads** (dragonfly).
- **Holometabolous** (complete): egg → **larva** → **pupa** → adult (butterfly, beetle, housefly, honeybee, mosquito).

steps.title: Hormonal control
steps.body: Brain **neurosecretory cells** release **PTTH** (prothoracicotropic hormone) via the corpora cardiaca → stimulates the **prothoracic glands** to secrete **ecdysone** (converted to 20-hydroxyecdysone), which triggers moulting. **Juvenile hormone (JH)** from the **corpora allata** decides the type of moult: high JH → larva-to-larva moult; low JH → larva-to-pupa; JH absent → pupa-to-adult. JH analogues (e.g. methoprene) are used as insect growth regulators in pest control.

steps.title: Social organisation in honeybee
steps.body: Colony of one **queen** (fertile female, develops from fertilised egg fed royal jelly throughout), thousands of **workers** (sterile females; nursing, wax making, foraging, guarding) and seasonal **drones** (males, from unfertilised eggs — **haplodiploidy**, arrhenotokous parthenogenesis). Communication by **round dance** (food near, under ~50–100 m) and **waggle dance** (direction relative to the sun, distance by duration of the waggle run) — Karl von Frisch. Termites have a caste system too (king, queen, workers, soldiers).

steps.title: Economic importance
steps.body: Beneficial: honey and wax (Apis), silk (Bombyx mori — mulberry; tasar, eri and muga silks from other moths), lac (Kerria lacca), pollination, prawn/shrimp fisheries. Harmful: crop pests (locust, rice stem borer, cotton bollworm), stored-grain pests, disease vectors (Anopheles — malaria, Aedes — dengue and chikungunya, Culex — filariasis, sandfly Phlebotomus — kala-azar, housefly — mechanical carrier).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing JH and ecdysone: ecdysone causes moulting; JH keeps it juvenile.
- Saying drones come from fertilised eggs.
- Calling the cockroach holometabolous.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Mollusca, Echinodermata and Hemichordata
courses.summary: Molluscan body plan, Pila globosa, torsion in gastropods, pearl formation, the echinoderm water vascular system and larvae, and Balanoglossus with its chordate affinities.
outcomes: Describe the molluscan body plan and classes
Explain torsion and its consequences
Describe the water vascular system of Asterias
Identify echinoderm larvae
Evaluate the affinities of Hemichordata

lessons.title: Mollusca and the type Pila globosa

story.title: The apple snail of Indian ponds

scenes.text: Pila globosa can breathe in water with a gill and in air with a lung — and survive drought sealed in mud.
Its distant cousin, the octopus, has a brain big enough to learn mazes.

steps.title: Molluscan body plan
steps.body: Soft unsegmented body (schizocoelous; coelom reduced to pericardium, gonad and kidney cavities), with **head**, ventral muscular **foot**, dorsal **visceral mass**, and a **mantle** (pallium) that secretes the CaCO₃ **shell** and encloses a mantle cavity with **ctenidia** (gills). Rasping **radula** (absent in bivalves). Open circulation (closed in cephalopods), haemocyanin. Trochophore and/or **veliger** larva.

steps.title: Classes
steps.body:
- **Monoplacophora** (Neopilina — serially repeated organs, 'living fossil').
- **Polyplacophora** (chitons; eight shell plates).
- **Aplacophora** (worm-like, no shell).
- **Gastropoda** (Pila, Aplysia, Doris, Limax; torsion).
- **Scaphopoda** (Dentalium, tusk shell).
- **Bivalvia/Pelecypoda** (Lamellidens, Mytilus, Pinctada pearl oyster, Teredo shipworm; no head or radula).
- **Cephalopoda** (Sepia, Loligo, Octopus, Nautilus; foot modified into arms and funnel).

steps.title: Pila globosa
steps.body: Shell dextral, spirally coiled with operculum. Mantle cavity divided into **branchial chamber** (with ctenidium) and **pulmonary sac** (lung); left **nuchal lobe** forms a siphon to take air at the surface — amphibious respiration. Radula with teeth in rows (taenioglossan formula 2·1·1·1·2). Kidney excretes mostly uric acid during aestivation. Sexes separate; eggs laid on land above water.

steps.title: Pearl formation
steps.body: When a foreign particle or parasite lodges between the mantle and shell, mantle epithelial cells surround it as a **pearl sac** and deposit concentric layers of **nacre** (aragonite + conchiolin). Pinctada fucata (Gulf of Mannar) is the Indian marine pearl oyster; culturing involves inserting a nucleus with a piece of donor mantle tissue.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying bivalves have a radula.
- Calling the molluscan shell chitinous: it is mostly calcium carbonate.
- Forgetting cephalopods have a closed circulation.

scenes.text: Early in development, a gastropod veliger larva twists its visceral mass through 180° in a few minutes to hours.
Why would an animal put its anus over its head?

steps.title: Definition and mechanism
steps.body: **Torsion** is the anticlockwise rotation (viewed from above) of the visceral mass and mantle through **180°** relative to the head and foot in the veliger larva. It is brought about by asymmetrical contraction of the larval **retractor muscle** (first 90°) and differential growth (next 90°). It is different from **coiling** (spiral growth of shell and visceral mass), which is a separate event.

steps.title: Consequences
steps.body:
- Mantle cavity, anus, gills, kidney openings move from posterior to **anterior**, above the head.
- Visceral nerve loop twisted into a figure 8 — **streptoneury** (chiastoneury), as in Prosobranchia such as Pila.
- Original left organs become right and vice versa; often loss of one gill, kidney and auricle (organs of the post-torsional right side reduced).
- **Detorsion** in Opisthobranchia (Aplysia) and Pulmonata partly reverses this, giving **euthyneury** (untwisted).

steps.title: Proposed advantages
steps.body:
- Larva can withdraw the head into the shell first (Garstang's protective hypothesis).
- Anterior mantle cavity receives clean water and its osphradium tests water ahead.
- Disadvantage: waste discharged over the head — offset by water currents and slit/hole shells (Haliotis).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating torsion and coiling as the same.
- Saying torsion occurs in the adult.
- Saying detorsion occurs in prosobranchs.

quiz.why: The visceral hump and mantle turn 180° relative to the head and foot.

quiz.why: Twisting of the visceral connectives by torsion produces streptoneury.

lessons.title: Echinodermata: water vascular system and larvae

scenes.text: A starfish glides over rocks on hundreds of tube feet driven by a hydraulic system.
It can pull a mussel's shell open just enough to slip its stomach inside.

steps.title: Characters
steps.body: Exclusively marine, enterocoelous deuterostomes; bilateral larvae but **pentaradial** adults; endoskeleton of calcareous **ossicles** with spines; unique **water vascular (ambulacral) system**; tube feet; no excretory organs; dermal branchiae (papulae) for gas exchange; pedicellariae. Classes: **Asteroidea** (Asterias), **Ophiuroidea** (brittle stars, Ophiothrix), **Echinoidea** (sea urchin Echinus, sand dollar), **Holothuroidea** (sea cucumber), **Crinoidea** (sea lily Antedon).

steps.title: Water vascular system of Asterias
steps.body: **Madreporite** (aboral sieve plate) → **stone canal** (calcified walls) → **ring canal** around the mouth with **Tiedemann's bodies** (9 in Asterias) and **Polian vesicles** (absent in Asterias but present in many others) → five **radial canals** along the arms → **lateral canals** with valves → **ampullae** + **tube feet (podia)**. Contraction of an ampulla with the valve closed forces fluid into the tube foot, extending it; longitudinal muscles retract it and the sucker grips. Functions: locomotion, attachment, food capture, gas exchange.

steps.title: Larvae
steps.body: Basic dipleurula type, then class-specific: **bipinnaria** and **brachiolaria** (Asteroidea), **ophiopluteus** (Ophiuroidea), **echinopluteus** (Echinoidea), **auricularia** (Holothuroidea), **doliolaria** (Crinoidea). Larval resemblance of auricularia to the **tornaria** of Balanoglossus supports the echinoderm–hemichordate–chordate link.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying echinoderms are radially symmetrical from origin: they are secondarily pentaradial, with bilateral larvae.
- Placing the madreporite on the oral surface (in starfish it is aboral).
- Forgetting that echinoderms are deuterostomes.

scenes.text: Buried in sandy shores, Balanoglossus leaves coiled castings like an earthworm.
Yet its gill slits and larva tie it to chordates and echinoderms.

steps.title: Structure of Balanoglossus
steps.body: Vermiform, marine, tubicolous body in three regions: **proboscis** (protocoel), **collar** (mesocoel), **trunk** (metacoel) — tricoelomate (archimeric) condition. Trunk shows branchiogenital, hepatic and abdominal regions. Paired **pharyngeal gill slits** (U-shaped). **Stomochord** (buccal diverticulum) once thought homologous to the notochord. A dorsal hollow collar nerve cord region. Glomerulus (proboscis gland) for excretion. Sexes separate; indirect development through a **tornaria** larva.

steps.title: Affinities
steps.body:
- **Chordate**: pharyngeal gill slits, dorsal tubular nerve cord in the collar, stomochord (now considered not homologous to the notochord). Hence earlier placed as a subphylum of Chordata.
- **Echinoderm**: tornaria resembles auricularia/bipinnaria; enterocoelous tripartite coelom; madreporic-type proboscis pore.
- **Annelid-like**: burrowing worm form (superficial).
Modern view: Hemichordata is a **separate phylum**, sister group of Echinodermata (together **Ambulacraria**), within the deuterostomes.

steps.title: Exam answer frame
steps.body: For 'Discuss the systematic position of Balanoglossus': (1) structure summary, (2) chordate features with critique of the stomochord, (3) echinoderm features especially tornaria, (4) conclusion — independent phylum close to Echinodermata.

scenes.text: Ten phyla, dozens of type studies — what do you actually need on one page?
Organise everything by body plan, and the details fall into place.

steps.title: Body-plan grid
steps.body:
- **Porifera**: cellular, asymmetric, no germ layers proper, choanocytes, canal system.
- **Cnidaria**: tissue, radial, diploblastic, cnidocytes, polyp/medusa.
- **Ctenophora**: biradial, comb plates, colloblasts.
- **Platyhelminthes**: organ grade, bilateral, triploblastic acoelomate, flame cells.
- **Nematoda**: pseudocoelomate, cuticle, complete gut, sexes separate.
- **Annelida**: schizocoelomate, metameric, nephridia, closed circulation.
- **Arthropoda**: jointed appendages, chitin, haemocoel, open circulation.
- **Mollusca**: mantle, shell, foot, radula, reduced coelom.
- **Echinodermata**: pentaradial adult, water vascular system, enterocoel.
- **Hemichordata**: tricoelomate, gill slits, stomochord, tornaria.

steps.title: Larvae at a glance
steps.body: Amphiblastula/parenchymula (sponges) · planula (cnidarians) · miracidium–sporocyst–redia–cercaria–metacercaria (Fasciola) · cysticercus (Taenia) · trochophore (polychaetes, many molluscs) · veliger (molluscs) · nauplius, zoea, mysis (crustaceans) · bipinnaria/brachiolaria, echinopluteus, ophiopluteus, auricularia, doliolaria (echinoderms) · tornaria (Balanoglossus).

steps.title: Respiratory and excretory organs
steps.body: Respiration: body surface (sponges to annelids), gills (crustaceans, molluscs), tracheae (insects), book lungs (scorpions), pulmonary sac (Pila), papulae and tube feet (starfish). Excretion: contractile vacuole (protists), flame cells (flatworms), renette/H-shaped canals (nematodes), nephridia (annelids), green glands (crustaceans), Malpighian tubules (insects, arachnids), organ of Bojanus/kidney (molluscs), none (echinoderms), glomerulus (Balanoglossus).

steps.title: Answer format for a spot
steps.body:
1. Name (genus, common name).

steps.title: Model spot: Euplectella
steps.body: Venus's flower basket. Phylum Porifera, Class Hexactinellida. scenes.text: An eyepiece scale has no units of its own — it must be calibrated against a stage micrometer.
Once calibrated, you can measure any cell under that same objective.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body:
A **stage micrometer** has a scale of known divisions (commonly 1 mm divided into 100 parts, so 1 stage division = 0.01 mm = 10 µm). The **ocular micrometer** in the eyepiece has arbitrary divisions. Superimpose both, find two coinciding lines, and compute:

**1 ocular division (OD) = (number of stage divisions × 10 µm) / (number of ocular divisions)**.

Calibration is valid only for that objective and microscope.

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Under 40× objective, 10 stage divisions coincide with 25 ocular divisions. 1 OD = (10 × 10)/25 = **4 µm**. A Paramecium spans 60 OD → length = 60 × 4 = **240 µm** (within the usual range of about 180–300 µm for P. caudatum).

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Under 10× objective, 30 stage divisions coincide with 20 ocular divisions. 1 OD = (30 × 10)/20 = **15 µm**. A Hydra tentacle segment spanning 42 OD = 42 × 15 = **630 µm** = 0.63 mm.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: Prepare a hay infusion culture; place a drop with a few cotton fibres (to slow ciliates) or a drop of methyl cellulose on a slide; cover; locate under low power; switch objective; record length in OD for at least five individuals and average.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a calibration from one objective for another.
- Forgetting to convert stage divisions to µm.
- Measuring a single individual rather than an average.

activity.prompt: Under 40×, 8 stage divisions (10 µm each) coincide with 20 ocular divisions. A Paramecium measures 55 ocular divisions. Its length in µm?

quiz.why: A 1 mm scale divided into 100 parts gives 0.01 mm, which equals 10 µm per division.

quiz.q: If 10 stage divisions = 50 ocular divisions, 1 OD =
quiz.why: 10 × 10 µm = 100 µm spread over 50 divisions gives 2 µm per ocular division.

lessons.title: Lab: Temporary mounts, viva and long-answer practice

scenes.text: The examiner hands you an earthworm and asks for a mount of its setae and nephridia.
Then comes the viva: 'Why is the earthworm called the farmer's friend?'

steps.title: Temporary mount protocol (general)
steps.body: Isolate the part → wash in water/normal saline → stain (e.g. borax carmine or eosin, 2–5 min) → wash off excess stain → dehydrate briefly if required → mount in glycerine → cover without air bubbles → seal/label → observe under low then high power and draw. Suitable mounts: earthworm setae, septal nephridia, ovary; cockroach mouthparts, salivary gland, trachea; prawn appendages; Spongilla spicules/gemmules; Obelia colony.

steps.title: Viva questions
steps.body:
- Why is Hydra called immortal? Interstitial cells continually renew tissues.
- What is the function of the clitellum? It secretes the cocoon.
- Why is Pila amphibious? It has both ctenidium and pulmonary sac.
- What is a living fossil? An organism that has changed little over long geological time, e.g. Limulus, Neopilina, Peripatus.
- What is haplodiploidy? Males haploid from unfertilised eggs, females diploid (honeybee).

uni-bsc-bio-plant-anatomy-embryology.title: Plant Anatomy & Embryology
uni-bsc-bio-plant-anatomy-embryology.description: Tissues, meristems, primary and secondary structure of root, stem and leaf, anomalous growth, and angiosperm embryology from anther and ovule to seed, with practical section work. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc. (Botany/Biology) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Tissues and meristems
courses.summary: Simple and complex permanent tissues, epidermal and secretory tissues, meristems and their classification, and theories of shoot and root apical organisation.
outcomes: Describe parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma with their functions
Explain the structure of xylem and phloem elements
Classify meristems by origin, position and function
Compare apical cell, histogen, tunica–corpus and quiescent centre theories
Describe stomata types and secretory structures

scenes.text: Pull a celery petiole and tough strings come away — collenchyma strands that let it bend without breaking.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Parenchyma
steps.body: Living, thin-walled (primary cellulose wall), isodiametric cells with intercellular spaces. Functions: storage, photosynthesis (chlorenchyma), buoyancy (aerenchyma in hydrophytes), healing and regeneration since they can dedifferentiate. Transfer cells have wall ingrowths for short-distance transport.

steps.title: Collenchyma
steps.body: Living cells with unevenly thickened primary walls rich in cellulose and pectin; gives flexible support to growing organs (hypodermis of dicot stems, petioles). Types: angular (thickening at corners, Cucurbita), lamellar/plate (tangential walls, Sambucus), lacunar (around intercellular spaces, Salvia), annular.

steps.title: Sclerenchyma
steps.body: Dead at maturity, with thick lignified secondary walls and simple pits. Fibres: long, tapering (jute, hemp, flax — bast fibres); sclereids: short — brachysclereids/stone cells (pear grit), macrosclereids (seed coat of legumes), osteosclereids (bone-shaped), astrosclereids (star-shaped, Nymphaea leaf), trichosclereids.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Collenchyma is living and lacks lignin; sclerenchyma is usually dead and lignified. Monocots generally lack collenchyma — their hypodermis is sclerenchymatous.

activity.prompt: Classify each feature.

items.text: Corner thickenings of cellulose and pectin

quiz.q: Grittiness of pear is due to
quiz.why: Clusters of short stone cells (brachysclereids) give pear flesh its gritty texture.

scenes.text: A teak tree moves water up through dead pipes and sugar down through living sieve tubes.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Xylem
steps.body: Four elements: tracheids (elongated, dead, lignified, tapering ends, pits; the only conducting cells in gymnosperms and pteridophytes), vessels (tubes of vessel members with perforation plates — simple or scalariform; typical of angiosperms), xylem fibres, and xylem parenchyma (only living element). Wall thickening patterns in order of development: annular, spiral (protoxylem), scalariform, reticulate, pitted (metaxylem). Exarch: protoxylem towards periphery (roots); endarch: protoxylem towards centre (stems); mesarch: in the middle (ferns).

steps.title: Phloem
steps.body: Sieve tube elements (living, enucleate at maturity, sieve plates with callose, P-protein), companion cells (nucleate, connected by plasmodesmata, regulate sieve tubes — angiosperms), phloem parenchyma (absent in most monocots) and phloem fibres (bast). Gymnosperms and pteridophytes have sieve cells with albuminous cells instead.

steps.title: Memory hook
steps.body: 'Exarch = exit-root': protoxylem lies outward in roots. Stems are endarch.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Xylem parenchyma is living; the rest of xylem elements are dead. Mature sieve tube elements have no nucleus but are alive.

activity.prompt: Living or dead at maturity?

quiz.why: Vessels are the main conducting elements of angiosperms (with a few exceptions like Gnetales).
Callose lines and can plug sieve plate pores of sieve tubes.
Protoxylem lies toward the periphery in roots.

quiz.q: Which thickening forms first in protoxylem?
quiz.why: Annular and spiral thickenings allow stretching during elongation, so form first.

scenes.text: Peeling a maize leaf shows dumb-bell guard cells; a bean leaf shows kidney-shaped ones.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Epidermis and stomata
steps.body: Usually one layer, covered by cuticle; bears trichomes and stomata. Guard cells are kidney-shaped in dicots and dumb-bell-shaped in grasses. Metcalfe and Chalk classification of dicot stomata by subsidiary cells: anomocytic (ranunculaceous — no distinct subsidiary cells, e.g. Ranunculus), anisocytic (cruciferous — three unequal, e.g. Brassica), paracytic (rubiaceous — two parallel to guard cells), diacytic (caryophyllaceous — two at right angles), actinocytic (radiating). Bulliform/motor cells in grass leaves help rolling.

steps.title: Secretory tissues
steps.body: External: glandular hairs, nectaries, hydathodes (guttation), osmophores. Internal: secretory cavities (lysigenous — Citrus oil glands; schizogenous — resin ducts of Pinus), laticifers — non-articulated (latex cells, Euphorbia, Nerium) and articulated (latex vessels, Hevea, Papaver).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Hydathodes are always open water pores and do not regulate; stomata regulate gas exchange. Hevea has articulated laticifers, not non-articulated.

activity.prompt: Match the stomatal type.

items.text: Two subsidiary cells parallel to the pore
Two subsidiary cells at right angles to the pore

quiz.why: Brassicaceae have three unequal subsidiary cells (anisocytic).
Lysigenous cavities arise when secretory cells dissolve, as in Citrus peel.
Hydathodes at leaf margins release liquid water under root pressure.
Loss of turgor in these large epidermal cells makes grass leaves roll and reduce water loss.

scenes.text: Cut the tip of an onion root and it stops lengthening — the root apical meristem is gone.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Classification of meristems
steps.body: By origin: promeristem, primary (apical) and secondary (cork cambium, interfascicular cambium). By position: apical, intercalary (grass nodes, mint), lateral (vascular and cork cambium). By function (Haberlandt): protoderm → epidermis, procambium → primary vascular tissue, ground meristem → cortex, pith.

steps.title: Theories of shoot apex
steps.body: Apical cell theory (Nägeli): a single tetrahedral apical cell (pteridophytes, bryophytes). Histogen theory (Hanstein 1868): dermatogen, periblem, plerome. Tunica–corpus theory (Schmidt 1924): outer tunica layers divide anticlinally (surface growth), inner corpus divides in all planes (volume growth). Cyto-histological zonation in gymnosperms (Foster).

steps.title: Root apex
steps.body: Histogen theory applied to roots with calyptrogen (root cap). Körper–Kappe theory (Schüepp). Quiescent centre concept (Clowes 1958): a group of slowly dividing cells at the root tip (shown by low thymidine uptake) acting as a reserve of initials.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Tunica divides anticlinally (walls perpendicular to surface), not periclinally. Quiescent centre cells are not dead; they divide rarely.

quiz.why: Grasses elongate from intercalary meristems at the base of internodes.
A. Schmidt proposed it in 1924 for angiosperm shoot apices.

In the histogen scheme for roots, calyptrogen produces the root cap.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Primary structure, secondary growth and anomalies
courses.summary: Primary anatomy of dicot and monocot root, stem and leaf, normal secondary growth by vascular and cork cambium, wood structure, and anomalous secondary growth in Boerhaavia, Dracaena and Bignonia.
outcomes: Distinguish dicot and monocot root, stem and leaf anatomy

lessons.title: Primary structure of root, stem and leaf

scenes.text: A sunflower stem section shows a neat ring of bundles; a maize stem shows bundles scattered like stars.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Roots
steps.body: Both: epiblema with root hairs, parenchymatous cortex, endodermis with Casparian strips, pericycle, radial vascular bundles with exarch xylem. Dicot root (gram, sunflower): xylem bundles 2–6 (diarch to hexarch), small or no pith. Monocot root (maize): polyarch (often more than 6) xylem bundles, large pith, endodermis with passage cells opposite protoxylem.

steps.title: Stems
steps.body: Dicot stem (sunflower): epidermis with multicellular hairs, collenchymatous hypodermis, cortex, endodermis (starch sheath), pericycle (sclerenchyma patches), ring of conjoint, collateral, open bundles (with cambium), endarch xylem, large pith. Monocot stem (maize): sclerenchymatous hypodermis, no clear cortex/endodermis/pith distinction (ground tissue), scattered conjoint collateral closed bundles, each with a bundle sheath, Y-shaped xylem and a lysigenous water cavity. Cucurbita has bicollateral bundles.

steps.title: Leaves
steps.body: Dicot leaf (dorsiventral, mango): upper epidermis with thick cuticle, palisade below upper epidermis, spongy mesophyll above lower epidermis, more stomata on lower surface, reticulate veins. Monocot leaf (isobilateral, grass): stomata on both surfaces, undifferentiated mesophyll, bulliform cells, parallel veins; C4 grasses show Kranz anatomy (bundle sheath cells with chloroplasts).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Root bundles are radial (xylem and phloem on different radii), not conjoint. Monocot stem bundles are closed — no cambium — so no normal secondary growth.

activity.prompt: Dicot stem or monocot stem?

quiz.why: Cucurbitaceae have phloem on both inner and outer sides of xylem.
Unthickened endodermal cells opposite protoxylem allow radial water flow.
A wreath of chloroplast-rich bundle sheath cells is the hallmark of C4 leaves.
Monocot roots have many xylem bundles, often more than six.

lessons.title: Normal secondary growth in dicot stem and root

story.title: How a sapling becomes a trunk

scenes.text: A neem sapling's stem is a pencil's width; in twenty years it is a trunk — thanks to two lateral meristems.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Vascular cambium in stem
steps.body: Intrafascicular cambium in bundles plus interfascicular cambium (from medullary ray parenchyma) join to form a complete cambial ring. Fusiform initials (elongated) produce secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward — more xylem than phloem; ray initials produce vascular rays. Primary phloem gets crushed; primary xylem stays near the pith.

steps.title: Cork cambium and periderm
steps.body: Phellogen arises in the cortex (often hypodermis). It produces phellem (cork, suberised, dead) outward and phelloderm (secondary cortex) inward: periderm = phellem + phellogen + phelloderm. Lenticels are lens-shaped openings filled with loose complementary cells for gas exchange. Bark = all tissues outside vascular cambium.

steps.title: Secondary growth in dicot root
steps.body: Cambium arises from conjunctive parenchyma inside phloem strands and from pericycle opposite protoxylem, first wavy then circular. Pericycle also gives phellogen.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Cork cambium in stems usually arises in the cortex, whereas in roots it arises from pericycle. Bark is not just cork.

activity.prompt: Order tissues in an old dicot stem from outside to centre.

quiz.why: Parenchyma between bundles dedifferentiates to join intrafascicular cambium.
These three layers together make up the periderm.
Loosely packed complementary cells let air through the corky bark.
Cambial activity is biased inward, giving much more secondary xylem.

scenes.text: A forest guard counts rings on a felled teak stump to estimate its age.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Growth rings
steps.body: In seasonal climates cambium forms wide, thin-walled early (spring) wood and narrow, dense late (autumn) wood. One early + one late band = one annual ring. Dendrochronology uses rings to date trees and reconstruct past climate. Tropical evergreen trees may lack distinct rings.

steps.title: Heartwood and sapwood; porosity
steps.body: Heartwood (duramen): inner, dark, non-conducting, with tyloses (balloon-like ingrowths of parenchyma into vessels) and deposits of tannins, resins — durable. Sapwood (alburnum): outer, light, conducting. Ring-porous wood: large vessels in early wood (teak); diffuse-porous: vessels uniform (mango). Gymnosperm wood is non-porous (no vessels) and called softwood; angiosperm wood is porous hardwood.

steps.title: Worked example: age and growth rate
steps.body: A stump shows 48 annual rings and a radius of 36 cm. Age ≈ 48 years. Average radial growth = 36 ÷ 48 = 0.75 cm per year.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Count one early + late wood pair as one ring, not two. Softwood (conifer) can be physically harder than some hardwoods — the terms refer to anatomy.

activity.prompt: A tree stump has 60 annual rings and a radius of 45 cm. Find its average radial growth in cm per year.

quiz.why: Parenchyma balloons into old vessels and blocks them in heartwood.
Teak forms large vessels mainly in early wood.
Gymnosperm wood lacks vessels and is called softwood.

scenes.text: Monocots have no vascular cambium, yet Dracaena trunks grow thick — an anomaly.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Boerhaavia (dicot stem)
steps.body: Shows three rings of bundles: inner medullary bundles (2 large), middle ring, outer ring; successive cambia from pericycle produce extra rings of bundles with interxylary (conjunctive) tissue — accessory cambia.

steps.title: Dracaena (monocot stem)
steps.body: A secondary cambium arises in the cortex outside the primary bundles; it forms secondary amphivasal (leptocentric — xylem surrounding phloem) bundles and conjunctive tissue inward and a little parenchyma outward.

steps.title: Bignonia (dicot climber)
steps.body: Cambium forms less xylem at four places and more phloem there, so phloem wedges project into the xylem forming a cross-shaped (furrowed) xylem — helping flexibility of the climber. Other examples: included phloem in Salvadora and Leptadenia.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Dracaena's secondary bundles are amphivasal, not collateral. Boerhaavia anomaly is due to abnormal cambial position/accessory cambia, not to monocot features.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Anther, ovule and gametophytes
courses.summary: Structure of the anther wall, microsporogenesis and the male gametophyte; structure and types of ovules, megasporogenesis and types of embryo sac.
outcomes: Describe the layers of the anther wall and their functions
Explain microsporogenesis and pollen development
Classify ovules by curvature, integuments and nucellus
Explain monosporic, bisporic and tetrasporic embryo sac development
Draw and label a Polygonum-type embryo sac

scenes.text: A young anther in section looks like a butterfly — four pollen sacs, each wrapped in four layers.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Anther wall
steps.body: A typical anther is bilobed, dithecous and tetrasporangiate. Wall layers from outside: epidermis; endothecium (fibrous thickenings, helps dehiscence); one to three middle layers (ephemeral); tapetum (innermost, nourishes microspores). Tapetum types: secretory/glandular (cells stay in place) and amoeboid/periplasmodial (protoplasts invade the locule). Tapetal cells are often bi- or multinucleate and contribute Ubisch bodies and sporopollenin precursors.

steps.title: Microsporogenesis
steps.body: Sporogenous cells → microspore mother cells (2n) → meiosis → microspore tetrads. Cytokinesis may be successive (after each division, isobilateral tetrads, monocots) or simultaneous (after meiosis II, tetrahedral tetrads, dicots). Tetrads usually separate; in Typha, Drosera and Ericaceae they stay as compound pollen; in Calotropis and orchids pollen forms pollinia.

steps.title: Pollen wall and male gametophyte
steps.body: Exine (sporopollenin, very resistant, with germ pores) and intine (cellulose and pectin). First mitosis gives a large vegetative cell and a small generative cell (2-celled pollen shed in ~60% of angiosperms). Generative cell divides into two male gametes — in the pollen grain (3-celled, e.g. grasses, crucifers) or in the pollen tube.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Endothecium, not tapetum, causes dehiscence. Exine is absent at germ pores, which is where the pollen tube emerges.

activity.prompt: Order the anther wall layers from outside to inside.

quiz.q: Nutritive layer of the anther is
quiz.why: The tapetum supplies nutrients, enzymes and wall materials to developing microspores.
The tough exine is made of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant biopolymers.
In Calotropis and orchids all pollen of a sac is bound into a pollinium.

quiz.q: The generative cell gives rise to
quiz.why: Mitosis of the generative cell forms two male gametes.

scenes.text: Most angiosperm ovules are turned upside down so the micropyle lies next to the funicle — the anatropous form.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Parts
steps.body: Funicle (stalk) joins ovule to placenta at the hilum; body has one or two integuments enclosing the nucellus, leaving a micropyle; chalaza is the base where integuments and nucellus meet; embryo sac lies in the nucellus. Raphe is the ridge formed when funicle fuses with the ovule body (anatropous).

steps.title: Types by curvature
steps.body: Orthotropous/atropous (straight — Polygonum, Piper), anatropous (inverted 180°, most common), hemianatropous (90°, Ranunculus), campylotropous (body curved, embryo sac not — Capsella, legumes), amphitropous (body and embryo sac curved horseshoe-like), circinotropous (funicle coils around ovule — Opuntia).

steps.title: Integuments and nucellus
steps.body: Unitegmic (sympetalous dicots), bitegmic (most polypetalous dicots and monocots). Crassinucellate: nucellus massive with parietal cells; tenuinucellate: thin nucellus, archesporial cell directly as megaspore mother cell. Special structures: obturator, caruncle (castor), aril (litchi, nutmeg mace).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: In campylotropous ovules only the body curves; in amphitropous the embryo sac also curves. Aril is an outgrowth of the funicle, not of the fruit wall.

activity.prompt: Match the ovule type.

quiz.q: Most common ovule type in angiosperms
quiz.why: Anatropous ovules are found in the majority of angiosperm families.

quiz.q: Caruncle is seen in seeds of
quiz.why: Castor seeds have a spongy outgrowth from the micropylar integument called caruncle.

quiz.why: The chalaza is the basal region of the ovule opposite the micropyle in orthotropous ovules.

scenes.text: From one surviving megaspore, three rounds of mitosis build an embryo sac of seven cells with eight nuclei.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Megasporogenesis
steps.body: Archesporial cell → megaspore mother cell (2n) → meiosis → linear tetrad of four megaspores; usually the chalazal one is functional and three degenerate.

steps.title: Polygonum type (monosporic, 8-nucleate)
steps.body: Functional megaspore undergoes three free-nuclear mitoses → 8 nuclei, 4 at each pole. One nucleus from each pole moves to the centre as polar nuclei. Micropylar end: egg apparatus = egg + two synergids (with filiform apparatus that guides the pollen tube). Chalazal end: three antipodals. Central cell has two polar nuclei. Result: 7 cells, 8 nuclei. Found in about 70% of angiosperms.

steps.title: Other types
steps.body: Monosporic: Polygonum (8-nucleate), Oenothera (4-nucleate, micropylar megaspore, no antipodals). Bisporic: Allium (dyad cell gives 8-nucleate sac after 2 mitoses). Tetrasporic: Adoxa, Fritillaria, Peperomia (16-nucleate), Plumbago, Penaea (16 nuclei in four groups).

steps.title: Worked example: counting divisions
steps.body: Polygonum type: meiosis (2 divisions) + 3 mitoses after meiosis. Bisporic Allium: meiosis I gives dyad, one dyad cell completes meiosis II (2 nuclei, both megaspore nuclei participate), then 2 mitoses → 8 nuclei. Tetrasporic: all 4 megaspore nuclei in one cell; 1 mitosis (Adoxa) → 8 nuclei.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Embryo sac (female gametophyte) is haploid except the central cell after polar fusion (2n secondary nucleus). Synergids, not antipodals, have the filiform apparatus.

activity.prompt: Order the development of a Polygonum-type embryo sac.
items: Linear tetrad forms; chalazal megaspore survives

quiz.why: The central cell holds two polar nuclei, so 7 cells contain 8 nuclei.

scenes.text: A bee pushes into a Salvia flower; a lever drops the anthers onto its back — a lever (turn-pipe) mechanism.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Pollination types and agents
steps.body: Self (autogamy, geitonogamy) and cross (xenogamy). Agents: wind (anemophily — light dry pollen, feathery stigma, maize, grasses), water (hydrophily — Vallisneria, Zostera), insects (entomophily — colour, scent, nectar, Salvia), birds (ornithophily), bats (chiropterophily). Outbreeding devices: dichogamy (protandry, protogyny), herkogamy, heterostyly (Primula), self-incompatibility, dicliny.

steps.title: Self-incompatibility
steps.body: Gametophytic SI (pollen genotype decides; pollen tube stops in style — Solanaceae, Rosaceae; controlled by S-RNases) and sporophytic SI (parent sporophyte genotype decides; pollen fails at stigma surface — Brassicaceae). Methods to overcome: bud pollination, mixed pollination, intraovarian pollination, in vitro fertilisation.

steps.body: Geitonogamy is genetically self-pollination even though it involves two flowers of the same plant.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Fertilisation, endosperm, embryo and seed
courses.summary: Pollen tube entry, double fertilisation, types of endosperm, dicot and monocot embryogeny, seed and fruit formation, apomixis, polyembryony and applied embryology.
outcomes: Explain pollen tube entry and double fertilisation
Classify endosperm into nuclear, cellular and helobial types
Trace dicot (Capsella) and monocot embryo development
Define apomixis, polyembryony and parthenocarpy with examples

scenes.text: In 1898 S. G. Nawaschin saw in Lilium and Fritillaria that one male gamete fuses with the egg and the other with the polar nuclei.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Pollen germination and tube entry
steps.body: Pollen absorbs water on the stigma and the tube grows through the style (solid or hollow) guided chemically. Entry into the ovule: porogamy (through micropyle, most common), chalazogamy (through chalaza, Casuarina — discovered by Treub), mesogamy (through integuments or funicle, Cucurbita). The tube enters one synergid via the filiform apparatus and discharges both male gametes.

steps.title: Double fertilisation and triple fusion
steps.body: Syngamy: male gamete (n) + egg (n) → zygote (2n). Triple fusion: second male gamete (n) + two polar nuclei (n + n) or secondary nucleus (2n) → primary endosperm nucleus (3n). Double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms (a form of it occurs in Ephedra but without endosperm).

steps.title: Worked example: ploidy
steps.body: A plant has 2n = 24. Egg = n = 12; zygote/embryo = 2n = 24; endosperm (Polygonum type) = 3n = 36; integuments/seed coat = maternal 2n = 24; nucellus/perisperm = 2n = 24.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Seed coat is maternal tissue (2n), not embryo tissue. Endosperm in Oenothera type is 2n because there is only one polar nucleus.

activity.prompt: In a plant with 2n = 16, what is the chromosome number of the endosperm cells (Polygonum-type embryo sac)?

quiz.why: S. G. Nawaschin reported it in 1898 in Lilium and Fritillaria.

A male gamete fuses with two polar nuclei, forming the 3n primary endosperm nucleus.

quiz.q: Pollen tube usually enters the embryo sac through
quiz.why: It penetrates one synergid, which degenerates and releases the gametes.

scenes.text: Tender coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm; the white kernel is cellular endosperm formed later.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: Nuclear: primary endosperm nucleus divides repeatedly without walls; walls form later from periphery (wheat, maize, coconut — the water is the liquid free-nuclear part). Cellular: every division followed by wall formation (Petunia, Datura, Balsam). Helobial: first division forms a large micropylar and small chalazal chamber; micropylar becomes nuclear (common in Helobiae/monocots, e.g. Eremurus).

steps.title: Endosperm haustoria and ruminate endosperm
steps.body: Haustoria extend from endosperm into surrounding tissue (Cucurbitaceae, Acanthaceae). Ruminate endosperm has an irregular, mottled surface due to ingrowth of seed coat (areca nut, nutmeg). In cereals the aleurone layer (protein-rich outer layer) secretes amylase on germination.

steps.title: Endospermic vs non-endospermic seeds
steps.body: Albuminous seeds retain endosperm (castor, cereals, coconut); exalbuminous seeds use it up during embryo growth and store food in cotyledons (pea, gram, groundnut). Perisperm is persistent nucellus (black pepper, beet).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Perisperm (2n, nucellar) and endosperm (3n) are different tissues.

activity.prompt: Albuminous or exalbuminous seed?

quiz.why: It is the liquid part of nuclear endosperm before cell walls form.
It is characteristic of the order Helobiae and many monocots.

scenes.text: Capsella bursa-pastoris is the classic dicot whose embryo goes from globular to heart to torpedo shape.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Dicot embryo (Capsella, Crucifer/Onagrad type)
steps.body: Zygote divides transversely → basal cell (towards micropyle) and terminal cell. Basal cell forms a suspensor (with large haustorial basal cell) whose last cell, the hypophysis, forms the radicle tip and root cap. Terminal cell → quadrant → octant → globular stage (dermatogen differentiates) → heart-shaped (two cotyledon primordia) → torpedo → mature curved embryo with two cotyledons, plumule, hypocotyl and radicle.

steps.title: Monocot embryo (grass)
steps.body: Single cotyledon called scutellum (shield-shaped, absorbs food from endosperm); plumule covered by coleoptile; radicle covered by coleorhiza; epiblast in some grasses. In Luzula/Sagittaria type monocot development the terminal cell forms the cotyledon and the plumule is lateral.

steps.title: Embryogeny types (Johansen/Maheshwari)
steps.body: Based on plane of first division of the terminal cell and roles of the basal cell: Crucifer (Onagrad), Asterad, Solanad, Caryophyllad, Chenopodiad, Piperad.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Hypophysis is from the suspensor (basal) lineage, not from the terminal cell.

activity.prompt: Order the stages of Capsella embryo development.

quiz.why: The single shield-shaped cotyledon of grasses absorbs endosperm reserves.
Coleorhiza is the protective sheath of the radicle.
This cell from the suspensor end gives the root tip and cap.

quiz.q: Two cotyledon primordia first appear at
quiz.why: The two bulges of cotyledons give the embryo its heart shape.

scenes.text: Plant a Citrus seed and several seedlings come up — extra embryos from nucellar cells.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Apomixis
steps.body: Seed formation without fertilisation. Recurrent agamospermy: diplospory (unreduced embryo sac from megaspore mother cell) and apospory (embryo sac from a nucellar cell, Hieracium); then parthenogenesis of the unreduced egg. Adventive embryony: embryos directly from nucellus or integument (Citrus, mango). Non-recurrent: haploid embryo from egg.

steps.title: Polyembryony and parthenocarpy
steps.body: Polyembryony: more than one embryo per seed — cleavage (gymnosperms), nucellar adventive (Citrus, mango, Opuntia), from synergids/antipodals. Parthenocarpy: fruit without fertilisation, seedless (banana, seedless grape — sometimes induced by auxins/gibberellins). Not the same as apomixis.

steps.title: Applied embryology
steps.body: Anther/pollen culture for haploids (Guha and Maheshwari, 1964, Datura); embryo rescue in wide crosses; endosperm culture for triploids; in vitro pollination; P. Maheshwari, the father of Indian embryology, wrote 'An Introduction to the Embryology of Angiosperms' (1950). Apomixis could fix hybrid vigour in crops.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Parthenocarpy gives seedless fruit; apomixis gives seeds. Nucellar embryos are genetically identical to the mother.

scenes.text: Priya condenses the whole syllabus into ten lines per topic.

steps.title: Anatomy at a glance
steps.body: Root: radial bundles, exarch. Stem: conjoint collateral; dicot open ring, endarch; monocot closed scattered. Leaf: dicot dorsiventral, monocot isobilateral. Secondary growth: vascular cambium (fusiform + ray initials) and phellogen. Anomalies: Boerhaavia (medullary bundles), Dracaena (amphivasal secondary bundles), Bignonia (phloem wedges).

steps.title: Embryology at a glance
steps.body: Anther wall: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum. Pollen: exine (sporopollenin) + intine; 2- or 3-celled. Ovule: anatropous most common. Embryo sac: Polygonum type 7 cells/8 nuclei. Double fertilisation: zygote 2n + PEN 3n. Endosperm: nuclear, cellular, helobial. Capsella embryo: globular → heart → torpedo. Apomixis, polyembryony, parthenocarpy.

steps.title: Diagram checklist
steps.body: T.S. drawings: show outline sector with labelled tissues; embryo sac: label egg, synergids, polar nuclei, antipodals, micropylar and chalazal ends.

lessons.title: Lab: Stomatal index from a leaf peel

scenes.text: Under 40× objective, Rahul counts stomata and epidermal cells in one field of a Tradescantia peel.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: Peel lower epidermis (Tradescantia/Rhoeo or bean leaf) with forceps, stain lightly with safranin, mount in glycerine. Under high power count stomata (S) and epidermal cells (E) in a field; repeat in 5 fields and average.

steps.title: Formula and worked example
steps.body: Stomatal index (Salisbury) SI = S ÷ (S + E) × 100. Example: S = 24, E = 96 → SI = 24 ÷ 120 × 100 = 20%. Stomatal frequency = stomata per mm² of field area.

steps.title: Viva FAQs
steps.body: Why use the index rather than frequency? SI stays relatively constant for a species because it is not affected by leaf expansion. Why lower epidermis? Dicot leaves usually have more stomata on the lower side.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Count guard-cell pairs as one stoma and do not count guard cells as epidermal cells.

activity.prompt: In one field you count 18 stomata and 102 epidermal cells. Calculate the stomatal index.

quiz.why: Salisbury defined SI as stomata divided by total stomata plus epidermal cells, times 100.

options: Is less affected by leaf expansion

quiz.why: Each pair with its pore forms a single stoma.

lessons.title: Lab: Pollen germination and embryo mounting

scenes.text: In a cavity slide of 10% sucrose with boric acid, Vinca pollen sends out tubes within an hour.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Pollen germination (hanging drop / cavity slide)
steps.body: Prepare 10% sucrose with about 100 ppm boric acid. Dust fresh pollen (Vinca, Hibiscus, Impatiens) into a drop, keep in a moist chamber 30–60 min, observe. A pollen grain is germinated when tube length exceeds its diameter. Germination % = germinated ÷ total × 100.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Total pollen counted = 120; germinated = 84. Germination % = 84 ÷ 120 × 100 = 70%.

steps.title: Embryo mounting (Capsella / Tridax)
steps.body: Dissect young fruits/ovules in a drop of water or 10% KOH, press gently under a cover slip to release embryos, stain lightly and identify globular, heart and torpedo stages.

steps.title: Viva FAQs
steps.body: Why sucrose? Osmotic support and energy. Why boric acid? Boron promotes tube growth. Why moist chamber? Prevents drying.

scenes.text: Boiling wood chips in Schultze's fluid separates tracheids, vessels and fibres for observation.

steps.title: Maceration
steps.body: Cut thin slivers of stem; warm in Jeffrey's fluid (equal parts 10% chromic acid and 10% nitric acid) or Schultze's mixture (conc. nitric acid with a few crystals of potassium chlorate) in a fume hood; wash thoroughly, tease, stain with safranin and mount. Observe tracheids, vessel members, fibres, sclereids. Safety: strong oxidising acids — gloves, goggles.

lessons.title: General characters and classification of algae

scenes.text: Meera scoops green water from the college pond and sees, under the microscope, swimming cells, long filaments and hollow balls.
All are algae — yet they differ in colour, stored food and flagella. Those three clues are how phycologists classify them.

steps.title: What are algae?
steps.body: Algae are chlorophyll-bearing, autotrophic, mostly aquatic thalloid organisms. The plant body is a thallus (not differentiated into root, stem and leaf), there is no vascular tissue, and sex organs are usually unicellular and not surrounded by a jacket of sterile cells. The zygote does not form an embryo inside the female organ. (Cyanobacteria, the 'blue-green algae', are prokaryotes and are now treated with bacteria, but most Indian syllabi still study them here.)

steps.title: Range of thallus organisation
steps.body: 1) Unicellular motile (Chlamydomonas) or non-motile (Chlorella). 2) Colonial: motile coenobium (Volvox) or non-motile (Hydrodictyon). 3) Palmelloid (Tetraspora) — cells in mucilage. 4) Dendroid (Prasinocladus). 5) Filamentous: unbranched (Ulothrix, Oedogonium, Spirogyra) or branched (Cladophora). 6) Heterotrichous — prostrate plus erect system (Fritschiella, Ectocarpus). 7) Siphonaceous/coenocytic — multinucleate tube without septa (Vaucheria). 8) Parenchymatous/foliose (Ulva) and complex differentiated thalli of kelps (Laminaria) and Sargassum.

steps.title: Pigments, reserve food, flagella
steps.body: Chlorophyceae (green): chl a + b, starch, 2–4 equal whiplash flagella. Phaeophyceae (brown): chl a + c, fucoxanthin, laminarin and mannitol, 2 unequal lateral flagella (one tinsel). Rhodophyceae (red): chl a (+d), phycoerythrin, floridean starch, no flagella at any stage. Xanthophyceae (yellow-green, e.g. Vaucheria): chl a, oil as reserve, unequal flagella. Bacillariophyceae (diatoms): silica frustule, chrysolaminarin and oil.

steps.title: Fritsch's classification (1935, 1945)
steps.body: F. E. Fritsch divided algae into 11 classes: Chlorophyceae, Xanthophyceae, Chrysophyceae, Bacillariophyceae, Cryptophyceae, Dinophyceae, Chloromonadineae, Euglenineae, Phaeophyceae, Rhodophyceae and Myxophyceae (Cyanophyceae). His main criteria were pigments, reserve food, flagella, thallus structure and reproduction.

steps.title: Reproduction and life cycles
steps.body: Vegetative: fragmentation, akinetes, hormogonia. Asexual: zoospores, aplanospores, autospores. Sexual: isogamy (similar gametes, Ulothrix), anisogamy (unequal motile gametes), oogamy (large non-motile egg + small sperm, Volvox, Oedogonium). Life cycles: haplontic (zygote is the only diploid stage; zygotic meiosis — Chlamydomonas, Spirogyra), diplontic (gametic meiosis — diatoms, Fucus), haplodiplontic with alternation of generations, isomorphic (Ulva, Ectocarpus) or heteromorphic (Laminaria).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not call cyanobacteria 'eukaryotic algae'. Do not write 'Rhodophyceae have flagellate sperm' — red algae have non-motile spermatia. Laminarin and mannitol are brown-algal reserves; floridean starch is red-algal.

activity.prompt: Place each character in the correct algal class.

items.text: Chlorophyll a and b, true starch
Pyrenoids surrounded by starch in a cup-shaped chloroplast

quiz.q: Fritsch classified algae into how many classes?
quiz.why: Fritsch recognised 11 classes based mainly on pigments, reserve food and flagellation.

quiz.q: Coenocytic siphonaceous thallus is seen in
quiz.why: Vaucheria has a multinucleate tubular thallus without cross walls, i.e. a coenocyte.

quiz.q: Reserve food of red algae is
quiz.why: Rhodophyceae store floridean starch, a branched glucan related to amylopectin.

quiz.q: In a haplontic life cycle meiosis is
quiz.why: In haplontic algae the zygote divides by meiosis, so it is the only diploid cell in the cycle.

lessons.title: Type studies: Chlamydomonas, Volvox and Oedogonium

scenes.text: A single swimming cell, then a ball of thousands of cells, then a long filament with caps on its cells — the green algae show increasing complexity.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Chlamydomonas
steps.body: Unicellular, motile, biflagellate (two equal whiplash flagella at the anterior end), cup-shaped chloroplast with one pyrenoid, red eyespot (stigma), two contractile vacuoles near the base of flagella. Asexual: zoospores formed in the parent cell; under unfavourable conditions a palmella stage. Sexual: isogamy (C. eugametos), anisogamy (C. braunii) or oogamy (C. coccifera). Zygote secretes thick wall, undergoes meiosis to give 4 haploid zoospores — haplontic.

steps.title: Volvox
steps.body: Motile coenobium of 500–60,000 biflagellate cells arranged in a single peripheral layer in mucilage; cells connected by cytoplasmic strands. Only a few cells in the posterior half are reproductive (gonidia). Asexual: gonidium divides to form a daughter colony that undergoes inversion. Sexual: oogamous — antheridia produce sperm bundles (plates), oogonia an egg. Species are monoecious (V. globator) or dioecious (V. aureus). Zygote (oospore) is red-orange due to haematochrome; meiosis is zygotic.

steps.title: Oedogonium
steps.body: Unbranched filament attached by a basal holdfast; cells with reticulate chloroplast and many pyrenoids. Characteristic 'cap cells' result from its unique ring-type cell division. Asexual by a single multiflagellate (stephanokont: a crown of flagella) zoospore per cell. Sexual: advanced oogamy. Species are macrandrous (normal-sized male filaments) or nannandrous (dwarf males formed from androspores that settle on the suffultory cell below the oogonium).

steps.title: Worked example: identify the specimen
steps.body: Slide shows a filament with several cells bearing striations at one end, and a swollen cell with a pore holding a large egg; a tiny filament is attached to the cell below. Step 1: striations = cap cells → Oedogonium. Step 2: swollen cell = oogonium. Step 3: tiny attached filament = dwarf male → nannandrous species. Answer: Oedogonium, nannandrous, showing oogonium and dwarf male.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Volvox is a coenobium (fixed cell number at birth), not just any colony. Oedogonium zoospores are multiflagellate, not biflagellate.

activity.prompt: Order the events in the sexual life cycle of Chlamydomonas.
items: Haploid vegetative cell divides to form gametes
Diploid zygote forms a thick wall and rests
Four haploid zoospores are released and grow into new cells

quiz.why: Ring-type cell division in Oedogonium leaves stacked caps of old wall at the anterior end of dividing cells.
Young daughter coenobia turn inside out (inversion) so that flagella point outward.
It bears a ring (crown) of many flagella at its anterior end, called stephanokont.
The red light-sensitive eyespot of Chlamydomonas is the stigma, which helps phototaxis.

lessons.title: Type studies: Vaucheria, Ectocarpus and Polysiphonia

scenes.text: On a rocky shore at Okha, brown tufts and red feathery threads cling to stones — Ectocarpus and Polysiphonia.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Vaucheria (Xanthophyceae)
steps.body: Coenocytic branched tube, many discoid chloroplasts without pyrenoids, oil as reserve. Asexual: a large compound multiflagellate zoospore (synzoospore) formed in a club-shaped zoosporangium; aplanospores and akinetes ('Gongrosira stage') in drying conditions. Sexual: oogamous; antheridium hooked, oogonium sessile and beaked, often side by side. Zygotic meiosis.

steps.title: Ectocarpus (Phaeophyceae)
steps.body: Heterotrichous branched filaments, ribbon-shaped chromatophores. Diploid sporophyte bears unilocular sporangia (meiosis → haploid zoospores) and plurilocular sporangia (mitotic diploid zoospores). Gametophyte is haploid and morphologically identical → isomorphic alternation of generations. Gametes are pear-shaped with two unequal laterally inserted flagella; fusion is isogamous to physiologically anisogamous.

steps.title: Polysiphonia (Rhodophyceae)
steps.body: Thallus with a central siphon surrounded by pericentral siphons, pit connections between cells. Triphasic life cycle: haploid gametophyte (male with spermatangia, female with carpogonium having trichogyne) → diploid carposporophyte on the female (cystocarp releasing carpospores) → free-living diploid tetrasporophyte that forms tetraspores by meiosis. Gametophyte and tetrasporophyte look alike (isomorphic).

steps.title: Memory hook
steps.body: Polysiphonia = three generations: Gametophyte (n) → Carposporophyte (2n, parasitic on female) → Tetrasporophyte (2n). 'G-C-T'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Unilocular sporangia of Ectocarpus are the site of meiosis; plurilocular sporangia on the sporophyte do not reduce chromosome number.

activity.prompt: Assign each structure to its genus.

quiz.q: Triphasic life cycle is seen in
quiz.why: Polysiphonia has gametophyte, carposporophyte and tetrasporophyte phases.
Unilocular sporangia on the diploid sporophyte undergo meiosis to form haploid zoospores.
In dry conditions Vaucheria cuts its thallus into thick-walled segments resembling the alga Gongrosira.

quiz.q: Female sex organ of red algae is
quiz.why: Red algae bear a flask-shaped carpogonium with a long receptive trichogyne.

lessons.title: Cyanobacteria and economic importance of algae

scenes.text: A Tamil Nadu farmer broadcasts dried blue-green algal flakes in his paddy field to save urea.
The ice cream he eats that evening contains alginate or carrageenan from seaweeds.

steps.title: Nostoc and Anabaena
steps.body: Filamentous cyanobacteria: trichomes of bead-like cells in mucilage with heterocysts (thick-walled, pale cells where nitrogenase fixes N₂ under low O₂) and akinetes (resting spores). Nostoc forms gelatinous balls; Anabaena azollae lives in leaf cavities of the fern Azolla. Reproduction is only vegetative/asexual (hormogonia, akinetes); no sexual reproduction.

steps.title: Biofertilisers
steps.body: Cyanobacterial inoculum (Anabaena, Nostoc, Tolypothrix, Aulosira) and Azolla–Anabaena are used in rice fields; they add fixed nitrogen and organic matter to the soil.

steps.title: Economic products
steps.body: Food: Porphyra (nori), Ulva, Spirulina (protein-rich supplement). Agar from red algae Gelidium and Gracilaria (culture media, jellies). Carrageenan from Chondrus and Kappaphycus (cultivated in Tamil Nadu). Alginates from brown algae Laminaria, Sargassum, Macrocystis. Diatomaceous earth (kieselguhr) from diatom frustules — filters, abrasives, insulation. Iodine was once extracted from kelps. Chlorella is a model organism and a candidate for biofuel. Harmful: algal blooms, eutrophication, toxins of Microcystis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Agar is from red algae, alginic acid is from brown algae — students often swap them.

activity.prompt: Match product to source group.

quiz.q: Nitrogen fixation in Anabaena occurs in
quiz.why: Heterocysts exclude oxygen and contain nitrogenase, the enzyme that fixes atmospheric nitrogen.
Gelidium and Gracilaria, both red algae, are the main commercial sources of agar.
It is the fossil accumulation of the siliceous cell walls (frustules) of diatoms.

quiz.q: Azolla is useful in rice fields because it harbours
quiz.why: The cyanobacterium Anabaena azollae lives in the fern's leaf cavities and fixes nitrogen.

questions.q: Pigment giving brown algae their colour
questions.why: Fucoxanthin, a xanthophyll, masks the chlorophyll in Phaeophyceae.

questions.q: Isomorphic alternation of generations occurs in
questions.why: Ulva gametophyte and sporophyte look the same.
Chlamydomonas cells lose flagella and divide inside mucilage under unfavourable conditions.
Nannandrous species form androspores that grow into dwarf male filaments.

questions.why: Gonidia in the posterior half of the coenobium form daughter colonies or gametangia.

questions.q: Which algal group lacks flagella at all stages?
questions.why: Red algae have no flagellate stage; even male gametes (spermatia) are non-motile.
Xanthophyceae like Vaucheria store oil droplets, not starch.

questions.q: Pit connections are a feature of
questions.why: Rhodophyte cells are linked by protein pit plugs called pit connections.
Laminaria has a large sporophyte and microscopic gametophyte.
They arise mitotically from the diploid carposporophyte formed after fertilisation.
Spirulina biomass is rich in protein and vitamins.
