courses.title: Unit 2 · Fungi and Lichens
courses.summary: General characters, hyphal organisation, nutrition and classification of fungi (Ainsworth 1973), type studies of Albugo, Rhizopus, Penicillium, Puccinia and Agaricus, lichens and the economic importance of fungi including plant diseases.
outcomes: List the general characters of fungi and types of mycelium
Classify fungi into subdivisions following Ainsworth
Describe life cycles of Rhizopus, Penicillium, Puccinia and Agaricus
Explain the structure, types and importance of lichens
Relate fungi to industry, medicine and plant disease

lessons.title: General characters and classification of fungi

scenes.text: Three-day-old bread grows a cottony white mass with black dots — Rhizopus. An orange turns blue-green — Penicillium.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: General characters
steps.body: Fungi are eukaryotic, achlorophyllous, heterotrophic (saprophytic, parasitic or symbiotic) organisms with absorptive nutrition. The body is a mycelium of hyphae — aseptate and coenocytic (Phycomycetes) or septate (Ascomycetes, Basidiomycetes). Cell wall is mainly chitin (cellulose in Oomycetes). Reserve food: glycogen and oil, never starch.

steps.title: Hyphal modifications
steps.body: Rhizoids (Rhizopus), haustoria (absorbing organs of parasites like Albugo), stolons, sclerotia (hard resting masses), rhizomorphs (root-like strands) and fruiting bodies. In Basidiomycetes, dikaryotic hyphae show clamp connections that ensure each cell keeps one nucleus of each mating type.

steps.title: Ainsworth (1973)
steps.body: Kingdom Fungi divided into Myxomycota (plasmodial, wall-less) and Eumycota. Eumycota has five subdivisions: Mastigomycotina (motile spores, e.g. Albugo, Phytophthora), Zygomycotina (zygospore, e.g. Rhizopus, Mucor), Ascomycotina (ascospores in asci, e.g. Saccharomyces, Penicillium, Aspergillus), Basidiomycotina (basidiospores on basidia, e.g. Puccinia, Agaricus, Ustilago) and Deuteromycotina (Fungi Imperfecti, no known sexual stage, e.g. Alternaria, Cercospora, Fusarium).

steps.title: Reproduction
steps.body: Asexual spores: sporangiospores, zoospores, conidia, chlamydospores, oidia. Sexual reproduction typically has three phases — plasmogamy, karyogamy and meiosis — by planogametic copulation, gametangial contact (Albugo), gametangial copulation (Rhizopus), spermatisation or somatogamy (Agaricus). In higher fungi plasmogamy and karyogamy are separated by a dikaryotic (n+n) phase.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Oomycetes (Albugo) have cellulose walls and are now placed outside true fungi, but syllabi still study them under Mastigomycotina. Fungi store glycogen, not starch.

activity.prompt: Place each genus in its Ainsworth subdivision.

quiz.why: True fungi have chitin walls; cellulose walls occur in Oomycetes.
Deuteromycotina are grouped because their sexual stage is unknown.
They maintain the dikaryotic condition during cell division in basidiomycete hyphae.
Haustoria of parasitic fungi penetrate host cells and absorb nutrients.

lessons.title: Type studies: Albugo, Rhizopus and Penicillium

scenes.text: In a Rajasthan mustard field, leaves show white shiny blisters — white rust caused by Albugo candida.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Albugo candida
steps.body: Obligate parasite on crucifers. Intercellular aseptate mycelium with knob-like haustoria. Asexual: sporangiophores beneath host epidermis cut off chains of sporangia (basipetal), rupturing the epidermis as white pustules; sporangia germinate by biflagellate zoospores. Sexual: oogamous by gametangial contact — antheridium sends a fertilisation tube into oogonium; oospore with warty wall; meiosis at germination.

steps.title: Rhizopus stolonifer
steps.body: Saprophytic 'bread mould'. Aseptate mycelium with stolons and rhizoids; sporangiophores arise in tufts above rhizoids, each ending in a sporangium with a columella. Sexual: heterothallic (+ and − strains); progametangia meet, gametangia fuse (gametangial copulation) to form a black warty zygospore, which on germination gives a germ sporangium.

steps.title: Penicillium
steps.body: Septate mycelium; asexual conidiophores branched like a brush (penicillus): metulae → phialides → chains of conidia. Sexual stage (in some species) forms cleistothecia with asci and 8 ascospores. P. notatum/P. chrysogenum produce penicillin (Fleming, 1928); P. roqueforti and P. camemberti ripen cheeses.

steps.title: Worked example: identify from a slide
steps.body: Observation: aseptate hyphae, unbranched sporangiophore with a dome-shaped columella, rhizoids at base. Step 1: aseptate + sporangia → Zygomycete. Step 2: stolon/rhizoid at sporangiophore base → Rhizopus (Mucor lacks rhizoids). Identification: Rhizopus, Zygomycotina.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not draw Penicillium conidia inside a sporangium; they are exogenous, in chains. Rhizopus zygospore is formed by gametangial copulation, not contact.

activity.prompt: Order the stages of sexual reproduction in Rhizopus.
items: Hyphae of + and − strains come close
Septa cut off terminal gametangia and suspensors
Gametangia fuse to form a zygote
Zygote develops a thick warty wall (zygospore)
Zygospore germinates after meiosis into a germ sporangium

quiz.q: White rust of crucifers is caused by
quiz.why: Albugo candida produces white pustules of sporangia on mustard and radish.

quiz.q: Columella is found in the sporangium of
quiz.why: Rhizopus sporangium has a central dome-shaped sterile columella.
Penicillium's branched conidiophore resembles a brush (penicillus).

scenes.text: Reddish then black streaks on wheat stems — Puccinia graminis tritici, a fungus that needs two hosts to finish its life.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Puccinia graminis: heteroecious and macrocyclic
steps.body: It completes its cycle on two hosts — wheat (primary) and barberry (alternate host) — and has five spore stages: on wheat, uredospores (dikaryotic, red rust, repeat infection) and teleutospores (two-celled, black, karyogamy then meiosis); on soil, basidiospores (haploid, from promycelium); on barberry, pycniospores (spermatia, upper leaf surface) and aecidiospores (dikaryotic, lower surface) which reinfect wheat. In India, barberry is not essential: uredospores survive in the hills and are carried to the plains.

steps.title: Agaricus (mushroom)
steps.body: Primary mycelium (monokaryotic) fuses by somatogamy → secondary dikaryotic mycelium → tertiary mycelium forming the basidiocarp: stipe, pileus, annulus and radiating gills. A section of a gill shows trama, subhymenium and hymenium of basidia and paraphyses. Each basidium: karyogamy → meiosis → 4 basidiospores on sterigmata. Agaricus bisporus is the cultivated button mushroom.

steps.title: Spore stage numbering
steps.body: 0 = pycnidial, I = aecial, II = uredial, III = telial, IV = basidial. Wheat carries II and III; barberry carries 0 and I.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Aecidiospores infect wheat, not barberry; basidiospores infect barberry. Students often reverse these.

activity.prompt: On which host or substrate does each spore of Puccinia graminis form?

quiz.q: Alternate host of black stem rust is
quiz.why: Puccinia graminis forms pycnia and aecia on barberry (Berberis).

quiz.q: Which spore is the repeating stage on wheat?
quiz.why: Uredospores reinfect wheat repeatedly during the growing season.

quiz.q: Number of basidiospores per basidium in Agaricus campestris
quiz.why: Meiosis of the diploid nucleus gives four basidiospores borne on sterigmata.

quiz.q: The ring on a mushroom stipe is the
quiz.why: The annulus is the remnant of the partial veil that covered the young gills.

scenes.text: On a granite boulder, grey crusts and leafy patches grow where nothing else can — lichens, an alga and a fungus living as one.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Lichens
steps.body: A lichen is a symbiotic association of a mycobiont (usually an ascomycete) and a phycobiont/photobiont (green alga such as Trebouxia, or cyanobacterium such as Nostoc). Growth forms: crustose (Graphis), foliose (Parmelia), fruticose (Usnea). A heteromerous thallus shows upper cortex, algal layer, medulla and lower cortex with rhizines. Reproduction by soredia and isidia (vegetative), and fungal fruiting bodies (apothecia).

steps.title: Uses of lichens
steps.body: Pioneers of xerosere succession on bare rock; sensitive indicators of SO₂ air pollution; litmus from Roccella; 'reindeer moss' (Cladonia) as fodder; Parmelia used as spice (kalpasi) in Indian cooking; usnic acid as antibiotic.

steps.title: Economic importance of fungi
steps.body: Beneficial: yeast in baking and brewing; penicillin (Penicillium), cephalosporins (Cephalosporium), griseofulvin; citric acid (Aspergillus niger); cyclosporin A (Tolypocladium) as immunosuppressant; edible mushrooms (Agaricus, Pleurotus, Volvariella); mycorrhiza in nutrient uptake; biocontrol (Trichoderma). Harmful: plant diseases (late blight of potato — Phytophthora infestans, rust of wheat, smut — Ustilago, tikka disease of groundnut — Cercospora), aflatoxins (Aspergillus flavus), ergotism (Claviceps), human mycoses (ringworm, candidiasis).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Lichen phycobiont may be a cyanobacterium, not always a green alga. Late blight of potato is caused by Phytophthora (an oomycete), not Alternaria (early blight).

courses.title: Unit 3 · Bryophytes
courses.summary: General characters and classification of bryophytes, type studies of Riccia, Marchantia, Anthoceros and Funaria, evolution of the sporophyte and the ecological and economic importance of bryophytes.
outcomes: List the general characters of bryophytes as amphibians of the plant kingdom
Classify bryophytes into Hepaticopsida, Anthocerotopsida and Bryopsida
Compare gametophyte and sporophyte of Riccia, Marchantia, Anthoceros and Funaria
Explain progressive sterilisation of sporogenous tissue
State the ecological and economic importance of bryophytes

scenes.text: After the monsoon, damp walls of a Pune college turn green with mosses and flat liverworts.
They need water for fertilisation — that is why bryophytes are called amphibians of the plant kingdom.

steps.title: General characters
steps.body: Bryophytes are non-vascular embryophytes. The dominant, independent plant is the haploid gametophyte — thalloid (liverworts, hornworts) or leafy (mosses) — anchored by rhizoids. Sex organs are multicellular and jacketed: antheridia (biflagellate antherozoids) and flask-shaped archegonia (neck and venter with egg). Water is needed for fertilisation. The diploid sporophyte (sporogonium: foot, seta, capsule) is attached to and partly dependent on the gametophyte. Spores germinate into a protonema (prominent in mosses).

steps.title: Classification (Proskauer 1957, as followed in many syllabi)
steps.body: Division Bryophyta: 1) Hepaticopsida (liverworts — Marchantiales: Riccia, Marchantia; Jungermanniales: Porella), 2) Anthocerotopsida (hornworts — Anthoceros), 3) Bryopsida (mosses — Sphagnum, Funaria, Polytrichum). Older systems (Eichler) recognised only Hepaticae and Musci.

steps.title: Alternation of generations
steps.body: Haploid gametophyte → gametes → zygote (2n) → embryo → sporophyte (2n) → spore mother cells → meiosis → haploid spores → protonema/gametophyte. The alternation is heteromorphic with gametophyte dominance — the reverse of pteridophytes and seed plants.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Rhizoids are not roots — they lack vascular tissue. The moss 'leaf' is part of the gametophyte, so it is haploid.

activity.prompt: Haploid or diploid?

quiz.why: The independent, long-lived plant body of bryophytes is the haploid gametophyte.
Biflagellate antherozoids must swim through water to reach the archegonium.
Hornworts form the separate class Anthocerotopsida.
The bryophyte sporophyte is differentiated into foot, seta and capsule (seta absent in Riccia).

scenes.text: Riccia forms small rosettes on wet soil; Marchantia carries umbrella-like stalks — the male and female receptacles.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Riccia
steps.body: Gametophyte: dichotomously branched thallus with a dorsal mid-rib groove; ventral scales and rhizoids (smooth and tuberculate). T.S.: upper photosynthetic zone of vertical assimilatory filaments with air canals, lower storage zone. Sex organs embedded in the dorsal groove. Sporophyte is the simplest: only a capsule (no foot, no seta), all inner cells sporogenous except the wall; no elaters. Spores released by decay of the thallus.

steps.title: Marchantia
steps.body: Dioecious thallus with gemma cups (vegetative reproduction by gemmae). Dorsal surface has barrel-shaped air pores; T.S. shows air chambers with photosynthetic filaments. Antheridiophore has a lobed disc bearing antheridia on the upper side; archegoniophore has 8–9 finger-like rays with archegonia hanging upside down beneath. Sporophyte: foot, short seta and capsule; sporogenous tissue forms spores and elaters (hygroscopic, help dispersal).

steps.title: Worked example: identification key
steps.body: Specimen: thallus with cup-like structures containing green discs on dorsal surface. Step 1: thalloid → liverwort or hornwort. Step 2: gemma cups present → Marchantia. Step 3: if a stalked lobed disc is present it is male (antheridiophore); rayed star-shaped head → female (archegoniophore).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Riccia sporophyte has no elaters and no seta. Marchantia archegonia face downward on the archegoniophore because of the growth of the receptacle.

activity.prompt: Riccia or Marchantia?

items.text: Capsule only, no foot or seta

quiz.why: Riccia's sporophyte is just a spherical capsule without foot or seta.

scenes.text: Anthoceros sends up green horn-like sporophytes that keep growing from their base for months.
Funaria, the cord moss, grows on burnt soil with capsules nodding on long setae.

steps.title: Anthoceros
steps.body: Thallus simple, without air chambers; each cell has a single large chloroplast with a pyrenoid (algal-like). Mucilage cavities house Nostoc colonies. Sex organs are endogenous (antheridia in chambers). Sporophyte: bulbous foot, meristematic zone (intercalary meristem) and long capsule; capsule has epidermis with stomata, chlorophyllous wall, a central columella of sterile cells, and archesporium producing spores and pseudo-elaters. Dehisces longitudinally from the tip. It is the most advanced bryophyte sporophyte: partly independent nutritionally.

steps.title: Funaria hygrometrica
steps.body: Gametophyte has two stages: branched filamentous protonema with buds, and the leafy gametophore (axis, spirally arranged leaves, multicellular rhizoids). Monoecious and autoicous: antheridial branch is the main shoot (with paraphyses), archegonial branch a lateral one. Capsule: apophysis (with stomata), theca (columella, spore sac, air spaces), operculum, peristome of two rings of 16 teeth (diplolepidous), annulus; covered by calyptra (from archegonial venter).

steps.title: Progressive sterilisation
steps.body: Bower's idea: from Riccia (almost all inner tissue fertile) → Marchantia (elaters sterile) → Anthoceros (columella, wall, foot sterile) → Funaria (much sterile tissue, elaborate dispersal mechanism) — sporogenous tissue becomes progressively a smaller fraction of the sporophyte.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Funaria calyptra is gametophytic (haploid), even though it sits on the diploid capsule. Peristome teeth are hygroscopic; they are not the operculum.

scenes.text: In wet Himalayan slopes, Sphagnum forms spongy mats that hold many times their weight of water.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Sphagnum (peat moss)
steps.body: Leaves have living green chlorophyllous cells and large dead hyaline cells with pores and thickening bands that absorb water. Capsule opens explosively; elevated on a pseudopodium (gametophytic stalk) because the seta is very short.

steps.title: Importance
steps.body: Pioneers on rocks (with lichens) in succession; soil formation and erosion control on slopes; Sphagnum peat used as fuel and as packing/horticultural medium thanks to high water-holding capacity; peat bogs store large amounts of carbon; mosses act as indicators of pollution and as bio-monitors of heavy metals; Sphagnum was used as an antiseptic dressing because of its absorbency and acidity.

steps.title: Origin and evolution
steps.body: Two main views: algal origin (from green algae like Coleochaete or heterotrichous forms like Fritschiella) and pteridophytic origin (bryophytes as reduced pteridophytes, Rhynia-like). The algal hypothesis is more widely accepted.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Pseudopodium in Sphagnum is gametophytic, not the seta.

activity.prompt: Gametophytic or sporophytic structure?

quiz.why: Partly decomposed Sphagnum accumulates in bogs to form peat.

quiz.why: Its parenchymatous habit and retained zygote suggest a green-algal origin.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Pteridophytes
courses.summary: General characters, classification, stelar evolution, heterospory and seed habit, and type studies of Rhynia, Lycopodium, Selaginella, Equisetum and Pteris (with Marsilea).
outcomes: State the general characters and classification of pteridophytes
Describe and trace the evolution of stelar types

lessons.title: General characters, classification and stelar system

scenes.text: In Rhynie chert from Scotland, 400-million-year-old Rhynia stems still show a central strand of xylem — the first vascular plants.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: General characters
steps.body: Pteridophytes are seedless vascular cryptogams. The dominant plant is the diploid sporophyte with true roots, stem and leaves (microphylls or megaphylls), xylem (tracheids) and phloem (no vessels in most, no companion cells). Sporangia on sporophylls, often aggregated in strobili or sori. Spores give an independent, small gametophyte (prothallus) bearing antheridia and archegonia; water is needed for fertilisation. Most are homosporous; Selaginella, Marsilea, Salvinia and Isoetes are heterosporous.

steps.title: Classification (Reimers 1954, widely taught)
steps.body: Pteridophyta divided into Psilophytopsida (Rhynia), Psilotopsida (Psilotum), Lycopsida (Lycopodium, Selaginella), Sphenopsida (Equisetum) and Pteropsida (ferns: Pteris, Marsilea). Sporne grouped them as Psilopsida, Lycopsida, Sphenopsida and Pteropsida (Filicopsida).

steps.title: Stelar types
steps.body: Protostele (no pith): haplostele (smooth xylem core, Rhynia, Selaginella spp.), actinostele (star-shaped xylem, Psilotum), plectostele (xylem plates, Lycopodium). Siphonostele (with pith): ectophloic (phloem outside only, Osmunda), amphiphloic/solenostele (phloem both sides, Marsilea rhizome). Dictyostele: siphonostele broken by overlapping leaf gaps into meristeles (Pteris, Adiantum). Eustele (collateral bundles in a ring, seed plants) and atactostele (scattered, monocots). Evolutionary trend: protostele → siphonostele → dictyostele, by medullation (pith formation).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Leaf gaps are associated with megaphylls; microphylls (Lycopodium) leave no leaf gaps. Equisetum stem has an eustele-like ring with carinal canals, not a dictyostele.

activity.prompt: Match the stele type to the example.

quiz.why: A solid smooth xylem core surrounded by phloem (haplostele) is the simplest protostele.
Overlapping leaf gaps dissect the siphonostele into a network of meristeles.

Like seed plants, the conspicuous independent plant is the diploid sporophyte.

scenes.text: On the Western Ghats, Selaginella carpets shady banks and Lycopodium hangs from tree trunks — the living club mosses.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Rhynia (fossil)
steps.body: Rootless, leafless dichotomous aerial axes arising from a rhizome with rhizoids; terminal sporangia (homosporous); stem with cuticle, stomata, cortex and haplostele. It shows how the first land vascular plants were built.

steps.title: Lycopodium
steps.body: Microphyllous, homosporous; plectostele/actinostele; kidney-shaped sporangia in the axils of sporophylls in terminal strobili. Gametophyte is long-lived, often subterranean and mycorrhizal.

steps.title: Selaginella
steps.body: Prostrate or erect, dorsiventral shoots with four rows of microphylls (two large lateral, two small dorsal), each with a ligule. Rhizophores (leafless downward branches bearing roots). Stem stele is a protostele suspended in an air cavity by trabeculae (endodermal cells). Strobilus with microsporophylls (many microspores) and megasporophylls (usually 4 megaspores per megasporangium). Endosporic, much-reduced gametophytes: the male develops within the microspore wall; the female gametophyte develops within the megaspore, often beginning while still in the sporangium — an approach towards seed habit.

steps.title: Seed habit — what Selaginella has and lacks
steps.body: Has: heterospory, reduction in megaspore number, retention of megaspore and early development of female gametophyte inside it. Lacks: an integument around the megasporangium and permanent retention of the megaspore on the parent plant — so it does not form a true seed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Rhizophore is not a root; it is a leafless branch that bears roots at its tip. The ligule is on the upper (adaxial) surface of the leaf base.

activity.prompt: Lycopodium, Selaginella or both?

quiz.q: Trabeculae in Selaginella stem are modified
quiz.why: Elongated endodermal cells called trabeculae suspend the stele in the air cavity.
Heterospory and retention of the megaspore are steps towards seed formation.
Rhynia had only dichotomous axes with rhizoids, no true roots or leaves.

quiz.q: Number of megaspores usually in a Selaginella megasporangium
quiz.why: Only one megaspore mother cell completes meiosis, giving four megaspores.

scenes.text: Equisetum stems are jointed and rough with silica — once used to scrub pots, hence 'scouring rush'.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Sporophyte
steps.body: Underground rhizome and aerial jointed, ribbed stems with nodes and internodes; leaves are small, scale-like and fused into a sheath at each node; branches in whorls. Stem T.S.: ridges and furrows, silica-impregnated epidermis with sunken stomata in furrows, sclerenchyma under ridges, chlorenchyma under furrows, vallecular canals (cortex, opposite furrows), central pith cavity, vascular bundles opposite ridges each with a carinal canal (protoxylem cavity).

steps.title: Reproduction
steps.body: Terminal strobilus of peltate (umbrella-shaped) sporangiophores, each bearing 5–10 sacs; homosporous. Spores have four hygroscopic elaters (bands of the outer wall) that coil and uncoil, aiding dispersal and keeping spores together. Gametophytes are green, lobed, often functionally unisexual.

steps.title: Worked example: identify a stem T.S.
steps.body: Section: wavy outline with ridges; two kinds of canals — larger ones in the cortex opposite furrows, smaller ones next to xylem opposite ridges; large central hollow. Step 1: ridged stem with canals → Equisetum. Step 2: cortical canals = vallecular, bundle canals = carinal. Identification: Equisetum stem T.S.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Vallecular canals are opposite furrows, carinal canals opposite ridges — not the other way round.

activity.prompt: Order the tissues in Equisetum stem T.S. from outside to centre (through a furrow).
items: Vascular bundle region with carinal canal

quiz.why: They form when protoxylem breaks down in bundles opposite the ridges.
They develop from the outermost spore wall layer and are hygroscopic.
Each sporangiophore has a stalk and a hexagonal disc bearing sporangia beneath.

options: Scale leaves fused into a sheath
quiz.why: Small scale-like leaves are fused at each node to form a toothed sheath.

scenes.text: Turning a Pteris pinna over, students see a brown continuous line at the margin — the sori protected by a false indusium.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Pteris
steps.body: Sporophyte: rhizome with dictyostele and ramenta (brown scales), pinnately compound megaphyllous fronds with circinate vernation (coiled young leaves). Sori are marginal, continuous, covered by the inrolled leaf margin (false indusium). Sporangium (leptosporangiate): stalk, capsule with an annulus (thick-walled cells) and stomium (thin-walled), 48–64 spores. Homosporous; heart-shaped green prothallus with rhizoids, antheridia among rhizoids and archegonia near the notch; multiflagellate sperms. Apogamy and apospory are known.

steps.title: Marsilea (water fern)
steps.body: Leaf with four leaflets like a clover; amphiphloic siphonostele in rhizome. Heterosporous: bean-shaped sporocarps (modified leaf segments) contain sori with both micro- and megasporangia. In water the sporocarp swells, a gelatinous sorophore carries the sori out. Very reduced endosporic gametophytes.

steps.title: Annulus mechanism
steps.body: As the annulus cells lose water, cohesion pulls their thin outer walls inward; the annulus straightens and tears the stomium, then snaps back, flinging spores — a catapult.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Pteris has a false indusium (leaf margin), not a true indusium. Marsilea sporocarp is a modified leaf segment, not a fruit.

activity.prompt: Order the life cycle of Pteris.

Spore germinates into a heart-shaped prothallus
Antherozoids swim to archegonia and fertilise eggs
Zygote grows into a young sporophyte on the prothallus

Its sporocarps produce separate microspores and megaspores.

quiz.q: Brown scales on fern rhizome are
quiz.why: Ramenta are multicellular brown scales that protect the rhizome and young fronds.

quiz.q: Archegonia on a fern prothallus are located
quiz.why: Archegonia develop behind the apical notch on the ventral surface.

questions.why: Apogamy bypasses gamete fusion.
Rhynia is named after Rhynie, Scotland.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Gymnosperms
courses.summary: General characters and classification of gymnosperms, type studies of Cycas, Pinus and Gnetum, fossil gymnosperms and economic importance.
outcomes: List general characters of gymnosperms and classify them
Describe morphology, anatomy and reproduction of Cycas and Pinus
Explain the structure of the gymnosperm ovule and seed
Identify angiosperm-like features of Gnetum

scenes.text: A pine cone scale carries two seeds lying openly on its surface — 'gymnos' naked, 'sperma' seed.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: General characters
steps.body: Gymnosperms are seed plants whose ovules are exposed on megasporophylls (not enclosed in an ovary). Mostly woody trees/shrubs with secondary growth; xylem with tracheids (vessels only in Gnetales), phloem without companion cells (albuminous cells instead). Heterosporous; microsporophylls and megasporophylls usually in cones (strobili). Pollination mainly by wind; pollen lands directly on the ovule (micropyle, pollination drop). Female gametophyte (endosperm) is haploid and formed before fertilisation. Archegonia present (except Gnetum and Welwitschia). Polyembryony is common.

steps.title: Classification (Sporne 1965)
steps.body: Cycadopsida: Pteridospermales (seed ferns, fossil), Bennettitales (fossil), Pentoxylales (fossil, described by Birbal Sahni from Rajmahal Hills), Cycadales (Cycas). Coniferopsida: Cordaitales (fossil), Coniferales (Pinus), Taxales, Ginkgoales (Ginkgo). Gnetopsida: Gnetales (Gnetum, Ephedra, Welwitschia).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Gymnosperm endosperm is haploid female gametophyte tissue, unlike the triploid endosperm of angiosperms. Double fertilisation does not occur in typical gymnosperms.

activity.prompt: Gymnosperm, angiosperm or both?

quiz.why: It is the female gametophyte, formed from a haploid megaspore before fertilisation.
Gnetum and Ephedra have vessels, an angiosperm-like feature.
Prof. Birbal Sahni described Pentoxylales from the Rajmahal Hills, Jharkhand.
Albuminous (Strasburger) cells take the role of companion cells.

story.title: A living fossil in the garden

scenes.text: The Cycas in the college garden looks like a palm, but its seeds are the size of eggs and it is a living fossil.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Morphology and anatomy
steps.body: Unbranched columnar stem covered by persistent leaf bases; crown of pinnate compound leaves with circinate vernation, plus scale leaves. Roots: tap root and coralloid roots (apogeotropic, harbouring cyanobacteria Anabaena/Nostoc in a cortical algal zone). Stem T.S.: large pith and cortex with mucilage canals, girdle traces, ring of conjoint collateral open bundles (manoxylic wood). Leaflet T.S.: xerophytic — thick cuticle, sunken stomata on lower side, hypodermis, palisade, transfusion tissue; mid-rib with a diploxylic bundle (centripetal and centrifugal xylem).

steps.title: Reproduction
steps.body: Dioecious. Male cone: large compact cone of microsporophylls, each bearing many microsporangia in sori on the lower side. Female: no cone — megasporophylls arise in a loose crown at the stem apex, each with ovules on its margins. Ovule: orthotropous, unitegmic, with three-layered integument (outer fleshy, middle stony, inner fleshy), nucellus with pollen chamber, large female gametophyte with 2–8 archegonia. Pollen tube is haustorial; male gametes are the largest known (top-shaped, multiciliate).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Female Cycas plants do not form a cone. Coralloid roots grow upward (apogeotropic), not downward.

activity.prompt: Root, stem or leaflet feature of Cycas?

quiz.why: An algal zone in the cortex houses nitrogen-fixing Anabaena or Nostoc.

quiz.q: Diploxylic bundle is found in Cycas
quiz.why: The leaflet mid-rib bundle has both centripetal and centrifugal xylem.
Cycas sperms are large and bear a spiral band of many cilia.
It is straight with a single three-layered integument.

scenes.text: Pinus roxburghii (chir) is tapped for resin in Uttarakhand; its needles come in bundles of three.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Morphology and anatomy
steps.body: Tall evergreen tree, branches of two kinds: long shoots (unlimited growth, scale leaves) and dwarf shoots (spurs) bearing needle leaves — 1 to 5 per spur depending on species (P. roxburghii 3, P. wallichiana 5). Needle T.S.: thick cuticle, sunken stomata, hypodermis, plicate (infolded) mesophyll, resin ducts, endodermis, transfusion tissue and 1–2 vascular bundles. Stem shows secondary growth with pycnoxylic wood (compact, mostly tracheids with bordered pits, resin ducts), growth rings.

steps.title: Reproduction
steps.body: Monoecious. Male cones in clusters on lower branches; each microsporophyll has two microsporangia; pollen is winged (two air sacs). Female cone: bract scale with ovuliferous scale bearing two inverted ovules. Pollination in spring; fertilisation about a year later. Embryo development includes polyembryony (simple and cleavage). Seeds winged; cone takes about two to three seasons to mature in many species.

steps.title: Worked example: which species?
steps.body: A spur shows 5 needles. Step 1: count = 5. Step 2: Indian pines — P. wallichiana (blue pine) has 5, P. roxburghii 3, P. gerardiana (chilgoza) 3. Answer: P. wallichiana.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Pycnoxylic (Pinus) vs manoxylic (Cycas): do not swap them. Pine pollen has two wings (air sacs), not one.

quiz.why: Needle leaves arise in bundles from short dwarf shoots (spurs).

scenes.text: In Assam forests, Gnetum climbs trees with broad net-veined leaves — easy to mistake for a flowering plant.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Gnetum
steps.body: Mostly climbers with opposite, broad, reticulately veined dicot-like leaves. Wood has vessels. Strobili with whorls of 'flowers' at nodes (collars); ovule with three envelopes; no archegonia — the female gametophyte has free nuclei, some acting as eggs. These angiosperm-like features make Gnetales important in discussions of angiosperm origin, though molecular data suggest they are closest to conifers.

steps.title: Fossil gymnosperms
steps.body: Lyginopteris (seed fern, Carboniferous), Williamsonia (Bennettitales, flower-like bisexual strobili), Cordaites, Pentoxylon (Rajmahal Hills). Fossilisation types: petrifaction, compression, impression, casts. Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences, Lucknow, honours Sahni.

steps.title: Economic importance
steps.body: Timber (deodar Cedrus deodara, pine, fir); resin, turpentine; paper pulp; edible seeds (chilgoza pine nuts — P. gerardiana); sago from Cycas pith; ephedrine (Ephedra) used as bronchodilator; taxol (paclitaxel) from Taxus as anticancer drug; ornamental (Thuja, Araucaria, Cycas); Ginkgo leaf extracts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Ephedrine comes from Ephedra, not Gnetum. Taxol comes from Taxus (yew).

story.title: One table to rule them all

scenes.text: The night before the exam, Arjun compresses five units into one comparison grid.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Dominant phase and vascular tissue
steps.body: Algae: thallus, no embryo, no vascular tissue; life cycles of all three kinds. Bryophytes: gametophyte dominant, embryo present, no vascular tissue. Pteridophytes: sporophyte dominant, vascular tissue, no seeds. Gymnosperms: sporophyte dominant, seeds naked, archegonia (mostly), haploid endosperm. Angiosperms: seeds in fruit, double fertilisation, triploid endosperm.

steps.title: Sex organ evolution
steps.body: Algae: unicellular, non-jacketed gametangia. Bryophytes and pteridophytes: jacketed antheridia and archegonia. Gymnosperms: archegonia reduced; male gametes delivered by pollen tube (siphonogamy) — motile in Cycas and Ginkgo, non-motile in Pinus. Archegonia lost in Gnetum and angiosperms.

steps.title: Answer-writing tip
steps.body: For a 10-mark life-cycle question: labelled diagram of the plant, T.S./L.S. of key structure, reproduction (asexual, sexual), life-cycle diagram showing n/2n and site of meiosis, and two lines of significance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Always mark the site of meiosis: zygote (haplontic algae), sporangium/sporogonium capsule (bryophytes, pteridophytes) or micro/megasporangium (seed plants).

steps.title: Materials
steps.body: Slides, cover slips, needle, brush, dropper, blotting paper, glycerine (10–20%), stains: iodine (starch), safranin (lignified/cellulose walls of plant tissue), cotton blue in lactophenol (fungi).

steps.title: Fungal mount
steps.body: Pick a little mould from bread with a needle, place in a drop of lactophenol cotton blue, tease apart, lower cover slip at 45° to avoid bubbles, warm gently, blot excess. Observe under low then high power. Rhizopus: aseptate hyphae, sporangia with columella; Penicillium: septate hyphae, brush-like conidiophores.

steps.title: Viva FAQs
steps.body: Why lactophenol? It kills, clears and preserves fungal material (phenol), and the cotton blue stains chitin walls. Why glycerine? It prevents drying. Why lower the cover slip slowly? To avoid air bubbles.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Too much stain hides detail; always blot and, if needed, wash with water before mounting in glycerine.

steps.title: Section cutting
steps.body: Hold material in pith (potato/carrot), keep razor wet, cut many thin transverse sections in one smooth stroke, transfer to watch glass with water, select the thinnest, stain with safranin (1–2 min), wash, optionally counter-stain with fast green, mount in glycerine.

steps.title: Spotter: identification and reasons
steps.body: Format for every spotter — Identification; Classification (division/class/order/genus); two to three diagnostic features. Example: Pinus needle T.S. — Gymnosperm, Coniferales; reasons: plicate mesophyll, sunken stomata, resin ducts, transfusion tissue, two vascular bundles.

uni-bsc-bio-plant-ecology-taxonomy.title: Plant Ecology & Taxonomy
uni-bsc-bio-plant-ecology-taxonomy.description: Ecological factors, ecosystems, energy flow, biogeochemical cycles, communities, succession and phytogeography of India, together with principles of plant taxonomy, botanical nomenclature, classification systems and study of major angiosperm families, with field and herbarium practicals. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Sc. (Botany/Biology) programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Ecological factors, adaptations and ecosystems
courses.summary: Climatic, edaphic, topographic and biotic factors, soil formation and profile, morphological and anatomical adaptations of hydrophytes and xerophytes, ecosystem structure, food chains, ecological pyramids, energy flow and biogeochemical cycles.
outcomes: Explain the main ecological factors and Liebig/Shelford laws
Describe soil formation, profile and texture
Relate hydrophyte and xerophyte adaptations to habitat
Analyse energy flow with the 10% law and ecological pyramids

scenes.text: On a Nilgiri hill, the shaded north slope carries moist forest while the sunny south slope carries grassland — topography shaping climate.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Factors
steps.body: Climatic: light (intensity, quality, duration; heliophytes vs sciophytes), temperature, water (rainfall, humidity), wind. Edaphic: soil. Topographic: altitude, slope, aspect. Biotic: interactions with plants, animals, microbes and humans. Liebig's law of the minimum: growth is limited by the nutrient in least supply. Shelford's law of tolerance: each organism has minimum and maximum limits; steno- vs eury- species (stenothermal, eurythermal).

steps.title: Soil
steps.body: Formed by weathering (physical, chemical, biological) of parent rock plus humus. Profile: O (litter/humus), A (topsoil, eluviation), B (subsoil, illuviation), C (weathered parent material), R (bedrock). Texture by particle size: sand (0.02–2 mm), silt (0.002–0.02 mm), clay (<0.002 mm) per the International system; loam is the best agricultural soil. Soil water: gravitational, capillary (available), hygroscopic (unavailable). Indian soils: alluvial, black (regur, cotton), red, laterite, desert, mountain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Capillary water is the plant-available water; hygroscopic water is held too tightly. Liebig = minimum; Shelford = tolerance range (both limits).

quiz.why: Capillary water is held in micropores at tensions roots can overcome.

quiz.why: Regur is the clay-rich black soil of the Deccan, good for cotton.

scenes.text: The lotus floats on ponds with air-filled petioles; Opuntia survives Thar heat with flat green stems and spines.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Hydrophytes
steps.body: Types: free-floating (Eichhornia, Pistia, Lemna), rooted floating (Nymphaea, Nelumbo), submerged (Hydrilla, Vallisneria), amphibious (Sagittaria, Ranunculus), emergent (Typha). Adaptations: reduced roots/root pockets (Eichhornia), poor vascular and mechanical tissue, abundant aerenchyma, thin or no cuticle, stomata on upper surface in floating leaves (none in submerged), heterophylly (Limnophila, Sagittaria), swollen petioles (Eichhornia).

steps.title: Xerophytes
steps.body: Types: ephemerals (drought escapers), succulents (drought avoiders — Opuntia, Aloe, Euphorbia), non-succulent perennials (drought endurers — Calotropis, Nerium, Zizyphus). Adaptations: deep roots, phylloclades/cladodes (Opuntia, Ruscus), phyllodes (Australian Acacia), spines, thick cuticle, multiple epidermis (Nerium), sunken stomata in pits/crypts with hairs (Nerium), rolled leaves (Ammophila), CAM, mucilage cells.

steps.title: Halophytes
steps.body: Mangroves (Rhizophora, Avicennia, Sundarbans): pneumatophores (negatively geotropic breathing roots), vivipary (seed germinates on parent), salt glands, succulent leaves.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Submerged hydrophytes have no stomata. Phylloclade is a modified stem, phyllode a modified petiole.

scenes.text: In a village pond, phytoplankton feed zooplankton, which feed small fish, which feed a kingfisher.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Term 'ecosystem' coined by A. G. Tansley (1935). Abiotic components (inorganic substances, organic compounds, climate) and biotic: producers (autotrophs), consumers (primary, secondary, tertiary), decomposers. Food chains: grazing and detritus; food webs. Productivity: GPP (total fixation) and NPP = GPP − respiration.

steps.title: Energy flow
steps.body: Unidirectional, obeys thermodynamics. Only about 1–2% of incident sunlight (often stated as ~2–10% of PAR) is fixed. Lindeman's 10% law (1942): roughly 10% of energy at one trophic level is passed to the next. Pyramids: number (upright in grassland, inverted in a tree ecosystem), biomass (inverted in ponds: phytoplankton biomass < zooplankton at a moment), energy (always upright).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Producers fix 20,000 kJ. With 10% transfer: herbivores 2,000 kJ, primary carnivores 200 kJ, secondary carnivores 20 kJ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Energy pyramid can never be inverted; biomass and number pyramids can. Energy flows, nutrients cycle.

activity.prompt: Producers in a grassland fix 50,000 kJ. Using the 10% law, how much energy (kJ) reaches the secondary consumers?

quiz.q: The term ecosystem was coined by
quiz.why: A. G. Tansley introduced it in 1935.

scenes.text: A carbon atom in a mango leaf may have been breathed out by a tiger last year.

steps.title: Carbon cycle
steps.body: Gaseous cycle. CO₂ fixed by photosynthesis; returned by respiration, decomposition, combustion of fossil fuels, volcanoes; oceans act as a major reservoir (bicarbonate, carbonates). Deforestation and fossil-fuel burning raise atmospheric CO₂ → greenhouse effect.

steps.title: Nitrogen cycle
steps.body: Fixation (biological, lightning, industrial Haber–Bosch) → ammonification (decomposers release NH₃) → nitrification (Nitrosomonas: NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻; Nitrobacter: NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻) → assimilation by plants → denitrification (Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus denitrificans: NO₃⁻ → N₂) under anaerobic conditions.

steps.title: Phosphorus cycle
steps.body: Sedimentary cycle (no significant gaseous phase): weathering of phosphate rocks → soil phosphate → plants → animals → decomposition → sediments; runoff causes eutrophication of lakes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Nitrosomonas makes nitrite; Nitrobacter makes nitrate. Phosphorus cycle is sedimentary, not gaseous.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Populations, communities, succession and phytogeography
courses.summary: Population attributes and interactions, quantitative and qualitative community characters with quadrat analysis, ecological succession (hydrosere and xerosere), phytogeographical regions and forest types of India, and biodiversity conservation.
outcomes: Define population growth forms and species interactions
Calculate frequency, density, abundance and Raunkiaer's frequency classes
Describe stages of hydrosere and xerosere
Name the phytogeographical regions and forest types of India
Explain in-situ and ex-situ conservation and biodiversity hotspots

scenes.text: On the college lawn, students lay 1 m × 1 m quadrats and count every plant of each species.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Population attributes and interactions
steps.body: Density, natality, mortality, age structure (pyramids: expanding, stable, declining), dispersion. Growth forms: J-shaped (exponential, dN/dt = rN) and S-shaped (logistic, dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K, K = carrying capacity). Interactions: mutualism (+/+, lichens, mycorrhiza), commensalism (+/0, epiphytes like Vanda), parasitism (+/−, Cuscuta), competition (−/−), amensalism (−/0, allelopathy), predation/herbivory.

steps.title: Quantitative characters
steps.body: Frequency (%) = number of quadrats in which species occurs ÷ total quadrats studied × 100. Density = total individuals ÷ total quadrats studied. Abundance = total individuals ÷ number of quadrats of occurrence. Raunkiaer's frequency classes: A 1–20%, B 21–40%, C 41–60%, D 61–80%, E 81–100%; law: A > B > C ≥ < D < E. Qualitative: physiognomy, phenology, stratification, life forms (Raunkiaer: phanerophytes, chamaephytes, hemicryptophytes, cryptophytes, therophytes).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Ten quadrats laid. Species X present in 6, total 30 individuals. Frequency = 6/10 × 100 = 60% (class C). Density = 30/10 = 3.0 per quadrat. Abundance = 30/6 = 5.0 per quadrat of occurrence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Density divides by ALL quadrats; abundance divides only by quadrats where the species occurs.

activity.prompt: In 20 quadrats, Cynodon occurs in 15 with 90 individuals in total. Calculate its abundance.

quiz.q: Species in 8 of 20 quadrats has frequency

quiz.why: Growth slows as population approaches carrying capacity K.

quiz.why: He classified plants by where buds survive the unfavourable season.

scenes.text: Over centuries an abandoned pond fills with plants and silt, becomes marsh, then meadow, then woodland.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body: Succession: orderly, directional change in community composition leading to a climax (Clements' monoclimax; Tansley's polyclimax; Whittaker's climax pattern). Primary (bare area) vs secondary (after disturbance, faster). Steps: nudation, invasion (migration, ecesis, aggregation), competition and coaction, reaction, stabilisation (climax). Seral stages and pioneer community.

steps.title: Hydrosere
steps.body: Phytoplankton → submerged (Hydrilla, Vallisneria) → floating (Nymphaea, Trapa, Pistia) → reed-swamp (Typha, Phragmites) → sedge-meadow (Carex, Cyperus) → woodland (Salix, Alnus) → climax forest.

steps.title: Xerosere (lithosere)
steps.body: Crustose lichens → foliose lichens → mosses → herbs (annual then perennial grasses) → shrubs → climax forest. Lichen acids and weathering build soil.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Both hydrosere and xerosere move towards mesic (moderate moisture) climax. Secondary succession starts with soil already present.

quiz.q: Pioneers of xerosere on bare rock
quiz.why: Crustose lichens colonise bare rock first and begin soil formation.

Ecesis is germination, growth and reproduction of invaders in the new site.

scenes.text: India spans deserts, mangroves, tropical rainforests and alpine meadows — and its plant geography reflects all of them.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Phytogeographical regions
steps.body: Chatterjee (1939) recognised regions such as Western Himalaya, Eastern Himalaya, Indus plain, Gangetic plain, Central India, Deccan, Malabar (Western Ghats), Assam and the Andaman–Nicobar islands (with Burma, Ceylon in the original scheme). Mountain and island regions show high endemism.

steps.title: Forest types (Champion and Seth, 1968)
steps.body: Major groups include tropical wet evergreen (Western Ghats, North-East, Andamans), tropical semi-evergreen, tropical moist deciduous (sal, teak), littoral and swamp (mangroves of Sundarbans), tropical dry deciduous, tropical thorn (Rajasthan — Acacia, Prosopis), subtropical pine (chir), montane wet temperate (shola of Nilgiris), Himalayan moist and dry temperate (deodar, oak), subalpine and alpine scrub.

steps.title: Biodiversity hotspots and endemism
steps.body: India includes parts of four global hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats–Sri Lanka, and Sundaland (Nicobar Islands). Endemics: Nepenthes khasiana (Meghalaya), many Western Ghats balsams (Impatiens) and orchids.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sal (Shorea robusta) is typical of moist deciduous forests of north and central India, not of the Western Ghats evergreen forests.

steps.title: Levels and threats
steps.body: Genetic, species and ecosystem diversity. Alpha (within community), beta (between communities), gamma (regional). Threats: habitat loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, invasive species (Lantana camara, Parthenium hysterophorus, Eichhornia crassipes), pollution, climate change. IUCN Red List categories: Extinct, Extinct in the Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Least Concern, Data Deficient.

steps.title: Conservation
steps.body: In-situ: national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves (core, buffer, transition zones; Nilgiri was India's first, 1986), sacred groves. Ex-situ: botanical gardens, seed banks, gene banks, cryopreservation (liquid nitrogen, −196 °C), tissue culture, field gene banks. Legal: Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (National Biodiversity Authority, Chennai).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sacred groves and biosphere reserves are in-situ; seed banks and cryopreservation are ex-situ.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Principles of taxonomy, nomenclature and classification
courses.summary: Aims and components of taxonomy, taxonomic hierarchy, the International Code of Nomenclature (ICN) and its principles, types and priority, artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems (Linnaeus, Bentham & Hooker, Engler & Prantl, APG IV), and taxonomic aids including herbaria, keys and modern data sources.
outcomes: Define taxonomy, systematics and the taxonomic hierarchy
Apply key ICN rules: binomials, priority, types, author citation
Compare Bentham & Hooker, Engler & Prantl and APG systems
Construct and use indented and bracketed dichotomous keys
Explain herbarium techniques and modern taxonomic evidence

scenes.text: Tulsi, holy basil, Krishna tulsi — but botanists everywhere write Ocimum tenuiflorum L.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Components and hierarchy
steps.body: Taxonomy = identification, nomenclature and classification (description included). Systematics also studies evolutionary relationships. Hierarchy: Kingdom → Division (-phyta) → Class (-opsida) → Order (-ales) → Family (-aceae) → Genus → Species, with intermediate ranks (sub-, tribe -eae).

steps.title: ICN principles
steps.body: The International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi and plants (ICN; so renamed at the Melbourne Congress, 2011) is revised after each International Botanical Congress. Six principles: independence from zoological and bacterial codes; application of names by nomenclatural types; priority of publication; each taxon with a particular circumscription, position and rank has one correct name; names are treated as Latin; rules are retroactive. Starting point for vascular plants: Linnaeus' Species Plantarum, 1 May 1753. Binomial: genus capitalised + specific epithet lowercase, italicised, with author citation (Mangifera indica L.). Tautonyms (genus repeated as epithet) are not allowed in botany.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: Holotype (single specimen designated by author), isotype (duplicate of holotype), lectotype (chosen later from original material when no holotype), neotype (chosen when all original material is lost), syntype (one of several cited when no holotype), paratype (cited but not holotype/isotype), epitype (interpretive support for an ambiguous type).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Alternative family names such as Leguminosae (Fabaceae), Compositae (Asteraceae), Cruciferae (Brassicaceae), Gramineae (Poaceae), Palmae, Umbelliferae, Labiatae and Guttiferae are conserved and correct. Genus and species names are italicised; family names are normally written in roman type.

activity.prompt: Match the type category.

items.text: Single specimen designated by the original author
Duplicate of the holotype from the same gathering
Chosen from original material when no holotype was designated

quiz.q: Starting date of botanical nomenclature for vascular plants
quiz.why: Linnaeus' Species Plantarum, published 1 May 1753, is the starting point.
ICN requires family names to end in -aceae, apart from conserved alternatives.

scenes.text: Many Indian herbaria still arrange their sheets by Bentham and Hooker's Genera Plantarum, written at Kew in 1862–1883.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Artificial — Linnaeus
steps.body: Sexual system (Species Plantarum, 1753): 24 classes based mainly on number, union and length of stamens. Simple but grouped unrelated plants.

steps.title: Natural — Bentham & Hooker (1862–1883)
steps.body: Genera Plantarum: seed plants divided into Dicotyledons (Polypetalae — Thalamiflorae, Disciflorae, Calyciflorae; Gamopetalae — Inferae, Heteromerae, Bicarpellatae; Monochlamydeae), Gymnospermae (placed between dicots and monocots) and Monocotyledons. 202 natural orders (families). Merits: practical, based on actual specimens; used in Indian herbaria. Demerits: gymnosperms placed between dicots and monocots; Monochlamydeae artificial; not phylogenetic.

steps.title: Phylogenetic — Engler & Prantl; APG
steps.body: Engler & Prantl (Die natürlichen Pflanzenfamilien, 1887–1915): gymnosperms before angiosperms, monocots before dicots, apetalous (Amentiferae) dicots treated as primitive — later criticised. Takhtajan and Cronquist placed Magnoliales as primitive. APG (Angiosperm Phylogeny Group, I 1998 → IV 2016) uses DNA sequences (rbcL, matK, 18S rDNA): ANA grade (Amborellales, Nymphaeales, Austrobaileyales), magnoliids, monocots, eudicots (rosids, asterids). APG IV recognises 64 orders and 416 families.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Bentham & Hooker was a natural, not phylogenetic, system. In APG, 'dicots' are not a single natural group — eudicots are.

activity.prompt: Which classification system?

items.text: Monocots placed before dicots; Amentiferae primitive

quiz.why: George Bentham and J. D. Hooker published it in three volumes, 1862–1883.

scenes.text: At Howrah, the Central National Herbarium of the Botanical Survey of India holds well over a million specimens.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Herbarium technique
steps.body: Collection (with field notes: locality, GPS, habitat, date, collector, number) → pressing and drying between blotters in a plant press → pest treatment (formerly mercuric chloride; now deep-freezing or naphthalene) → mounting on standard sheets (about 42 × 29 cm) → labelling → identification → accession and storage by a classification system. Indian herbaria: CAL (BSI, Howrah), DD (FRI, Dehradun), Blatter Herbarium Mumbai. World: Kew (K).

steps.title: Keys
steps.body: Dichotomous keys offer contrasting couplets. Indented (yoked) key: alternatives are indented progressively. Bracketed (parallel) key: couplets are kept together with numbers. Polyclave/multi-access keys (computer-based) allow any order. Rules: use contrasting, positive, measurable characters; start with general features.

steps.title: Worked example: bracketed key

steps.title: Sources of evidence
steps.body: Morphology; anatomy (wood, stomata, trichomes); embryology; palynology (pollen morphology); cytology (chromosome number, karyotype); phytochemistry/chemotaxonomy (betalains in most Caryophyllales instead of anthocyanins; alkaloids, flavonoids); molecular data (DNA sequences).

steps.title: Numerical taxonomy and cladistics
steps.body: Numerical (phenetic) taxonomy (Sneath and Sokal, 1963): many equally weighted characters, operational taxonomic units (OTUs), similarity coefficients, phenograms. Cladistics (Hennig): groups by shared derived characters (synapomorphies); monophyletic (common ancestor and all descendants), paraphyletic, polyphyletic groups; cladograms.

steps.title: DNA barcoding
steps.body: Plant core barcode = rbcL + matK (CBOL Plant Working Group, 2009), with ITS and trnH–psbA as supplementary. Used to detect adulteration in herbal medicines and identify species.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Phenetics uses overall similarity; cladistics uses only shared derived characters. Plesiomorphies (ancestral characters) do not define clades.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Study of angiosperm families
courses.summary: Floral description technique, floral formula and diagram, and diagnostic features, examples and economic importance of Brassicaceae, Malvaceae, Fabaceae, Apiaceae, Asteraceae, Solanaceae, Lamiaceae, Apocynaceae, Euphorbiaceae, Liliaceae and Poaceae.
outcomes: Describe a flower in semi-technical terms and write its floral formula
Draw and interpret floral diagrams
Identify major dicot and monocot families from diagnostic features
Distinguish the three subfamilies of Fabaceae
Name economically important plants of each family

scenes.text: Four sepals, four petals in a cross, six stamens — four long and two short. The mustard flower writes its own formula.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Floral description order
steps.body: Habit → root → stem → leaf (phyllotaxy, type, venation, stipules) → inflorescence → flower (bracteate?, pedicellate?, symmetry: actinomorphic ⊕ / zygomorphic %, sex ⚥ ♂ ♀, merous, ovary position: hypogynous, perigynous, epigynous) → calyx (K) → corolla (C) → perianth (P) → androecium (A) → gynoecium (G) → fruit → seed.

steps.title: Floral formula conventions
steps.body: Brackets ( ) = fusion (connation); a line or arc linking whorls = adnation (e.g. epipetalous stamens); ∞ = many; G with a line above the number = inferior ovary, line below = superior ovary (in print often written G(2) superior, Ḡ inferior). Example (Brassicaceae): ⊕ ⚥ K2+2 C4 A2+4 G(2).

steps.title: Floral diagram
steps.body: Ground plan seen from above: mother axis at top (dot), bract below, whorls drawn as concentric rings — sepals, petals (with aestivation: valvate, twisted, imbricate, vexillary/descendingly imbricate), stamens (with anther orientation), T.S. of ovary showing placentation (marginal, axile, parietal, free-central, basal).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Always describe from the actual specimen; e.g. twisted aestivation in Malvaceae corolla is diagnostic, so check it carefully.

activity.prompt: Order the parts in a semi-technical description of a flower.

quiz.why: ⊕ denotes radial symmetry (actinomorphic flower).
Two short outer and four long inner stamens are tetradynamous.
Ovules are borne on the walls of the bicarpellary ovary divided by a false septum (replum).

quiz.q: Brackets in a floral formula denote
quiz.why: Parts written in brackets are united (connate).

scenes.text: The hibiscus has its stamens fused into a column; the pea has a butterfly corolla with one standard petal.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Brassicaceae (Cruciferae)
steps.body: Herbs with pungent juice; racemes; cruciform corolla; tetradynamous stamens; bicarpellary syncarpous superior ovary with parietal placentation and false septum (replum); fruit siliqua or silicula. ⊕ ⚥ K2+2 C4 A2+4 G(2). Examples: mustard (Brassica nigra, B. juncea), cabbage, cauliflower, radish (Raphanus), Iberis.

steps.title: Malvaceae
steps.body: Mucilage, stellate hairs; epicalyx; valvate calyx, twisted corolla; numerous monadelphous stamens (staminal tube) with monothecous, reniform anthers; superior multicarpellary syncarpous ovary with axile placentation. ⊕ ⚥ Epi-K(5) C5 A(∞) G(5–∞). Examples: Hibiscus rosa-sinensis, cotton (Gossypium), okra (Abelmoschus esculentus).

steps.title: Fabaceae (Leguminosae) — three subfamilies
steps.body: Monocarpellary superior ovary, marginal placentation, legume fruit, root nodules. Papilionoideae (Faboideae): papilionaceous corolla with standard, wings, keel; vexillary aestivation; diadelphous (9)+1 stamens — % ⚥ K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1 (pea, gram, groundnut). Caesalpinioideae: ascending imbricate, 10 free stamens (Cassia, Tamarindus). Mimosoideae: actinomorphic, valvate, many free stamens, head inflorescence (Mimosa, Acacia). (APG treats the family with six subfamilies; syllabi use the classical three.)

steps.title: Apiaceae (Umbelliferae)
steps.body: Hollow furrowed stems, sheathing petioles, compound umbels; epigynous pentamerous flowers; bicarpellary inferior ovary with stylopodium; fruit cremocarp splitting into two mericarps. ⊕ ⚥ K5 C5 A5 Ḡ(2). Examples: coriander, cumin, carrot, fennel.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Malvaceous anthers are monothecous (one lobe); Papilionoideae stamens are diadelphous, Malvaceae monadelphous.

activity.prompt: Assign the diagnostic feature to its family.

quiz.why: A long dry fruit with a replum dehiscing from below upward is a siliqua.
Nine fused and one free stamen characterise Papilionoideae.
Mimosoid flowers are small, regular and have numerous protruding stamens.
Apiaceae have a swollen style base over the inferior ovary.

scenes.text: Pull apart a sunflower head: yellow ray florets around the edge and hundreds of tubular disc florets inside.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Asteraceae (Compositae)
steps.body: Head (capitulum) inflorescence with involucre of bracts; ray florets (ligulate, often female/neuter) and disc florets (tubular, bisexual); calyx modified into pappus; syngenesious stamens (anthers fused, filaments free), epipetalous; bicarpellary inferior unilocular ovary with one basal ovule; fruit cypsela. Disc floret: ⊕ ⚥ K pappus C(5) A(5) Ḡ(2). Examples: sunflower, marigold, Tridax, lettuce, safflower.

steps.title: Solanaceae
steps.body: Bicollateral bundles; flowers ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 (epipetalous) G(2); ovary obliquely placed, swollen axile placentation; fruit berry or capsule. Examples: potato, tomato, brinjal, chilli, Datura, tobacco, Withania (ashwagandha).

steps.title: Lamiaceae (Labiatae)
steps.body: Quadrangular stems, opposite-decussate aromatic leaves; verticillaster inflorescence; bilabiate corolla; didynamous stamens (2 long, 2 short), epipetalous; gynobasic style; ovary 4-lobed, fruit of 4 nutlets. % ⚥ K(5) C(2/3) A4 G(2). Examples: tulsi (Ocimum), mint (Mentha), Salvia, Leucas.

steps.title: Apocynaceae
steps.body: Latex; twisted corolla; stamens with anthers often adhering to stigma (gynostegium-like); bicarpellary apocarpous ovary united by style; fruit follicles; comose seeds. Examples: Catharanthus roseus (vinblastine, vincristine), Nerium, Rauvolfia serpentina (reserpine), Calotropis (now included under APG).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Syngenesious = anthers fused (Asteraceae); synandrous = whole stamens fused (Cucurbita). Didynamous (Lamiaceae) ≠ tetradynamous (Brassicaceae).

scenes.text: A rice flower has no petals — just lemma, palea, two tiny lodicules, six stamens and a feathery stigma.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Euphorbiaceae
steps.body: Often latex; unisexual flowers; cyathium inflorescence in Euphorbia (cup-shaped involucre with one central female flower and many male flowers each reduced to a single stamen); tricarpellary superior syncarpous ovary with axile placentation; fruit regma (schizocarpic capsule). ♀: G(3). Examples: castor (Ricinus), rubber (Hevea), cassava (Manihot), Euphorbia, Jatropha. Phyllanthus (amla) is now placed in Phyllanthaceae by APG.

steps.title: Liliaceae (classical sense)
steps.body: Bulbs/rhizomes; parallel venation; trimerous flowers, perianth of 6 tepals (3+3); stamens 3+3, epiphyllous; tricarpellary syncarpous superior ovary with axile placentation; fruit capsule or berry. ⊕ ⚥ P3+3 A3+3 G(3). Examples: Lilium, Gloriosa, Asparagus, Allium (onion, garlic — now Amaryllidaceae in APG), Aloe (now Asphodelaceae).

steps.title: Poaceae (Gramineae)
steps.body: Fibrous roots; cylindrical jointed culms with hollow internodes; leaf with sheath, ligule and blade; spikelets in spikes/panicles; florets with lemma and palea, 2–3 lodicules (perianth); stamens 3 (6 in rice and bamboo) with versatile anthers; monocarpellary superior ovary with feathery stigmas; fruit caryopsis. Examples: rice, wheat, maize, sugarcane, bamboo, Cynodon.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Lodicules are the reduced perianth of grasses; caryopsis has pericarp fused with seed coat. Note APG name changes when writing modern classification answers.

scenes.text: Ananya reviews her one-page sheet on the way to the exam hall.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Ecology
steps.body: Liebig (minimum), Shelford (tolerance). Soil horizons O-A-B-C-R. Hydrophyte: aerenchyma, reduced roots, no cuticle. Xerophyte: sunken stomata, thick cuticle, CAM, phylloclade. Lindeman 10% law. Energy pyramid always upright. Nitrosomonas → nitrite, Nitrobacter → nitrate. Frequency = quadrats of occurrence/total × 100; Density = individuals/total quadrats; Abundance = individuals/quadrats of occurrence. Hydrosere and xerosere stages. Champion & Seth forest types; four hotspots in India.

steps.title: Taxonomy
steps.body: ICN: 1 May 1753, priority, types (holo-, iso-, lecto-, neo-), no tautonyms. Systems: Linnaeus (artificial, 24 classes), Bentham & Hooker (natural, 202 families), Engler & Prantl (phylogenetic attempt), APG IV (2016: 64 orders, 416 families). Families: Brassicaceae (tetradynamous, siliqua), Malvaceae (monadelphous, monothecous), Fabaceae (legume; (9)+1), Apiaceae (umbel, cremocarp), Asteraceae (capitulum, syngenesious, cypsela), Solanaceae (oblique ovary), Lamiaceae (didynamous, gynobasic style), Apocynaceae (latex, follicles), Euphorbiaceae (cyathium, regma), Liliaceae (P3+3 A3+3 G(3)), Poaceae (caryopsis, lodicules).

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

lessons.title: Lab: Quadrat analysis and minimum quadrat size

scenes.text: Students lay ten 1 m² quadrats randomly in the campus grassland and tabulate species counts.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Minimum quadrat size (species–area curve)
steps.body: Start with a small quadrat (e.g. 10 cm × 10 cm), list species, then double area repeatedly and record cumulative species. Plot species vs area; where the curve flattens, the area is the minimum quadrat size (often about 1 m² for grasslands).

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: Lay quadrats randomly (e.g. throw over shoulder or random coordinates). Record every species present and count individuals. Tabulate per species: quadrats of occurrence, total individuals. Compute frequency, density, abundance; assign Raunkiaer frequency class.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: 10 quadrats. Cynodon dactylon: present in 9, total 135 → F = 90% (E), D = 13.5, A = 15.0. Tridax procumbens: present in 4, total 12 → F = 40% (B), D = 1.2, A = 3.0. Parthenium: present in 2, total 10 → F = 20% (A), D = 1.0, A = 5.0.

steps.title: Viva FAQs
steps.body: Why random placement? To avoid bias. Why minimum quadrat size? Smaller quadrats miss species; larger waste effort. What is IVI? Importance Value Index = relative frequency + relative density + relative dominance (max 300).

activity.prompt: In 25 quadrats, Euphorbia hirta occurred in 10 with 40 individuals in total. What is its density (individuals per quadrat)?

quiz.why: The point where new species stop appearing gives the adequate quadrat size.

quiz.q: Frequency of a species present in 9 of 10 quadrats

quiz.why: It is the sum of three relative values, each up to 100.

lessons.title: Lab: Soil water-holding capacity and pH

scenes.text: Sandy riverbank soil drains in minutes; garden loam stays moist — the WHC experiment shows why.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Water-holding capacity (Keen's box / funnel method)
steps.body: Weigh oven-dried soil (W1). Saturate with water in a perforated box/funnel on filter paper, let excess drain until dripping stops, weigh wet soil (W2). WHC (%) = (W2 − W1) ÷ W1 × 100.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: W1 = 50 g dry soil, W2 = 70 g after drainage. Water held = 20 g. WHC = 20 ÷ 50 × 100 = 40%.

steps.title: Soil pH
steps.body: Mix soil and distilled water 1:2.5 (w/v), stir, allow to settle, measure with calibrated pH meter or universal indicator. Interpretation: <6.5 acidic (laterite, hill soils), 6.5–7.5 neutral, >7.5 alkaline (black, saline soils).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Use oven-dried soil weight as the base, not wet weight. Calibrate the pH meter with buffers (pH 4, 7, 9.2) before use.

quiz.why: Fine particles and humus have large surface area and micropores.

scenes.text: The examiner hands over a flowering twig of Datura: describe, draw floral diagram, write formula and identify the family.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Identification answer format
steps.body: Classification (Bentham & Hooker: Class – Subclass – Series – Order – Family) → diagnostic reasons (5–6 features) → floral formula → floral diagram → L.S. of flower → T.S. of ovary. Example Datura: Dicotyledonae, Gamopetalae, Bicarpellatae, Polemoniales, Solanaceae — reasons: pentamerous, gamosepalous, gamopetalous, epipetalous stamens, bicarpellary syncarpous superior ovary obliquely placed with swollen axile placentation (ovary appears 4-chambered by false septa in Datura).

steps.title: Long answers
steps.body: 1) Hydrosere stages. 2) Energy flow and ecological pyramids. 3) Nitrogen cycle. 4) Adaptations of xerophytes. 5) Principles of ICN. 6) Bentham & Hooker system — merits and demerits. 7) Diagnostic features and economic importance of Fabaceae. 8) Compare Asteraceae and Lamiaceae.

steps.title: Short notes
steps.body: Ecotone; IVI; biosphere reserve; Raunkiaer's life forms; lectotype; herbarium; DNA barcoding; cyathium; cremocarp; lodicule.

steps.title: Viva FAQs
steps.body: What is the replum? False septum in Brassicaceae. What are lodicules? Reduced perianth of grasses. Why is Datura's ovary 4-celled? False septa divide the bilocular ovary.
